laag: In this lesson, students add two parts to find the total without story context. They self- select tools and strategies. After sharing and discussing their work, students find the total of a new expression in a different way. They compare their experiences with the tools and strategies.

title: Understand taking away as a type of subtraction.
objectives: Understand taking away as a type of subtraction.
i_can: I can take some away and write how many are left.
language_objectives: Given a subtraction problem, orally describe the part that is taken away and the part that is left.
key_questions: What happens when we take things away, or subtract?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: This is the first formal lesson on subtraction. The familiar song “Farmer Brown Had Ten Red Apples” provides context that allows students to experience subtraction as taking away. They model subtraction by crossing out the part that goes away and recording the part that is left. This lesson introduces the term subtraction.

title: Represent take from with result unknown story problems by using drawings and numbers.
objectives: Represent take from with result unknown story problems by using drawings and numbers.
i_can: I can tell or draw a subtraction story. I can write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: Listen to a story problem and orally describe the total and the parts in the problem. Use a number sentence to orally explain the relationship between the total and its parts by using the terms minus and equals.
key_questions: What happens when we take away, or subtract?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: Students use drawings and number sentences to represent take from with result unknown story problems. They transition from reading number sentences as “3 take away 1 is 2” to “3 minus 1 equals 2.” Students recontextualize the number sentence by using it to tell the story. This lesson introduces the term minus.

title: Represent and solve take from with result unknown story problems.
objectives: Represent and solve take from with result unknown story problems.
i_can: I can choose a tool to help me find how many are left. I can write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: Orally share strategies for solving a story problem (including hands, cubes, and a rekenrek). Orally compare and connect each strategy to a number sentence.
key_questions: Why do you think mathematicians use number sentences?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction.", "Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD4] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod5.AD6] Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools.
laag: The class writes a story problem based on a video. Students self-select tools to show and solve the problem. They write a number sentence to match. The class shares and compares solution strategies.

title: Represent decomposition situations by using number bonds and subtraction sentences.
objectives: Represent decomposition situations by using number bonds and subtraction sentences.
i_can: I can show the parts and total with a number bond and a subtraction sentence. I can sort the same total into different parts.
language_objectives: Use a number bond and a number sentence to orally explain the relationship between a total and its parts.
key_questions: Where is the total in the subtraction sentence? Where are the parts?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: Students identify the parts and total in a subtraction number sentence through familiar sorting contexts. They begin with the total and sort to take one part away. The action of taking a part away is key to understanding the sort as a subtraction situation. Students relate the parts and total of a number bond to the parts and total of a subtraction sentence.

title: Relate parts to total in subtraction situations.
objectives: Relate parts to total in subtraction situations.
i_can: I can choose a tool to help me find how many are left. I can show the parts and total with a number bond and a subtraction sentence.
language_objectives: Use a number bond and a number sentence to orally explain the relationship between the total and the parts in a story problem. Orally explain why a number sentence can show which part is taken away and which part is left but a number bond cannot. Given a shape puzzle, orally conjecture about what might have led to its shape and what would happen to the shape if it were manipulated further.
key_questions: How do the parts in a number sentence tell about the story?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction.", "Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD4] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod5.AD6] Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools.
laag: Students use subtraction stories to write number sentences and number bonds. They identify the part that goes away and the part that is left in the number sentence. Students see that number sentences show this information, but number bonds do not.

title: Tell subtraction story problems starting from number sentence models.
objectives: Tell subtraction story problems starting from number sentence models.
i_can: I can tell a math story that matches a number story. I can match number sentences and pictures.
language_objectives: Orally generate a story context based on the numbers and operations in a number sentence. Orally explain how a number sentence matches a story context by describing the total and the parts.
key_questions: How do you know when a subtraction sentence matches a story or a picture?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: Students solidify their understanding of the relationship between a number sentence and a subtraction story. In previous lessons, they began with a story and wrote number sentences to match. In this lesson, they begin with a number sentence and tell a story to match or identify a matching picture. This directs attention to the structure of the number sentence, requiring students to identify the total and the part that went away.

title: Find the difference in a subtraction sentence.
objectives: Find the difference in a subtraction sentence.
i_can: I can choose a tool to help me find how many are left. I can write how many are left in a subtraction sentence.
language_objectives: Orally share strategies for finding the difference (including hands and a number path). Orally compare and connect each strategy to a number sentence.
key_questions: How do you subtract when there is no story?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Subtract fluently within 5."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD10] Subtract fluently within 5.
laag: In this lesson, students subtract to find the difference without the context of stories. They look at a number sentence and choose strategies and tools to subtract. The class discusses different students’ work. Then students are asked to try new tools or strategies.

title: Identify the action in a problem to represent and solve it.
objectives: Identify the action in a problem to represent and solve it.
i_can: I can show what happens in a math story. I can write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: Listen to a story and orally explain how to solve the problem it presents by acting it out, using tools, and writing a number sentence.
key_questions: How do you decide whether to write an addition sentence or a subtraction sentence for a story?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction.", "Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD2] Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD4] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod5.AD6] Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools.
laag: After studying addition and subtraction separately, students are ready to work with these operations in the same lesson. They make sense of different problem types by acting out stories or modeling the action with tools. Modeling the action helps students determine whether to write an addition sentence or a subtraction sentence to represent the story.

title: Relate addition and subtraction through word problems.
objectives: Relate addition and subtraction through word problems.
i_can: I can show how addition and subtraction are alike with a number bond. I can show how they are different with a number sentence.
language_objectives: Listen to a story and orally discuss how addition and subtraction are related by using a number bond and a number sentence.
key_questions: How are addition and subtraction alike? How are addition and subtraction different?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction.", "Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD2] Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD4] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod5.AD6] Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools.
laag: In this lesson, students use the context of word problems, number bonds, and number sentences to see how addition and subtraction are related. They see that by using the same numbers, they can subtract to undo an addition problem. Students play a game and strategize whether to move forward or backward on a number path to reach the target number.

title: Reason about different units to solve story problems.
objectives: Reason about different units to solve story problems.
i_can: I can choose tools to solve a story problem with equal groups. I can tell how I know.
language_objectives: Orally share different strategies for representing and solving a problem (including drawings, cubes, fingers, and number bonds). Orally compare each representation and solution and connect them to the story context.
key_questions: How can we use groups to help us count or solve problems?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction.", "Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD4] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems within 10 by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod5.AD6] Add and subtract within 10 by using objects, drawings, or other math tools.
laag: This lesson explores story problems and pictures that involve reasoning about different units within the same situation. For example, if you can see 8 legs, how many giraffes are there? Students self-select tools to represent the situations by making equal groups for counting. The class writes number sentences to represent thinking.

title: Count starting from a number other than 1 to find the total.
objectives: Count starting from a number other than 1 to find the total.
i_can: I can start counting from different numbers to find the total.
language_objectives: As a class, orally compare the efficiency of counting from 1 with counting on from another number.
key_questions: What does it mean to count on?
ad_texts: ["Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: Counting from a number other than 1 is foundational to the Level 2 counting on strategy. In this lesson, students use their subitizing skills to count a group starting from a number other than 1. Students have a chance to compare the efficiency of counting from 1 with counting from another number.

title: Represent and solve take from with change unknown problems.
objectives: Represent and solve take from with change unknown problems.
i_can: I can choose tools to find a hidden part.
language_objectives: Orally share and discuss solution pathways for finding a hidden part (including fingers and number paths). Orally compare and connect each solution pathway to the story context.
key_questions: Why can some problems be solved by using either addition or subtraction?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD2] Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: This lesson introduces a problem type that students are not expected to master until grade 1. The goal is to make sense of the context and consider entry points for solving the problem. Students practice explaining their thinking by using models, drawings, and number sentences and through playing a game.

title: Find the number that makes 10 and record with a number sentence.
objectives: Find the number that makes 10 and record with a number sentence.
i_can: I can choose tools to find partners to 10 with weight and length.  I can write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to use weight, length, and fingers to find partners to 10. With a partner, orally discuss ways to find an unknown partner to 10 and write a number sentence to match.
key_questions: What are some ways to find partners to 10?
ad_texts: ["Find the partner to 10 for any number 1\u20139."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD8] Find the partner to 10 for any number 1–9.
laag: This lesson builds on the comparison work of module 3. Students apply what they know about comparing weight and length to find partners to 10. Given a number of cubes, they add more to balance the scale or match the length of a 10-stick of cubes. Students write number sentences to represent the partners to 10 that they find.

title: Organize drawings to solve problems efficiently.
objectives: Organize drawings to solve problems efficiently.
i_can: I can draw to show the parts and total. I can write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: Orally compare how efficient different kinds of math drawings are when they are used to represent and solve a story problem. Orally compare and connect each representation and solution to the story context.
key_questions: Why is it helpful to organize drawings?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD2] Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: Students make math drawings to represent and solve a story problem that involves partners to 10. Students discuss and compare different math drawings that show the same problem. They begin to identify the features of a useful math drawing. This lesson introduces the term organize.

title: Identify and extend linear patterns.
objectives: Identify and extend linear patterns.
i_can: I can find a pattern. I can add more to a pattern.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions to identify a pattern unit. Orally describe, create, and extend a pattern.
key_questions: How can you tell when something is a pattern?
ad_texts: ["Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: This lesson expands student understanding of part–whole relationships to include patterns. Students look for a pattern unit, the part that repeats, in linear patterns. They replicate and extend patterns by using movements, materials, and letters. This lesson introduces the term pattern.

title: Use a pattern to make a prediction.
objectives: Use a pattern to make a prediction.
i_can: I can use a pattern to decide what comes next.  I can create a pattern.
language_objectives: Orally describe characteristics of a pattern and generalize how to use patterns to make predictions. With a partner, orally describe a pattern and how to extend a pattern.
key_questions: What is a pattern? Why is a pattern helpful?
ad_texts: ["Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: Students continue to engage with patterns by watching a video of a toy car going down a set of three ramps. Students organize data as they watch the video. They discuss what makes a pattern and use patterns to make predictions. The structure of this lesson makes use of the Five Framing Questions routine.

title: Solve story problems by using repeated reasoning.
objectives: Solve story problems by using repeated reasoning.
i_can: I can use a pattern to solve a story problem. I can find groups of 2 and write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: As a class, orally analyze relationships in a story context to find and extend patterns.
key_questions: How do we describe a pattern?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD2] Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
laag: Students return to the familiar bouncy house story from lesson 17. They use repeated addition to find how many shoes are outside, given different numbers of children inside. Students discuss the relationship between the number of children and the number of shoes and find patterns. They use repeated reasoning to extend the pattern.

title: Extend growing patterns.
objectives: Extend growing patterns.
i_can: I can find a number pattern. I can use the pattern to decide what comes next.
language_objectives: Orally describe patterns found in the environment. As a class, orally analyze relationships in a story context to find and extend growing patterns.
key_questions: What is the same about number patterns and other kinds of patterns?
ad_texts: ["Compose shapes to form larger shapes."]
ad_full: [K.Mod4.AD5] Compose shapes to form larger shapes.
laag: Students activate their knowledge about patterns by analyzing a quilt. Students then work with a number, or growing pattern. They look at a birthday picture album and discover a growth pattern of 1. Then students build towers from triangles and discover a more complex growing pattern.

title: Reason about numbers to add and subtract.
objectives: Reason about numbers to add and subtract.
i_can: I can find patterns to solve problems. I can use numbers to make true number sentences. I can find different partners to 10.
language_objectives: Orally generalize about numbers to find and extend a pattern. With a partner, orally discuss ways to find an unknown partner to 10 and write a number sentence to match.
key_questions: In what ways did you get better at adding and subtracting?
big_idea: Being Flexible Within 10 Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.", "Find the partner to 10 for any number 1\u20139."]
ad_full: [K.Mod5.AD2] Represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD3] Represent subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations. [K.Mod5.AD8] Find the partner to 10 for any number 1–9.
laag: This lesson includes three activities to present as stations or rotations. Each activity invites students to practice adding or subtracting in different ways. For example, in one activity they look for and apply growth patterns, and in another they manipulate Hide Zero cards to make true number sentences. There is no Fluency component in this lesson.

title: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
objectives: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
i_can: I can use groups of 5 or 10 to count a collection. I can write a number sentence to show how I counted.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe strategies to use to organize, count, and record a collection of objects, including by using number sentences, groups of 5, and groups of 10.
key_questions: How can a number sentence help us explain how we counted?
ad_texts: ["This lesson supports K.CC.1\u20135, the counting and writing numeral standards. These concepts build from the work in module 1 and get more sophisticated as the counting quantities get larger in subsequent modules. This content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module."]
ad_full: This lesson supports K.CC.1–5, the counting and writing numeral standards. These concepts build from the work in module 1 and get more sophisticated as the counting quantities get larger in subsequent modules. This content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module.
laag: This lesson invites students to count and record a collection of objects by using tools and strategies of their choice. Students demonstrate and celebrate growth with counting concepts and written recordings while the teacher gathers formative assessment data. Class discussion focuses on recording with number sentences and counting from a number greater than 1. There is no Fluency component in this lesson.

title: Describe teen numbers as 10 ones and ones.
objectives: Describe teen numbers as 10 ones and ones.
i_can: I can count past 10 by making a group of 10. I can use 10 ones and some ones to tell how many.
language_objectives: As a class, orally compare what it is like to count with and without organizing objects into a group of 10 ones. Orally describe different strategies to determine how many objects by using the terms 10 ones and some more ones.
key_questions: How did making a group of 10 help you count?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Count to answer how many questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle configuration.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD5] Count to answer how many questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle configuration. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.
laag: Module 6 introduces students to basic place value concepts as they engage with teen numbers. Students count and describe groups of 10–19 objects as 10 ones and some more ones. Comparing the organization of different groups of objects helps students recognize the value of making a group of 10 to help them count. This lesson introduces the term ones.

title: Find 10 ones in a teen number.
objectives: Find 10 ones in a teen number.
i_can: I can find 10 ones in a larger number. I can use a number path to find numbers with 10 ones in them.
language_objectives: As a class, orally compare the efficiency of counting objects in different configurations. Use a number bond to record the numbers that have 10 ones inside, and orally justify why those numbers were identified.
key_questions: When do numbers have 10 inside?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.
laag: Students continue to explore place value concepts by searching for groups of 10 inside collections of 1–20 objects. Students use a number path to track which numbers contain a group of 10 and which do not. The number path provides a visual record that allows students to reason about the results of their tracking.

title: Write numerals 11–20.
objectives: Write numerals 11–20.
i_can: I can write how many. I can tell how many groups of 10 ones and some ones are in a number.
language_objectives: As a class, analyze and orally describe the patterns associated with counting from 1 to 30. Orally explain how to write numerals greater than 10.
key_questions: What does the 1 in a teen number represent?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Write numbers from 11 to 20.", "Represent a group of objects with a written numeral 0\u201320.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD2] Write numbers from 11 to 20. [K.Mod6.AD3] Represent a group of objects with a written numeral 0–20. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.
laag: Once students have organized collections of 10–20 objects as 10 ones and some more ones, they are better prepared to understand the meaning of the digit in the tens place. In this lesson, an authentic counting context provides reason for writing numerals to 20. Hide Zero cards and math tools highlight the underlying structure of ten in our counting as students learn to represent their count with a written numeral.

title: Order numerals 0–20.
objectives: Order numerals 0–20.
i_can: I can say the next number when I count past 10. I can count back from 20 to 0. I can show the number that comes before or after.
language_objectives: Orally explain the pattern of 1 more in the forward count sequence within teen numbers. Orally describe the movement on a number path as the quantity increases or decreases.
key_questions: How do you know which number comes next in the count sequence? How do you know which number comes before?
big_idea: How Many? Bigger or Equal? Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Recognize that each successive number is one more when counting within 20.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD4] Recognize that each successive number is one more when counting within 20. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: Students continue to think about patterns in the counting sequence as they write and order numbers. They return to the 1 more and 1 less patterns embedded in the forward and backward count sequences. Students expand the number stairs into the teen numbers to see if the pattern continues.

title: Reason about a number’s position in the number sequence.
objectives: Reason about a number’s position in the number sequence.
i_can: I can put numbers in order. I can tell how I know.
language_objectives: Orally justify the placement of a number within the teen number sequence.
key_questions: How do you know where to put a number on the number path?
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens.", "Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens. [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: Students apply their understanding of the relationship among teen numbers to determine a number’s position on the number path. They become number detectives and strategize to identify an unknown number within the teen number sequence.

title: Count out a group of objects to match a numeral.
objectives: Count out a group of objects to match a numeral.
i_can: I can make a group of 10 ones and some ones to match a number greater than 10.
language_objectives: Orally justify the choice of a math tool to model teen numbers and explain how it is helpful. Orally explain how to match a numeral to a group of ten ones and some more ones.
key_questions: How can tools help you see how many without having to count by ones? How can organizing help you count out the right number of objects?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Count out a given number of up to 20 objects from a larger group.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD6] Count out a given number of up to 20 objects from a larger group. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: Now that students can count an existing group of up to 20 objects to answer how many questions, they are ready to count out a group of 11–20 objects from a larger group. This lesson invites students to show teen numbers in different ways by using drawings and tools that use the structure of ten. Emphasis is placed on organizing so others can easily see the total.

title: Decompose numbers 10–20 with 10 as a part.
objectives: Decompose numbers 10–20 with 10 as a part.
i_can: I can use a number bond to break apart numbers greater than 10 into 10 ones and some ones.
language_objectives: Use a number bond to orally describe teen numbers with words and number statements, such as 17 is 10 and 7.
key_questions: How can number bonds help us better understand numbers?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Count to answer how many questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle configuration.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD5] Count to answer how many questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle configuration. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: This lesson brings what students already know about number bonds together with their emerging understanding of teen numbers. Students use the structure of the number bond to represent a teen total as 10 ones and some more ones. Practice decomposing teen numbers in this way supports place value understanding and prepares students to use Level 3 strategies in grade 1.

title: Represent teen number compositions and decompositions as addition sentences.
objectives: Represent teen number compositions and decompositions as addition sentences.
i_can: I can choose a tool to put together 10 ones and some ones in a story. I can write an addition sentence to match a story or picture.
language_objectives: Orally share strategies to represent and solve a story problem involving teen numbers. Orally compare and connect each strategy to a number sentence.
key_questions: How do you know when a number bond or number sentence matches a story or picture?
big_idea: Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD7] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: Students solve an add to with result unknown problem by using self-selected tools to represent the parts. A video sets the context for the problem. Then students use what they know about the structure of teen numbers to compose and decompose. They discuss how their thinking can be represented by using number sentences and number bonds.

title: Represent teen number decompositions as subtraction sentences.
objectives: Represent teen number decompositions as subtraction sentences.
i_can: I can choose a tool to break apart a number into 10 ones and some ones in a story. I can write a subtraction sentence to match a story or picture.
language_objectives: Orally share a story problem and justify why a subtraction sentence can be used to represent the story. Orally compare and connect each representation to a number sentence.
key_questions: How do you know when a subtraction sentence matches a story or picture?
big_idea: Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD7] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: Students use what they know about subtraction to decompose a teen number. In this lesson, each decomposition includes 10 as a part. Students solve a take away with result unknown problem by using tools to represent the action. They see that the story can be represented with a subtraction sentence.

title: Make sense of word problems involving teen numbers.
objectives: Make sense of word problems involving teen numbers.
i_can: I can use a drawing to solve story problems. I can match a drawing to a number sentence.
language_objectives: Listen to and solve a story problem. Orally make a statement to put the answer in context.
key_questions: How do you decide whether to write an addition or subtraction sentence for a story?
big_idea: Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD7] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: Students listen to a series of story problems and determine a solution pathway. They model each problem first by drawing and then by writing an addition or subtraction number sentence as a class.

title: Represent teen number decompositions as 10 ones and some ones and find a hidden part.
objectives: Represent teen number decompositions as 10 ones and some ones and find a hidden part.
i_can: I can use tools to break apart a number greater than 10 into 10 ones and some ones. I can find the hidden part.
language_objectives: Listen to a story problem and orally explain strategies for finding the hidden part, including the use of math tools. Orally explain the relationship between the total and parts in a story problem by using a number bond and a number sentence.
key_questions: How can tools help you find a hidden part?
big_idea: Place and Position of Numbers Model with Numbers
ad_texts: ["Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction.", "Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones.", "Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD7] Solve add to, take from, put together, and take apart with result unknown story problems with 10 as one of the parts by using addition and subtraction. [K.Mod6.AD8] Compose and decompose teen numbers 11 to 19 as ten ones and some more ones. [K.Mod6.AD9] Record teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones with a drawing or number sentence.
laag: This lesson reinforces place value concepts as students find a hidden part within teen numbers. Based on their understanding of the structure of teen numbers as 10 ones and some ones, students are able to figure out the hidden part. They model problems with various tools and by writing number sentences.

title: Investigate different ways to decompose teen numbers.
objectives: Investigate different ways to decompose teen numbers.
i_can: I can break apart numbers in different ways. I can write a number sentence to match.
language_objectives: Orally analyze the relationship between container size and the number of containers. Orally justify why teen numbers do not always have to be decomposed into 10 ones and some more ones.
key_questions: Does 10 always have to be a part when we decompose teen numbers? How do you know?
big_idea: How Many? Bigger or Equal? Place and Position of Numbers
ad_texts: ["Count to answer how many questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle configuration."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD5] Count to answer how many questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle configuration.
laag: This optional lesson provides a doughnut shop context that invites students to decompose teen numbers in many different ways. They see that 10 is not always one part. Students explore basic area concepts as they consider different ways to fit doughnuts into boxes of varied sizes.

title: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
objectives: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
i_can: I can use groups to count and record a collection of things.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe strategies to organize, count, and record a collection of objects, including making groups of 2 or groups of 10.
key_questions: How can you group objects to make counting easier?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers
ad_texts: ["This lesson supports K.CC.1\u20135, the counting and writing numeral standards. These concepts build from the work in module 1 and get more sophisticated as the counting quantities get larger in subsequent modules. This content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module."]
ad_full: This lesson supports K.CC.1–5, the counting and writing numeral standards. These concepts build from the work in module 1 and get more sophisticated as the counting quantities get larger in subsequent modules. This content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module.
laag: This lesson invites students to count and record a collection of objects by using tools and strategies of their choice. Students demonstrate and celebrate growth with counting concepts and written recordings while teachers gather formative assessment data. Class discussion focuses on how to use groups to make counting easier. There is no Fluency component in this lesson.

title: Count by tens.
objectives: Count by tens.
i_can: I can count by tens and write the total.
language_objectives: Orally describe ways to organize tools to count by ones and tens. Orally justify why it is more efficient to count by tens in certain situations.
key_questions: When is counting by tens helpful?
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens.
laag: Students make rekenrek bracelets with exactly 10 beads. They use their bracelets as tools to count by ones and tens. This lesson reinforces the efficiency of counting by tens rather than ones in certain situations.

title: Count by tens by using math tools.
objectives: Count by tens by using math tools.
i_can: I can use tools to count by tens and ones.
language_objectives: Orally describe patterns to determine missing numbers in a sequence. Orally justify when to count by tens and when to count by ones by explaining how efficient or precise each unit is in a given counting situation.
key_questions: How do you decide whether to count by tens or ones?
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens.
laag: Students search for math tools that allow them to easily see and count by tens. They model numbers by using ones or tens and decide which unit to use by thinking about the efficiency and precision of each type of counting. A Math Past exploration of infinity appeals to students’ curiosity about counting beyond 100.

title: Use the structure of ten to count to 100.
objectives: Use the structure of ten to count to 100.
i_can: I can use tools to count by tens and to find the next number.
language_objectives: Analyze and orally describe patterns to determine missing numbers in a sequence. Orally explain how counting by tens relates to counting by ones.
key_questions: How can you use what you know about counting by tens to help you count by ones to 100?
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens.", "Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens. [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: The activities in this lesson are presented as stations. Students practice counting to 100 by using what they know about counting by tens to help cross each decade number.

title: Use patterns in the number sequence to count by ones within 100.
objectives: Use patterns in the number sequence to count by ones within 100.
i_can: I can use patterns to tell how I count by ones up to 100. I can put numbers in order.
language_objectives: Generalize and orally explain the patterns in a number sequence and how patterns are used to count by ones.
key_questions: How can the repeating pattern of numbers 0–9 help us count to 100?
big_idea: How Many? Place and Position of Numbers
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens.", "Count forward from a number other than 1.", "Represent a group of objects with a written numeral 0\u201320."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens. [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1. [K.Mod6.AD3] Represent a group of objects with a written numeral 0–20.
laag: After multiple experiences with choral counting, students notice the repetition of numbers 0–9 as they count to 100. They use this foundational place value understanding to count to 100 and order numbers in a series of stations.

title: Count within and across decades when counting by ones, part 1.
objectives: Count within and across decades when counting by ones, part 1.
i_can: I can use tools to tell what number comes next. I can put numbers in order.
language_objectives: Orally make a prediction about a number’s placement in a sequence.
key_questions: How do you know where to put a number on the number path?
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens.", "Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens. [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: The activities in this lesson are presented as stations. Students practice counting within and across tens by ones. The familiar patterns that students see and highlight during a choral counting activity help them count, order, and represent numbers independently while at the stations.

title: Count within and across decades when counting by ones, part 2.
objectives: Count within and across decades when counting by ones, part 2.
i_can: I can use tools and patterns to tell what number comes next. I can put numbers in order.
language_objectives: Orally conjecture about numbers to determine their placement in a sequence. Orally explain how math tools and patterns aid in determining what number comes next.
key_questions: How can math tools and patterns help you know what number comes next?
ad_texts: ["Count to 100 by ones and tens.", "Count forward from a number other than 1."]
ad_full: [K.Mod6.AD1] Count to 100 by ones and tens. [K.Mod5.AD1] Count forward from a number other than 1.
laag: To count across decade numbers, students combine understanding of the repeating pattern of 0–9 in the count sequence with the ability to count by tens. They practice the skill up to 100 by using the same stations from previous lessons. The familiar patterns that students see and highlight during a choral counting activity help them count, order, and represent numbers independently while working in stations.

title: Compare totals in story situations.
objectives: Compare totals in story situations.
i_can: I can compare groups with more than one part. I can compare totals or compare the parts that are in a different story.
language_objectives: Orally justify when to compare the parts of a problem and when to compare the totals in a story context.
key_questions: What are some ways to compare groups that have more than one part?
ad_texts: ["Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies."]
ad_full: [K.Mod3.AD1] Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies.
laag: Earlier this year, students learned ways to compare groups and numbers. This lesson introduces the idea of comparing groups with more than one part. Students discover when they need to add and find totals to compare versus when they can simply compare parts. The structure of this lesson makes use of the Five Framing Questions routine.

title: Count and compare sets with more than 10 objects.
objectives: Count and compare sets with more than 10 objects.
i_can: I can choose tools to compare groups with more than 10 things.
language_objectives: Orally share strategies for comparing groups, including by using cubes, 10-frames and counters, and the counting sequence. Orally compare and connect each strategy used to compare teen numbers.
key_questions: What are some ways to compare groups with more than 10 objects?
ad_texts: ["Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies."]
ad_full: [K.Mod3.AD1] Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies.
laag: Students use comparison strategies from earlier this year to compare groups with more than 10 objects. While some totals in this lesson exceed grade-level expectations, the comparisons can be made through direct modeling. These experiences help students recall comparison strategies and create a need for the more efficient place value comparison strategies in grade 1.

title: Compare area by comparing number.
objectives: Compare area by comparing number.
i_can: I can use cubes to compare shapes. I can write how many square units each shape has. I can show which shape takes up more space.
language_objectives: Orally share strategies for comparing the area of different shapes. Orally compare and connect each strategy used to compare area.
key_questions: How can we compare shapes to see which takes up more space?
ad_texts: ["Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies."]
ad_full: [K.Mod3.AD1] Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies.
laag: Students informally find the area of two shapes by covering them with cubes. They use comparison strategies from earlier in the year to compare the areas. Students discover that shapes that look different can have the same area.

title: Compare lengths of objects by using 10-sticks and individual cubes.
objectives: Compare lengths of objects by using 10-sticks and individual cubes.
i_can: I can use 10-sticks and more cubes to find length. put things in order by length. I can
language_objectives: Orally describe how to use cubes to compare the lengths of objects by using the terms more, less, greater, or fewer. Orally evaluate how to count efficiently in each situation, such as counting by tens, by ones, or by tens and ones.
key_questions: How can you compare the lengths of objects? How can you count by tens and ones?
ad_texts: ["Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies."]
ad_full: [K.Mod3.AD1] Compare the number of objects in two groups by using the terms more than, fewer than, or the same number as, e.g., by using matching or counting strategies.
laag: Students use 10-sticks and individual cubes to create cube sticks that are the same length as classroom objects. They count the total cubes in the stick. Students compare and order objects from shortest to longest by using cube sticks or number.

title: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
objectives: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
i_can: I can show how I count things in a picture.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe strategies to organize, count, and record a collection of objects, including counting by ones and counting by tens.
key_questions: Why does counting by tens sometimes make it easier to count?
big_idea: How Many? Bigger or Equal? Place and Position of Numbers
ad_texts: ["This lesson supports K.CC.1\u20135, the counting and writing numeral standards. These concepts build from the work in module 1 and get more sophisticated as the counting quantities get larger in subsequent modules. This content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module."]
ad_full: This lesson supports K.CC.1–5, the counting and writing numeral standards. These concepts build from the work in module 1 and get more sophisticated as the counting quantities get larger in subsequent modules. This content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module.
laag: This lesson invites students to count and record a collection of pregrouped objects. They use tools and strategies of their choice. Class discussion focuses on how groups can make counting easier. Students demonstrate and celebrate growth with counting concepts and written recordings while teachers gather formative assessment data. There is no Fluency component in this lesson.

title: Organize to find how many and compare.
objectives: Organize to find how many and compare.
i_can: I can use a number path to help me count and compare.
language_objectives: Orally compare totals by using the word more. Orally explain how organizing objects linearly helps with finding the total and making comparisons.
key_questions: How can we show objects so they are easy to count and compare?
content_standards: Builds from K.CC.C.6; Builds from K.CC.C.7
ad_texts: ["This lesson is foundational to the work of grade 1 and builds from K.CC.C.6 and K.CC.C.7. Lesson content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in grade 1."]
ad_full: This lesson is foundational to the work of grade 1 and builds from K.CC.C.6 and K.CC.C.7. Lesson content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in grade 1.
laag: Students explore ways to organize by counting a set. With guidance, they organize their set on a number path. Students compare and reason about the totals on the number path and discover the usefulness of linear organization. Finally, they use color to represent and compare sets on number paths.

title: Organize and represent data to compare two categories.
objectives: Organize and represent data to compare two categories.
i_can: I can use number paths to organize. I can compare two groups.
language_objectives: Respond to a survey orally, pictorially, and by using gestures. Orally explain how a graph helps with comparing totals and analyzing survey results.
key_questions: What can we tell from a graph?
big_idea: Make Sense of Data Reasoning About Equality
ad_texts: ["Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4)", "Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD8] Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4) [1.Mod1.AD9] Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category.
laag: The class collects data about student preferences and makes a graph by representing each student choice with a cube on a number path. Students represent and compare a new set of data pictorially by coloring squares on a number path. Each time they represent data, students label categories and totals and use the graphs to answer questions. This lesson introduces the term graph and the symbol >.

title: Sort to represent and compare data with three categories.
objectives: Sort to represent and compare data with three categories.
i_can: I can sort objects. I can create a graph. I can compare three groups.
language_objectives: Orally compare category totals by using the words greater and more. Orally explain what a graph tells about.
key_questions: What can we tell from a graph?
big_idea: Make Sense of Data Reasoning About Equality
ad_texts: ["Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4) and", "Organize represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD8] Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4) and [1.Mod1.AD9] Organize represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category.
laag: Students work in pairs to sort cubes into three categories and graph the data by coloring number paths. Using a completed graph, the class answers comparison questions about which category has more. Students read their comparisons as number sentences with the greater than symbol, >.

title: Find the total number of data points and compare categories in a picture graph.
objectives: Find the total number of data points and compare categories in a picture graph.
i_can: I can create a picture graph. I can compare groups and find the total.
language_objectives: Orally compare category totals by using the words more, greater than, and equal. Using the word represents, orally explain that the pictures on the graph stand for objects.
key_questions: How can we find the total of all the groups in a graph? How can a graph help us compare groups?
big_idea: Make Sense of Data Reasoning About Equality
ad_texts: ["Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4)", "Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD8] Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4) [1.Mod1.AD9] Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category.
laag: Students sort a set by varied attributes. With guidance, they represent the sorted data by drawing pictures on a number path. Students use these picture graphs to compare categories with both the > and = symbols. Students also share strategies for finding the total number of data points. This lesson introduces the term represent.

title: Organize and represent categorical data.
objectives: Organize and represent categorical data.
i_can: I can show how I count a group of objects in different ways.  I can tell how I know.
language_objectives: With a partner, listen to and orally describe a strategy to estimate, count, and record a collection of objects.
key_questions: Why can it be helpful to show sorted objects by using a graph or chart?
ad_texts: ["Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD9] Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category.
laag: This student-driven lesson invites partners to sort a set of about 50 items into categories. The class shares and compares their strategies for organizing and counting each category. Students then choose either a chart or graph to represent their categories and discuss what their representation shows about the greater set. Because of the time needed to sort and count sets, the Problem Set and Exit Ticket are not included in this lesson. Use student representations as formative assessment. There is no Exit Ticket for this lesson. Instead, use students’ recordings to analyze their work after the lesson.

title: Use tally marks to represent and compare data.
objectives: Use tally marks to represent and compare data.
i_can: I can use tally marks to show and compare information.
language_objectives: Orally explain how tally marks are used to organize data. Orally compare category totals by using the words more than, fewer than, same number of, and less than.
key_questions: How do tally marks make counting and comparing easier?
big_idea: Make Sense of Data Reasoning About Equality
ad_texts: ["Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4)", "Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD8] Compare category totals in graphs by using the symbols >, =, and <. (1.NBT.B.3, 1.MD.C.4) [1.Mod1.AD9] Organize and represent data with up to three categories and write how many are in each category.
laag: The class collects data from a video and represents the data concretely by placing craft sticks on a chart. Students form tallies by organizing the sticks into fives and ones. They then represent the tallies pictorially by drawing tally marks to complete their own tally charts. They continue to count and compare category totals. This lesson introduces the < symbol.

title: Count all or count on to solve put together with total unknown situations.
objectives: Count all or count on to solve put together with total unknown situations.
i_can: I can find the total. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe counting representations and strategies that can be used to find a total, including counting all and counting on. Orally compare and connect counting strategies.
key_questions: What is the same and what is different about counting all and counting on?
ad_texts: ["Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD2] Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.
laag: This lesson invites students to solve put together with total unknown situations by using strategies of their choice. Through discussion, the class compares and connects representations and strategies. Expect a range of student understanding at this stage, and advance student thinking from counting all toward counting on from a known, trusted part. This lesson provides an opportunity for formative assessment.

title: Count on from a known part and identify both parts in a total.
objectives: Count on from a known part and identify both parts in a total.
i_can: I can count on from a part.
language_objectives: Orally count to find a total while playing a partner game. Orally explain how counting on and counting all are different and why counting on from a known part is helpful.
key_questions: Why should we count on from a part we know?
ad_texts: ["Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD2] Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.
laag: Partners play a game, Roll a Total, to practice counting on from a known part to find a total. They record the parts and total in a number bond.

title: Count on from both parts and record part–total relationships.
objectives: Count on from both parts and record part–total relationships.
i_can: I can count on from both parts. I can show the parts and total.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally explain how counting on from either part results in the same total, and record by writing a number bond or number sentence. Orally explain that there is only one way to count on when adding doubles.
key_questions: Why do we get the same total no matter which part we count on from?
ad_texts: ["Apply the commutative property of addition as a strategy to add.", "Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD1] Apply the commutative property of addition as a strategy to add. [1.Mod1.AD2] Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.
laag: Students explore counting on from both parts and discover that either starting point will result in the same total. As partners play the familiar Roll a Total game, they count on from a part, make a number bond, and write a matching number sentence. Students are introduced to the term doubles, and they notice that counting on from either part is exactly the same.

title: Count on from 5 within a set.
objectives: Count on from 5 within a set.
i_can: I can see 5 and count on.
language_objectives: Orally count on from 5 to find a total and write a number sentence to match. Orally explain how counting on from 5 is helpful.
key_questions: How is seeing 5 within a set helpful for finding the total?
ad_texts: ["on to find the", "Count total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence."]
ad_full: on to find the [1.Mod1.AD2] Count total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.
laag: Students identify and count on from 5 by using hands, 5-groups, and dot patterns. They show the parts and total on a number bond and write a number sentence to record the count. Students apply counting on from 5 to find totals in graphs and charts. Students learn that seeing a part within a set, such as 5, and using it to count on makes finding the total easier.

title: See any part in a set and count on.
objectives: See any part in a set and count on.
i_can: I can see a part. I can count on to find the total.
language_objectives: Orally describe different ways to count on to find the total. Write a number bond and number sentence to represent a counting strategy and orally explain how they match.
key_questions: How can we use number bonds to show how we find totals? How can we use number sentences to show how we find totals?
ad_texts: ["Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD2] Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.
laag: Students identify parts they know within a set and use them to count on. Through partner practice and discussion, students solidify the understanding that there are many ways to see parts within a set and to count on to find the total.

title: Count on from 10 to find an unknown total.
objectives: Count on from 10 to find an unknown total.
i_can: I can count on from 10. I can find the total.
language_objectives: Orally count on from 10 to find a total and write a number sentence to match. Orally explain how counting on from 10 is helpful.
key_questions: Why are fingers helpful tools for counting on when we can’t see a part?
ad_texts: ["Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.", "Count on from 10 to find totals between 11 and 19. (1.NBT.B.2, 1.NBT.B.2.b)"]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD2] Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence. [1.Mod1.AD7] Count on from 10 to find totals between 11 and 19. (1.NBT.B.2, 1.NBT.B.2.b)
laag: Students count on from 10 to find a total when the objects in the second part are hidden or not visible. They use their fingers to keep track of the hidden part, and they record their count as a number bond and a number sentence. Partners practice these skills by playing a game. This lesson introduces the term unknown.

title: Count on from an addend in add to with result unknown situations.
objectives: Count on from an addend in add to with result unknown situations.
i_can: I can solve story problems by counting on.
language_objectives: Listen to and retell stories about add to with result unknown situations to model and solve story problems. Listen to and orally describe solution strategies (including counting all, counting on, and using known facts), and compare and connect solution strategies.
key_questions: What are some ways to represent counting on by using tools and numbers?
ad_texts: ["Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD2] Count on to find the total number of objects in a set and represent the total with an addition number sentence.
laag: Students solve add to with result unknown problems by using strategies of their choice. After solving independently, the class compares work and makes connections among representations and strategies. This lesson supports students as they transition from counting on from a part of a set to counting on from an addend.

title: Count on to find the total of an addition expression.
objectives: Count on to find the total of an addition expression.
i_can: I can count on to find the total.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to count on to find a total by using fingers or a number path.
key_questions: Why are fingers helpful tools for counting on when we can’t see the parts?
ad_texts: ["Add within 20 by using strategies such as counting on or by creating an equivalent but easier problem. (1.OA.C.5, 1.OA.C.6)"]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD3] Add within 20 by using strategies such as counting on or by creating an equivalent but easier problem. (1.OA.C.5, 1.OA.C.6)
laag: Students count on to find the total of two addends. They practice “holding” the first addend and using their fingers to track as they count on the second addend. Then they relate counting on with fingers to counting on with hops on the number path. This lesson introduces the term expression.

title: Use the commutative property to count on from the larger addend.
objectives: Use the commutative property to count on from the larger addend.
i_can: I can count on from the larger part. I can find the total.
language_objectives: Listen to stories about add to with result unknown situations, and explain orally and in writing whether two expressions are equal and why. Orally explain what the commutative property is and how it can be used to find a total efficiently.
key_questions: Why can we add numbers in any order?
ad_texts: ["Apply the commutative property of addition as a strategy to add."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD1] Apply the commutative property of addition as a strategy to add.
laag: Students explore commutativity as they consider what statements are true. They notice that expressions with the same total are equal because the parts are the same and can be added in any order. With guidance, students use the number path and fingers to count on from either addend. The class discusses how it is more efficient to count on from the larger part. This lesson introduces the academic verb convince.

title: Use the commutative property to find larger totals.
objectives: Use the commutative property to find larger totals.
i_can: I can count on from the larger part. I can find totals up to 20.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe counting strategies (including counting on efficiently from the larger addend) to find unknown totals greater than 10, and compare and connect counting strategies. Identify equivalent expressions using the commutative property, and orally explain why they are equal.
key_questions: Is it easier to count on from the larger or smaller part? Why?
ad_texts: ["Apply the commutative property of addition as a strategy to add."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD1] Apply the commutative property of addition as a strategy to add.
laag: Students continue to count on from the larger addend, this time with totals greater than 10. With partners, students count on from both addends by using various tools. The class discusses strategies and confirms that it is easier to count on from the larger part because there are fewer numbers to count.

title: Add 0 and 1 to any number.
objectives: Add 0 and 1 to any number.
i_can: I can add 0 or 1. I can explain the patterns.
language_objectives: Orally tell time to the hour on an analog clock using the term o’clock, and orally compare telling time to counting on with a number path. Orally and in writing, generate statements about patterns when adding 0 and 1 to a number and test the statements’ validity.
key_questions: What happens when we add 1 to any number? What happens when we add 0 to any number?
ad_texts: ["Add within 20 by using strategies such as counting on or by creating an equivalent but easier problem. (1.OA.C.5, 1.OA.C.6)", "Add fluently within 10."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD3] Add within 20 by using strategies such as counting on or by creating an equivalent but easier problem. (1.OA.C.5, 1.OA.C.6) [1.Mod1.AD4] Add fluently within 10.
laag: Students apply their counting skills to telling time to the hour by using an analog clock. They notice patterns in sequences of +1 and +0 problems. They generalize to make conjectures about the total for each type of problem. They test their ideas on different problems to see whether their conjectures hold true. Students are introduced to the terms hour hand, minute hand, and o’clock.

title: Determine whether number sentences are true or false.
objectives: Determine whether number sentences are true or false.
i_can: I can decide if a number sentence is true or false.
language_objectives: Listen to stories about put together with both addends unknown situations to model and solve them by using manipulatives, drawings, and number sentences. Orally and in writing, use the meaning of the equal sign to justify why a number sentence is true or false.
key_questions: What makes a number sentence true or false?
ad_texts: ["Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false.
laag: Students represent a put together with both addends unknown situation by generating two-part expressions that total 5, which are familiar from kindergarten. They work in pairs to prove the equality of these expressions by using cubes and number bonds. Students determine whether number sentences are true or false and explain their reasoning.

title: Reason about the meaning of the equal sign.
objectives: Reason about the meaning of the equal sign.
i_can: I can explain why a number sentence is true or false.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, use the meaning of the equal sign to justify why a number sentence is true or false. Listen to peers’ justifications to evaluate their thinking.
key_questions: What does the equal sign mean?
ad_texts: ["Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false.
laag: Students practice matching equal expressions as a class and then in pairs. They reason about equality and the meaning of the equal sign as they evaluate whether a variety of number sentences are true or false.

title: Find all two-part expressions equal to 6.
objectives: Find all two-part expressions equal to 6.
i_can: I can show all the ways that two parts make 6.
language_objectives: Orally describe different ways to make 6 and write number sentences to match. Identify patterns when finding all two-part expressions equal to 6, and orally explain how the patterns help ensure every possible combination was found.
key_questions: How can we use the pattern on the Addition Totals chart to be sure that we found all the ways to make 6?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 10.", "Fluently decompose totals within 10 in more than one way."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD4] Add fluently within 10. [1.Mod1.AD5] Fluently decompose totals within 10 in more than one way.
laag: Students study a picture of items with a variety of attributes and sort, graph, and write a two-addend expression that totals 6. They identify the finite set of two-part expressions that total 6 through a guided, systematic approach. They play a game to develop fluency with facts that total 6.

title: Find all two-part expressions equal to 7 and 8.
objectives: Find all two-part expressions equal to 7 and 8.
i_can: I can show all the ways that two parts make 7 or 8.
language_objectives: Orally describe different ways to make 7 or 8 and write number sentences to match. Identify patterns when finding all two-part expressions equal to 7 or 8, and orally explain how the patterns help ensure every possible combination was found.
key_questions: How can we use the patterns on the Addition Totals chart to be sure that we found all the ways to make 7? 8?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 10.", "Fluently decompose totals within 10 in more than one way."]
