ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD4] Compare two-digit numbers by using the symbols >, =, and <.
laag: Students compare two quantities, either presented as pictures or written in unit form. They reason about the number of tens and ones in the totals and use that information to compare the quantities. Students represent their comparisons by writing comparison number sentences.

title: Use place value reasoning to write and compare 2 two-digit numbers.
objectives: Use place value reasoning to write and compare 2 two-digit numbers.
i_can: I can use tens and ones to compare the same two digits. I can show which number is greater or less.
language_objectives: Through a partner game, explain why a comparison statement is true and confirm a partner’s comparison statement by using a place value chart, a drawing, and a number sentence.
key_questions: How do you know which are the smallest and which are the biggest two-digit numbers we can make?
big_idea: Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones

title: Compare two quantities and make them equal.
objectives: Compare two quantities and make them equal.
i_can: I can compare two numbers and make them equal by adding to the smaller number. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Listen to and then build on the reasoning of others. Orally ask questions and analyze other students’ solutions based on the comparison of possible coin combinations. Orally explain how to make two sets of coins have equal values.
key_questions: How can we make a smaller total equal to a greater total?
big_idea: Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Compare two-digit numbers by using the symbols >, =, and <."]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD4] Compare two-digit numbers by using the symbols >, =, and <.
laag: Students reason about how the value of a smaller set of coins can be greater than the value of a larger set of coins. Students make the value of each set equal by adding pennies to compose ten and by trading for a dime. This lesson prepares students for making the next ten in topic C.

title: Add the ones first.
objectives: Add the ones first.
i_can: I can add two numbers by breaking one apart into tens and ones. I can add the ones first and then add the tens.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe how to break apart an addend to add the ones first. Orally generalize how adding ones first makes an easier problem.
key_questions: Why can it be helpful to break up a number into tens and ones to add it to another number?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones

Then they add the total to the tens. Students draw models and write number sentences to show how they decompose to make an easier problem.

title: Add the ones to make the next ten.
objectives: Add the ones to make the next ten.
i_can: I can use partners to ten to add two numbers. Using partners to ten helps me add the ones to make the next ten.
language_objectives: Orally, in writing, and by using manipulatives, describe how to break apart an addend to add the ones first and make the next ten. Orally analyze patterns related to partners to ten and predict how the tens place will change. Orally generalize how knowing partners to ten helps to make an easier problem.
key_questions: How is knowing partners to 10 helpful when adding a two-digit number to a one-digit number?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD7] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.

title: Decompose an addend to make the next ten.

i_can: I can make the next ten to add. I can show how I know.

key_questions: How can we make an easier problem when adding a two-digit number to a one-digit number?

ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD7] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.

title: Reason about related problems that make the next ten.
objectives: Reason about related problems that make the next ten.
i_can: I can make the next ten to add. I can use patterns to help me add larger parts and totals.
language_objectives: Orally analyze a list of number sentences to look for patterns and describe similarities. Orally describe how to find the total of a two-digit addend and a one-digit addend.
key_questions: How does the make the next ten strategy help us add?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones

ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD7] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.

title: Determine which equations make the next ten.

big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD7] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students analyze and find the totals for related addition problems. They use repeated reasoning to help them recognize when they can make ten or make the next ten. They test the patterns they find on additional sets of problems to confirm their thinking.

title: Count on and back by tens to add and subtract.

language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe solution strategies, including take away tens, count back by tens, and count on by tens, to find an unknown. Compare and connect solution strategies.
key_questions: What are some ways to add tens or take away tens?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones

title: Use related single-digit facts to add and subtract multiples of ten.
objectives: Use related single-digit facts to add and subtract multiples of ten.

language_objectives: Orally relate equations written in standard form and equations written in unit form. Orally explain how known facts can help add and subtract multiples of ten.
key_questions: How can facts we know help us add and subtract multiples of ten?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add or subtract multiples of 10. (1.NBT.C.4, 1.NBT.C.6)"]

objectives: Use tens to find an unknown part.
i_can: I can use tens to help me find an unknown part. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Listen to others’ reasoning about their choice of solution strategy and compare strategies. Orally describe how to use tens to find an unknown part.
key_questions: What strategies can we use to find an unknown part?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add or subtract multiples of 10. (1.NBT.C.4, 1.NBT.C.6)"]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD5] Add or subtract multiples of 10. (1.NBT.C.4, 1.NBT.C.6)

key_questions: How can we tell if a number sentence is true or false?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones

ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false. [1.Mod5.AD5] Add or subtract multiples of 10. (1.NBT.C.4, 1.NBT.C.6)
laag: Students determine whether number sentences are true or false and discuss their reasoning. They calculate the addition or subtraction expression on either side of the equal sign to find whether both sides represent the same amount.

title: Add tens to a two-digit number.
objectives: Add tens to a two-digit number.
i_can: I can add tens to a number. I can tell how the digits change.
language_objectives: Orally generalize how the digits in a two-digit number change when adding tens within 100. Listen to others’ reasoning about adding tens to find an unknown.
key_questions: What happens to the digits when you add tens to a number?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a multiple of 10 that have a sum within 100."]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD6] Add a two-digit number and a multiple of 10 that have a sum within 100.
laag: Students use the rekenrek and drawings to show adding tens to two-digit numbers. They represent the addends and the total by using place value charts, and they discuss how the digits in the tens place change but the digits in the ones place stay the same.

title: Add ones and multiples of ten to any number.
objectives: Add ones and multiples of ten to any number.
i_can: I can add tens and ones to a number. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally identify patterns in a choral count to describe how digits change when ones or tens are added. Through whole-class discussion and a partner game, describe how to add tens and ones to get to 100. Orally justify why two expressions are equal by using reasoning about tens and ones.
key_questions: How does looking at the digits in the tens and ones places help you to add?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a multiple of 10 that have a sum within 100.", "Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD6] Add a two-digit number and a multiple of 10 that have a sum within 100. [1.Mod5.AD7] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students engage in choral counting and notice patterns in the tens and ones places. Then they add a string of numbers, two at a time, to get to 100 (or more). Students self-select strategies to use in a variety of problems, including adding ones to a multiple of ten and adding ones or a multiple of ten to a two-digit number.

title: Use varied strategies to add 2 two-digit addends.
objectives: Use varied strategies to add 2 two-digit addends.
i_can: I can break apart tens and ones and combine them in different ways. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Listen to others’ reasoning about their choice of solution strategy to compare strategies. Orally justify the choice of a solution strategy for adding 2 two-digit numbers.
key_questions: What are some ways to combine groups of cubes to find the total?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod5.AD8] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students use place value strategies to combine pairs of two-digit numbers. They represent the addends with cubes, and then they self-select ways to combine the parts using tens and ones. Students share and discuss their strategies.

title: Decompose both addends and add like units.
objectives: Decompose both addends and add like units.
i_can: I can break apart the addends into tens and ones. Then  I can add the tens and add the ones.
language_objectives: Listen to the reasoning of others and build on it to orally explain how to find the total of two sets of coins. Through whole-class discussion and a partner game, orally explain how to use tens and ones to break apart numbers and add like units.
key_questions: How does breaking up two-digit addends into tens and ones help us to add?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false. [1.Mod5.AD8] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students add 2 two-digit numbers by decomposing both addends into tens and ones and then combining tens with tens and ones with ones. After guided practice using quick tens and number bonds to model problems, students practice doing this with a partner.

title: Decompose an addend and add tens first.
objectives: Decompose an addend and add tens first.
i_can: I can break up an addend into tens and ones. Then I can show how I add the tens first when finding the total.
language_objectives: Through whole-class discussion and a partner game, orally explain how to decompose an addend and use it to add the tens first.
key_questions: How does breaking up one addend into tens and ones help us to add?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false. [1.Mod5.AD8] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students watch a video that shows adding 2 two-digit numbers by decomposing the second addend into tens and ones, adding the tens to the first addend, and then adding the ones. Students practice this as a class by modeling problems with drawings and number bonds. Then they play a new game to practice adding two-digit numbers.

title: Decompose an addend to make the next ten.
objectives: Decompose an addend to make the next ten.
i_can: I can break apart an addend to make the next ten. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Through whole-class discussion and a partner game, orally explain how to decompose an addend and use it to make the next ten.
key_questions: How is breaking up an addend helpful?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false. [1.Mod5.AD8] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students watch a video that is similar to the one they viewed during lesson 23. The video shows adding 2 two-digit numbers by decomposing the second addend to make the next ten with the first addend. Students practice this as a class by modeling problems with drawings and number bonds. Then they play a game to practice adding two-digit numbers.

title: Compare equivalent expressions used to solve two-digit addition equations.
objectives: Compare equivalent expressions used to solve two-digit addition equations.
i_can: I can combine parts in different ways. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Write or make a drawing of a number bond or tens and ones to record how to add 2 two-digit numbers. Listen to and orally describe solution strategies, including add like units, add tens first, and make the next ten, for finding a total. Compare and connect solution strategies.
key_questions: What are some ways to make an easier problem?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod1.AD6] Determine whether addition and/or subtraction number sentences are true or false. [1.Mod5.AD8] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 50, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of operations.
laag: Students use self-selected strategies and tools to solve a two-digit addition problem. Then they share and discuss their work and find that different strategies result in the same total. Students analyze a number sentence with expressions that represent two ways to decompose two-digit addends. They determine that the expressions are equal and that the number sentence is true.

title: Name two-dimensional shapes based on the number of sides.
objectives: Name two-dimensional shapes based on the number of sides.
i_can: I can tell the name of a shape by counting its sides. I can draw a shape when I know its number of sides.
language_objectives: Orally classify two-dimensional shapes as triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, or hexagons based on the number of sides. Orally determine a category in which three shapes belong and justify why one shape does not belong by using the names of shapes and the number of straight sides.
key_questions: What can we notice about a shape to help us name it?
ad_texts: ["Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD2] Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes.
laag: Students count the number of sides on shapes and use that information to sort them into four categories: triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons. Students see that shapes that look different but have the same number of sides share a name. This lesson introduces the academic verb sketch.

title: Sort and name two-dimensional shapes based on attributes.
objectives: Sort and name two-dimensional shapes based on attributes.
i_can: I can count parallel sides and square corners. I can name shapes and tell about them.
language_objectives: Orally compare and classify shapes based on common attributes and use terms such as square corners and parallel sides to identify different types of quadrilaterals. Listen to build on the reasoning of others and describe shapes by using attributes.
key_questions: What are different ways to describe a shape? How can we describe this shape?
ad_texts: ["Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD2] Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes.
laag: Students identify the attributes of various quadrilaterals and test different shapes to see whether the sides are parallel and the corners are square (right angles). They use their knowledge of attributes to sort and discuss a variety of shapes. The terms parallel, rhombus, trapezoid, and square corner are introduced in this lesson. There is no Fluency component in this lesson. This allows students to spend more time exploring shape attributes.

title: Draw two-dimensional shapes and identify defining attributes.
objectives: Draw two-dimensional shapes and identify defining attributes.
i_can: I can name and tell about a shape. I can use tools to help me draw a shape.
language_objectives: Orally name and describe a rhombus, trapezoid, square, rectangle, hexagon, or triangle based on its attributes by using terms such as square corners, parallel, and sides.
key_questions: How does what we know about a shape help us to draw it? Which tools are helpful for precisely drawing shapes?
ad_texts: ["Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes.", "Draw two-dimensional shapes that have certain defining attributes."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD2] Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes. [1.Mod6.AD3] Draw two-dimensional shapes that have certain defining attributes.
laag: Students analyze shapes used in a floor plan. They name each shape and discuss its attributes. Then they use dots, cubes, and a straightedge to draw shapes precisely. There is no Problem Set in this lesson. This allows students to spend more time using their tools to draw a variety of shapes.

title: Name solid shapes and describe their attributes.
objectives: Name solid shapes and describe their attributes.
i_can: I can look at the faces of a solid shape to tell about the shape. I can name solid shapes.
language_objectives: Orally name and describe a rectangular prism, cone, triangular prism, cube, cylinder, or pyramid based on its attributes by using terms such as face.
key_questions: What are some ways to describe a solid shape?
ad_texts: ["Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD2] Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes.
laag: Students identify and name six solid shapes: cubes, cylinders, cones, square pyramids, rectangular prisms, and triangular prisms. Students describe the flat shapes they see on nets, or unfolded solid shapes, to make good guesses about which solid shape the net will become when it is folded. Students work with a partner to describe solid shapes, guess what unfolded solid shapes will become when folded, and fold nets into solid shapes. This lesson omits the Problem Set to allow more time for students to explore solid shapes.

title: Reason about the functionality of three‑dimensional shapes based on their attributes.
objectives: Reason about the functionality of three‑dimensional shapes based on their attributes.
i_can: I can tell about a solid shape and how it can move. I can tell if it will roll or stack and how I know.
language_objectives: Through listening and speaking, choose a shape for a given scenario and justify the choice based on the shape’s attributes and how it might function. Orally explain whether a three-dimensional shape can roll or stack by using attributes such as flat faces, curves, and points.
key_questions: Which solid shapes roll and stack? Why?
ad_texts: ["Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD2] Identify the defining attributes of two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional shapes.
laag: Students discuss the attributes of objects that are shaped like spheres, such as balls or globes. Students reason about attributes to compare solid shapes. They notice which attributes cause solid shapes to roll and stack, and they discuss how a shape’s attributes affect how it functions.

title: shapes within two- and three-dimensional composite shapes.
objectives: shapes within two- and three-dimensional composite shapes.
i_can: I can use smaller shapes to compose a larger flat or solid shape. I can find and count smaller shapes inside a larger shape.
language_objectives: Listen to and engage with the reasoning of others to describe composed shapes.
key_questions: How can smaller shapes be used to compose a larger shape?
ad_texts: ["Compose two\u2011dimensional and three\u2011dimensional shapes to create a composite shape."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD4] Compose two‑dimensional and three‑dimensional shapes to create a composite shape.
laag: Students study various composed shapes, including those in artwork, and recognize that larger shapes can be composed of other smaller shapes. They make this discovery in both flat shapes and solid shapes. Students create their own composite two‑ and three‑ dimensional shapes. This lesson revisits the term compose. There is no Problem Set in this lesson, and additional time is provided for students to complete the Exit Ticket.

title: Create new composite shapes by adding a shape.
objectives: Create new composite shapes by adding a shape.
i_can: I can use patterns to help me add to composed shapes. I can name the new shape and tell about it.
language_objectives: Orally predict the next composite shape in a pattern and justify the choice of shape. With a partner, orally describe growing patterns and number patterns in composed shapes.
key_questions: What happens when shapes are added to a composed shape?
ad_texts: ["Compose two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD4] Compose two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape.
laag: Students compose new shapes by adding one square at a time to a composite shape. They discuss how the new shape is composed, as well as its name and attributes. Students record their work and notice patterns in the compositions.

title: Combine identical composite shapes.
objectives: Combine identical composite shapes.
i_can: I can use copies of smaller shapes to make a composed shape. I can name the new shape and tell about it.
language_objectives: Orally form a conjecture about how many smaller two-dimensional shapes are needed to create a larger composite shape.
key_questions: What happens when you put together copies of the same composed shape?
ad_texts: ["Compose two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD4] Compose two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape.
laag: Students analyze and identify identical composite shapes within larger composite shapes. They manipulate triangles to compose new shapes. Then students combine their composed shape with a partner’s composed shape and identify the new shape.

title: Relate the size of a shape to how many are needed to compose a new shape.
objectives: Relate the size of a shape to how many are needed to compose a new shape.
i_can: I can compose the same shape in different ways. I can tell why I need more or fewer blocks to make a new shape.
language_objectives: Through listening and speaking, form a conjecture that more small shapes than large shapes are needed to compose a new shape, and justify the reasoning.
key_questions: Why does the number of blocks we need to compose a shape change?
ad_texts: ["Compose two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD4] Compose two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes to create a composite shape.
laag: Students make composed shapes and share solutions. They reason about why the same composed shape requires more of some blocks and fewer of others. They develop and test a conjecture: the smaller the shape, the more of them are needed to compose a new shape.

title: Reason about equal and not equal shares.
objectives: Reason about equal and not equal shares.
i_can: I can tell how a shape is composed of equal parts. I can partition a shape into equal parts.
language_objectives: Orally evaluate whether a shape or food item is partitioned into equal shares by using terms such as same-size, equal, fair, and equal shares.
key_questions: How do you know if a shape is composed of equal parts?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, fourths, or quarters."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD5] Partition circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, fourths, or quarters.
laag: Students watch a video that presents a situation about sharing and discuss equal shares in terms of fairness. They find fair ways to share by cutting paper that represents brownies, and then they use equal parts to compose shapes. They reason about different ways to partition shapes and talk about whether the representations show equal shares. The term partition is introduced in this lesson.

title: Name equal shares as halves or fourths.
objectives: Name equal shares as halves or fourths.
i_can: I can tell how a shape is partitioned into halves or fourths. I can partition a shape into halves or fourths.
language_objectives: Listen to follow a set of steps to fold paper into halves and fourths. Orally justify whether a shape or food item is partitioned into halves or fourths by using terms such as equal shares, equal parts, halves, and fourths.
key_questions: How do you know if something is partitioned into halves or fourths?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, fourths, or quarters."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD5] Partition circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, fourths, or quarters.
laag: Students fold origami owls to create, identify, and discuss halves and fourths. Then they identify halves and fourths in partitioned shapes. The terms halves and fourths are introduced in this lesson.

title: Partition shapes into halves, fourths, and quarters.
objectives: Partition shapes into halves, fourths, and quarters.
i_can: I can partition shapes into equal parts. I can tell if a shape is partitioned into halves or fourths, or quarters.
language_objectives: Listen to the reasoning of others and evaluate whether an object is cut into halves. Support agreement or disagreement by explaining reasoning with terms such as equal share, equal part, and halves. With a partner, orally justify whether a food item is partitioned into halves or quarters.
key_questions: How do you know if a shape is partitioned into halves? How do you know if a shape is partitioned into fourths (quarters)?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, fourths, or quarters."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD5] Partition circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, fourths, or quarters.
laag: Students are presented with a sharing scenario and engage in discussion about whether an object is partitioned into halves. They view different pictures of partitioned objects and determine whether they show halves or fourths. The term quarters is introduced in this lesson.

title: Relate the number of equal shares to the size of the shares.
objectives: Relate the number of equal shares to the size of the shares.
i_can: I can tell what happens to the size of the parts when a shape is partitioned into more equal parts. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Through listening and speaking, form a conjecture that the parts of a whole get smaller when the whole is shared among an increasing number of people, and justify the reasoning. Orally tell a sharing story and demonstrate by partitioning rectangles into 2, 3, and 4 equal shares.
key_questions: As a whole is partitioned into more equal parts, what happens to the size of the parts?
ad_texts: ["Draw or write to show that decomposing the same whole into more equal shares creates smaller shares."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD6] Draw or write to show that decomposing the same whole into more equal shares creates smaller shares.
laag: Students hear a sharing scenario that engages them in thinking about what happens to equal shares of a whole when the whole is partitioned into more equal parts. They draw to model the story and discuss their observations. Students craft and tell their own equal sharing story.

title: Tell time to the half hour with the term half past.
objectives: Tell time to the half hour with the term half past.
i_can: I can tell time to the half hour. I can tell what half past an hour means.
language_objectives: Orally tell time to the half hour on an analog clock by using the term half past. Through a partner game, match times shown in word form and presented on a clock by using terms such as half past both orally and in writing.
key_questions: What does it mean if the time is half past the hour?
big_idea: Clocks and Time Equal Parts Inside Shapes
ad_texts: ["Tell time to the half hour, including using the term half past."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD1] Tell time to the half hour, including using the term half past.
laag: Students relate the phrase half past to their understanding of half of a circle. They recognize that half past can also be stated as a time, such as 2:30. Students practice reading and matching times to the hour and half hour on digital and analog clocks.

title: Reason about the location of the hour hand to tell time.
objectives: Reason about the location of the hour hand to tell time.
i_can: I can tell time to the half hour. I can tell about the hour hand when the time is half past the hour.
language_objectives: Listen to build on the reasoning of others and orally describe similarities among, differences among, and attributes of time-telling tools. Orally tell time to the half hour on an analog clock and describe the position of the hour hand.
key_questions: How does the hour hand show half past an hour?
big_idea: Clocks and Time Equal Parts Inside Shapes
ad_texts: ["Tell time to the half hour, including using the term half past."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD1] Tell time to the half hour, including using the term half past.
laag: Students study time-telling tools from long ago. They look carefully at the shadow on a sundial to help them focus on the hour hand. Using an analog clock, students analyze the movement and location of the hour hand at the hour and half hour.

title: Count and record totals for collections greater than 100.
objectives: Count and record totals for collections greater than 100.
i_can: I can make groups of tens and ones to count my collection. I can tell how many tens and ones are in a number that is greater than 100.
language_objectives: With a partner, listen to and orally describe a strategy for estimating, counting, and recording a collection of objects. Write or draw to record how to organize and count a collection of objects. Include an estimate of how many in the collection of objects and the actual number in the collection. Listen to and orally describe strategies for counting accurately, including composing groups of ten. Compare and connect strategies.
key_questions: Where can we see the tens and ones when we write numbers that are greater than 100?
ad_texts: ["Represent a set of up to 120 objects with a written numeral by composing tens."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD8] Represent a set of up to 120 objects with a written numeral by composing tens.
laag: • Copy or print the counting collection recording The class works together to notice, count, write, and read numbers greater sheet to use for demonstration. than 100. Then partners organize, count, and record their collections of objects with totals greater than 100. The class shares and discusses student • Use small everyday objects to assemble at least one counting collection per student pair. Place work. They model the totals greater than 100 with Hide Zero cards and each collection in a bag or box. Each collection read them. should contain 100 to 120 objects. Assemble collections that have different digits in the There is no Fluency component, Problem Set, or Exit Ticket for this lesson. tens place of the total (e.g., 1 hundred, 0 tens, Instead, use classroom observations and students’ written representations some ones; 1 hundred, 1 ten, some ones; to analyze student thinking after the lesson. 1 hundred, 2 tens, 0 ones). Vary the number of objects in each collection based on the needs of your students.

title: Read, write, and represent numbers greater than 100.
objectives: Read, write, and represent numbers greater than 100.
i_can: I can show and write numbers greater than 100. I can read numbers and tell how many tens and ones are in them.
language_objectives: Orally explain patterns used to determine missing numbers in a sequence. Orally describe strategies that can help with reading and writing three-digit numbers.
key_questions: What helps us read and write numbers that are greater than 100?
ad_texts: ["Represent a set of up to 120 objects with a written numeral by composing tens.", "Write missing numbers in a sequence within 120."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD8] Represent a set of up to 120 objects with a written numeral by composing tens. [1.Mod6.AD10] Write missing numbers in a sequence within 120.
laag: Students make math drawings and use number bonds to represent numbers that are greater than 100. They show that the numbers have two parts: 100 and some more. Their drawing matches the way they hear the numbers being said, which helps them read the numbers accurately. Students also practice writing numbers to 120 by using the patterns in a number chart.

title: Count up and down across 100.
objectives: Count up and down across 100.
i_can: I can use patterns to help me find missing numbers. I can count up or down by tens or ones.
language_objectives: Orally analyze numbers in a sequence, determine whether they can be counted by ones or tens, and describe the patterns seen in each sequence. Orally describe strategies that can be used to help determine missing numbers in a sequence.
key_questions: How can we tell what number comes before or after a number in the count sequence?
ad_texts: ["Write missing numbers in a sequence within 120."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD10] Write missing numbers in a sequence within 120.
laag: Student pairs play a game to practice counting up and down the number path, starting at 100. Then they work with number sequences and count up and down by ones and tens. They read numbers, notice patterns, and determine which numbers come just before and just after a given number.

title: Write totals for collections larger than 100 shown in various groups of tens and ones.
objectives: Write totals for collections larger than 100 shown in various groups of tens and ones.
i_can: I can count and match collections that have the same total shown in different ways. I can write the total in tens and ones.
language_objectives: Through whole-class discussion and a partner game, listen to and orally describe counting strategies for finding a total, including identifying groups of ten. Orally explain why a number can be described both in tens and ones and in standard form (e.g., 8 tens 25 ones is equal to 105).
key_questions: How can we tell if different representations show the same number?
ad_texts: ["Represent a set of up to 120 objects with a written numeral by composing tens.", "Represent three-digit numbers within 120 as tens and ones."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD8] Represent a set of up to 120 objects with a written numeral by composing tens. [1.Mod6.AD9] Represent three-digit numbers within 120 as tens and ones.
laag: Students look at different ways the same total is represented. They reason about how they know the total is the same even though the representations are different. The lesson leads students through exploratory discussion, guided practice, and a game that students play with a partner. There is no Exit Ticket for this lesson. Instead, use students’ recordings to analyze their work after the lesson.

title: Represent and solve put together and take apart word problems.
objectives: Represent and solve put together and take apart word problems.
i_can: I can use a tape diagram to solve word problems. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Orally compare a tape diagram and a number bond. Write and draw to represent the parts, whole, and unknown in a story problem and orally describe how the models match the context. Orally generalize why a tape diagram is helpful for solving story problems.
key_questions: Why is a tape diagram helpful for solving problems?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD7] Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students represent different problem types by drawing and labeling tape diagrams. They analyze the part–whole relationships the tapes show and write equations they use to solve the problems. There is no Problem Set in this lesson to give students sufficient time to work with the new model.

title: Represent and solve add to and take from word problems.
objectives: Represent and solve add to and take from word problems.
i_can: I can use a tape diagram to help me solve word problems. I can show if Im finding a part or a total.
language_objectives: Write and draw to represent the parts, whole, and unknown in a story problem and orally describe how the models match the context. Orally explain why a tape diagram is helpful for determining whether an unknown is a part or a total.
key_questions: How does drawing a tape diagram help us to tell whether we need to find a part or the total?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD7] Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students represent different problem types by drawing and labeling tape diagrams. They analyze the part—whole relationships shown by the tapes and write equations they use to solve the problems. This lesson uses different types of word problems than those used in lesson 20.

title: Represent and solve add to and take from with start unknown word problems.
objectives: Represent and solve add to and take from with start unknown word problems.
i_can: I can use a tape diagram to know where to start in a word problem. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Write and draw to represent the parts, whole, and unknown in a story problem and orally describe how the models match the context. Through partner and whole-group conversations, orally explain how to find the unknown in a start unknown problem by using the words part and total. Listen to and orally retell story problems to imagine the action of the context and to represent it accurately by using a tape diagram.
key_questions: Why is a tape diagram helpful for solving problems?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD7] Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students are introduced to start unknown problem types. The quantity at the start, which is either a part or the total, is unknown. Students will first be guided through a concrete experience, and then they will work through representing word problems with tape diagrams and equations.

title: Represent and solve comparison word problems.
objectives: Represent and solve comparison word problems.
i_can: I can use a comparison tape diagram to help me compare totals in a word problem. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to organize models in order to compare. Orally generalize about why a tape diagram is helpful for comparing.
key_questions: How can a tape diagram help us to compare?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD7] Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students work with two different types of comparison situations in this lesson. They learn to draw comparison tape diagrams to represent the problems. They analyze the relationships the diagrams show and write equations they use to solve the problems.

title: Reason with nonstandard measurement units.
objectives: Reason with nonstandard measurement units.
i_can: I can tell why it takes more of a smaller tool than a larger tool to measure an object. I can solve word problems with lengths.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to organize models in order to compare nonstandard measurement units. Orally conjecture about why it takes more of a smaller unit than it does of a larger unit to measure the length of a given object.
key_questions: Why does it take more of a smaller tool than it does of a larger tool to measure the length of an object?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD7] Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students measure the length of an object twice by using a different nonstandard unit each time. They discover that they need more shorter units than longer units to measure the same object. Students also solve comparison word problems involving nonstandard units when the language of the problem suggests the opposite operation.

title: Solve nonroutine problems.
objectives: Solve nonroutine problems.
i_can: I can use tools to solve a problem that can be solved in different ways. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Write or draw to record how to solve problems with multiple correct responses that invite students to consider multiple perspectives. Listen to and orally describe solution strategies and representations for finding a total and compare and connect the representations.
key_questions: How do mathematicians solve problems?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD7] Represent and solve word problems within 20 involving all addition and subtraction problem types by using drawings and an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students act like mathematicians to solve nonroutine problems that have many solution pathways. They use information they know and self-select strategies and tools to solve a problem. Students share their solution and discuss their thinking. They relate the problem-solving process to the work that mathematicians do.

title: Make a total in more than one way.
objectives: Make a total in more than one way.
i_can: I can find the same total by adding in different ways. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Orally explain why two addends make 65 by using strategies such as composing or decomposing addends. Orally analyze patterns in ways to make 65 by using ten-sticks, cubes, and expressions.
key_questions: Why do we get the same total even when we combine addends in different ways?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD12] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.
laag: Students study pictures of numbers represented in terms of tens and ones. They try to figure out which two numbers can be combined to make a given total. Then students systematically move tens from one addend to the other. They find patterns in the resulting expressions and see that the total stays the same.

title: Add two-digit numbers in various ways, part 1.
objectives: Add two-digit numbers in various ways, part 1.
i_can: I can break apart addends and add the parts in different ways. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Write or draw to record how to add two-digit numbers, including by using quick tens and ones and by using number sentences. Listen to and orally describe solution strategies for finding the total, including add like units, add tens first, and add ones first to make the next ten. Compare and connect solution strategies. With a partner, examine sample student work to identify an error in making an easier problem, and orally explain how to correct the error.
key_questions: What are ways to make an easier problem?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD11] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations. [1.Mod6.AD12] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.
laag: Students use concrete materials to decompose addends and compose parts to solve addition problems with 2 two-digit addends. Through class discussion they share and compare various ways to solve the problems. They relate their work to number sentences. Students critique a flawed response that shows a common error.

title: Add two-digit numbers in various ways, part 2.
objectives: Add two-digit numbers in various ways, part 2.
i_can: I can break apart addends and add the parts in different ways. I can use drawings to show how I know.
language_objectives: Write or draw to record how to add two-digit numbers, including by using quick tens and ones and by using number sentences. Listen to and orally describe solution strategies for finding the total, including add like units, add tens first, and add ones first to make the next ten. Compare and connect solution strategies.
key_questions: What are ways to make an easier problem?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD11] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations. [1.Mod6.AD12] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.
laag: This lesson parallels lesson 27. The difference is that students use pictorial models rather than concrete ones to decompose addends and compose parts to solve problems that use 2 two-digit addends. Through class discussion they share and compare various ways to solve the problems. They relate their work to number sentences. Students critique a flawed response that shows a common error.

title: Add tens to make 100.
objectives: Add tens to make 100.
i_can: I can use partners to 10 to help me make 100 in different ways. I can show how I know.
language_objectives: Orally describe different ways to group tens to make 100 and listen to build on the reasoning of others. Read and orally retell an add to with start unknown problem, and write or draw to record how to find the total.
key_questions: How are partners to 10 helpful when finding ways to make 100?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD12] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.
laag: Students watch a video and reason about tens to find the value of a set of dimes. Students use their knowledge of partners to 10 to find all the ways to make 100 with two addends that are both multiples of 10. Students apply this thinking to solve word problems.

title: Make the next ten and add tens to make 100.
objectives: Make the next ten and add tens to make 100.
i_can: I can make the next ten and then add tens to get to 100. I can use tools to show how I know.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to make 100 by using a number path to get to the next ten and then to 100. Write to record thinking by using the arrow way and a number sentence.
key_questions: What are some strategies we can use to get to 100 from any number?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD11] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations. [1.Mod6.AD12] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.
laag: Students start from different two-digit numbers and add tens and ones to make or get to 100. They either add ones to make the next ten and then add tens to make 100, or they add tens first and then add the ones. They use the arrow way and number sentences to record their thinking.

title: Add to make 100.
objectives: Add to make 100.
i_can: I can add different numbers to make 100. I can use a number sentence to show how I know.
language_objectives: Through a partner game, orally justify why two numbers were chosen to make 100 by using place value understanding. Orally explain how to count and add a group of objects to find the total.
key_questions: What addends make 100? How do you know?
big_idea: Equal Expressions Reasoning About Equality Tens and Ones
ad_texts: ["Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.", "Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations."]
ad_full: [1.Mod6.AD11] Add a two-digit number and a one-digit number that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations. [1.Mod6.AD12] Add 2 two-digit numbers that have a sum within 100, relate the strategy used to a written method, and explain the reasoning used. Use concrete models, drawings, strategies based on place value, and/or properties of equations.
laag: Students study pictures of numbers represented in terms of tens and ones. They try to figure out which two numbers in the pictures can be combined to make 100. To culminate the year, students consider where they see math in the world around them and reflect on their learning during the year. There is no Problem Set in this lesson. This allows students to spend more time exploring ways to make 100.

title: Draw and label a picture graph to represent data.
objectives: Draw and label a picture graph to represent data.
i_can: I can make a picture graph to show data.
language_objectives: With a partner, orally ask and answer questions about picture graphs. Read and write to create a picture graph by using the terms table, data, title, category, and key.
key_questions: Why are graphs useful?
ad_texts: ["Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD8] Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories.
laag: Students vote on a personal favorite to generate data and make a class picture graph. They create a graph by using symbols to represent votes. Then students read and interpret picture graphs to answer questions. This lesson introduces the terms table, data, category, and key.

title: Draw and label a bar graph to represent data.
objectives: Draw and label a bar graph to represent data.
i_can: I can make a bar graph to show data.
language_objectives: Orally compare representations of the same data shown vertically and horizontally in picture and bar graphs. Read data from a table and write to represent it by using the terms bar graph and scale.
key_questions: How are bar graphs similar to picture graphs? How are bar graphs different from picture graphs?
ad_texts: ["Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD8] Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories.
laag: Students compare data presented vertically and horizontally. They discover that the data stays the same even when the orientation changes. They record data on a bar graph with a scale. Then they use bar graphs to answer questions. This lesson introduces the terms bar graph and scale.

title: Use information presented in a bar graph to solve put together and take apart problems.
objectives: Use information presented in a bar graph to solve put together and take apart problems.
i_can: I can use a bar graph to answer questions and find totals.
language_objectives: With a partner and as a class, orally explain strategies for finding a sum or a difference using data from a bar graph.
key_questions: How can a bar graph help us solve problems?
ad_texts: ["Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories.", "Solve addition, subtraction, and comparison problems by using information from a bar graph."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD8] Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories. [2.Mod1.AD9] Solve addition, subtraction, and comparison problems by using information from a bar graph.
laag: Students use a set of sorted objects to make a bar graph. They use the graph to solve put together and take apart problems. The class discusses strategies and writes addition or subtraction number sentences to show their thinking.

title: Use information presented in a bar graph to solve compare problems.
objectives: Use information presented in a bar graph to solve compare problems.
i_can: I can use a bar graph to compare data and answer questions.
language_objectives: Orally make comparison statements by using the phrases how many more and how many fewer with a partner. Read and write to create a bar graph and orally explain different strategies to compare the data.
key_questions: How does a bar graph help us compare?
ad_texts: ["Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories.", "Solve addition, subtraction, and comparison problems by using information from a bar graph."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD8] Draw and label picture and bar graphs to represent a data set with up to four categories. [2.Mod1.AD9] Solve addition, subtraction, and comparison problems by using information from a bar graph.
laag: Students represent data on a bar graph and use the graph to solve comparison problems that use the phrases how many more and how many fewer. Students find the difference between categories by matching and then counting the missing spaces or extra boxes in a row.

title: Connect measurement to physical units by iterating a centimeter cube.
objectives: Connect measurement to physical units by iterating a centimeter cube.
i_can: I can measure lengths with a 1 centimeter cube.
language_objectives: Through partner and whole-class discussions, orally describe features of a ruler by using the terms same size, length unit, space, and tick mark. Orally state the measurements of objects that are not whole-centimeter lengths.
key_questions: What do we count when we measure?
ad_texts: ["Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD1] Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students experiment with two ways of making a ruler, which is introduced as a new measurement tool. They place centimeter cubes side by side and make a tick mark where each cube ends. Then students make another ruler by iterating 1 cube to learn that the length of an object is measured by the total number of length units. This lesson introduces the term tick mark.

title: Make a 10 cm ruler and measure objects.
objectives: Make a 10 cm ruler and measure objects.
i_can: I can make a 10 centimeter ruler and use it to measure lengths.
language_objectives: After creating a ruler, through a class discussion orally describe the meaning of the numbers on a ruler and how they relate to equal spaces. Write to explain that tick marks on rulers show same-size length units.
key_questions: What do the numbers on a ruler tell us?
ad_texts: ["Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD1] Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students apply the mark-and-move-forward technique to make and label a 10 cm ruler. They work in pairs to use this new, more efficient tool to measure objects in the classroom. The focus of the lesson is on clarifying the meanings of, and the relationship between, the spaces, numbers, and tick marks on a ruler.

title: Measure lengths and relate 10 cm and 1 cm.
objectives: Measure lengths and relate 10 cm and 1 cm.
i_can: I can measure lengths in more than one way by using 10 centimeter rulers and cubes. 1 centimeter
language_objectives: Orally explain that one 10 cm ruler has the same length as ten 1 cm cubes. Orally justify statements about the relationship between different measurement units.
key_questions: What is the relationship between a 10 cm ruler and a 1 cm cube?
big_idea: Measure and Compare Objects Problem Solving with Measure
ad_texts: ["Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD1] Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students put together several 10 cm rulers to measure the lengths of objects longer than 10 cm. With guidance, they reason about the relationship between a 10 cm ruler and a 1 cm cube. This lesson introduces the term support as an academic verb.

title: Make a meter stick and measure with various tools.
objectives: Make a meter stick and measure with various tools.
i_can: I can make a meter stick and choose a tool that makes sense to measure lengths.
language_objectives: Orally explain that ten 10 cm rulers are the same length as 1 meter or 100 centimeters. Through listening to and speaking with a partner, create a meter stick by using alternating colored 10 cm rulers. With a partner, orally justify the selection of measurement tools and provide a rationale based on the size and shape of the object being measured.
key_questions: What is the same about making a meter stick, or 100 cm ruler, and a 10 cm ruler? How does the size and shape of an object help you select the best measurement tool?
ad_texts: ["Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD1] Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students use 10 cm cards to make a meter stick and deepen their understanding of units within units. They discuss the size and shape of classroom objects and use what they notice to select appropriate measurement tools. This lesson introduces the term meter.

title: Relate 1 cm, 10 cm, and 100 cm.
objectives: Relate 1 cm, 10 cm, and 100 cm.
i_can: I can write lengths in more than one way.
language_objectives: With a partner, listen to and orally reason about ways to express the same measurement with different units by using measurement tools. Read comparison statements that use the phrase is the same length as and orally explain whether they are true.
key_questions: How are 1 cm, 10 cm, and 100 cm related?
ad_texts: ["This lesson is foundational to the work of 2.NBT.A.1. Its content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in part 1 of this module."]
ad_full: This lesson is foundational to the work of 2.NBT.A.1. Its content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in part 1 of this module.
laag: Students reason about the relationship between metric units. Through problem solving, students discuss ways to express lengths in terms of different units: 1 m 25 cm, 125 cm, etc. Then students play a matching game where they find more than one way to express the same measurement.

title: Reason about the relationship between the size of the unit and the number of units needed to measure.
objectives: Reason about the relationship between the size of the unit and the number of units needed to measure.
i_can: I can measure lengths in more than one way.
language_objectives: Model and orally explain the meaning of the length units cubit, palm, and digit. Orally describe the relationship between the size of the unit and the number of units.
key_questions: What is the relationship between the size of the length unit and the number of units needed to measure? When we record measurements, why is it important to include the number and the unit?
ad_texts: ["This lesson is foundational to the work of 2.MD.A.2. Its content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in part 1 of this module."]
ad_full: This lesson is foundational to the work of 2.MD.A.2. Its content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in part 1 of this module.
laag: Students measure with ancient Egyptian length units and notice similarities to the metric system—that larger units are composed of smaller units. When students measure the same object twice, they reason about the relationship between the size of the length unit and the number of units needed to measure.

title: Estimate and compare lengths.
objectives: Estimate and compare lengths.
i_can: I can estimate and measure to compare lengths.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally explain the meanings of the terms benchmark and estimate. Read word problems involving length, and write or draw to find the difference between an estimate and a measurement.
key_questions: How can we tell if an estimate makes sense? How do benchmarks help make better estimates?
big_idea: Measure and Compare Objects Problem Solving with Measure
ad_texts: ["Estimate lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).", "Measure and find a difference in length by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD2] Estimate lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters). [2.Mod1.AD3] Measure and find a difference in length by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students use benchmark lengths, such as the width of their pinkie, to estimate the lengths of objects. They compare estimates with actual measurements and model the difference in length by using a tape diagram. This lesson introduces the terms benchmark and estimate.

title: Model and reason about the difference in length.
objectives: Model and reason about the difference in length.
i_can: I can show the difference in length in more than one way.
language_objectives: Orally explain two ways to find the difference in length between two objects. Identify the difference between lengths on a tape diagram and use the term difference to orally explain what it means in a measurement context.
key_questions: How does relating subtraction to addition help us find the difference in length?
big_idea: Measure and Compare Objects Problem Solving with Measure
ad_texts: ["Measure and find a difference in length by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD3] Measure and find a difference in length by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students use a tape diagram to compare an estimate with an actual measurement. They find the difference in length either by taking from the total length or by using the relationship between addition and subtraction to count on from the smaller length. Students write number sentences to match their models and reasoning. The term difference is introduced in this lesson.

title: Estimate and measure height to model metric relationships.
objectives: Estimate and measure height to model metric relationships.
i_can: I can measure and write heights in more than one way.
language_objectives: With a partner and as a class, listen to and orally describe how tall a partner is by using the word height. Orally and in writing, express measurements in different units and draw tape diagrams to represent the relationship between them.
key_questions: How can we express a measurement in more than one way? What is the relationship between measurement tools and units?
big_idea: Measure and Compare Objects Problem Solving with Measure
ad_texts: ["Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).", "Estimate lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD1] Measure lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters). [2.Mod1.AD2] Estimate lengths of objects by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: Students estimate and then measure a partner’s height. They select appropriate tools and experiment with strategies for measuring. Students express measurements in centimeters, and then in meters and centimeters. They use a tape diagram to model the relationships between units.

title: Represent and compare students’ heights.
objectives: Represent and compare students’ heights.
i_can: I can compare heights and show the difference in height.
language_objectives: Orally ask and answer comparison questions using the words taller and shorter. Through listening to and orally participating in a class discussion, compare and connect strategies to find the difference.
key_questions: What does it mean to find the difference in height? How does a tape diagram help us compare?
big_idea: Measure and Compare Objects Problem Solving with Measure
ad_texts: ["Measure and find a difference in length by using metric units (centimeters and meters)."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD3] Measure and find a difference in length by using metric units (centimeters and meters).
laag: The class compares two students’ heights, given in centimeters. Students use a tape diagram to represent and find the difference in height, and then write an addition or subtraction equation to match their drawing.

title: Use a measuring tape as a number line to add efficiently.
objectives: Use a measuring tape as a number line to add efficiently.
i_can: I can use a number line and benchmark numbers to add.
language_objectives: With a measuring tape, orally explain and demonstrate to a partner how to add efficiently using the terms benchmark numbers and number line.
key_questions: How can we use benchmark numbers and a number line to add efficiently?
ad_texts: ["Represent whole numbers within 100 on a number line.", "Represent sums within 100 by using a number line."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD5] Represent whole numbers within 100 on a number line. [2.Mod1.AD6] Represent sums within 100 by using a number line.
laag: Students use linear models, such as a measuring tape and a number line, to add efficiently. They recognize the efficiency of getting to a benchmark number. The terms benchmark number and number line are introduced in this lesson.

title: Use a measuring tape as a number line to subtract efficiently.
objectives: Use a measuring tape as a number line to subtract efficiently.
i_can: I can use a number line and benchmark numbers to subtract.
language_objectives: With a measuring tape, orally explain and demonstrate to a partner how to subtract efficiently using the terms benchmark numbers and number line. Through listening to and orally participating in a class discussion, compare and connect subtraction strategies on a number line to reason about the efficiency of using benchmark numbers.
key_questions: How can benchmark numbers and the number line be used to subtract efficiently?
ad_texts: ["Represent whole numbers within 100 on a number line.", "Represent differences within 100 by using a number line."]
ad_full: [2.Mod1.AD5] Represent whole numbers within 100 on a number line. [2.Mod1.AD7] Represent differences within 100 by using a number line.
laag: Students model subtracting efficiently on a linear model, such as a measuring tape or a number line. They recognize the efficiency of getting to a benchmark number.

title: Represent and solve comparison problems by using measurement contexts.
objectives: Represent and solve comparison problems by using measurement contexts.
i_can: I can answer questions about comparing lengths.
language_objectives: Orally reason about how to solve a comparison problem, compare similarities and differences between solution strategies, and reason about their efficiency by using benchmark numbers on a number line. Write to explain why a given solution strategy is incorrect.
key_questions: How can number lines and tape diagrams be used to represent and solve comparison problems? How can the same problem be solved with different equations?
big_idea: Measure and Compare Objects Problem Solving with Measure Number Strategies
