ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students use place value understanding to add like units. Expanded form and unit form are used to support adding like units. Students use number bonds and expressions to record and explain their thinking. The term decompose is introduced in this lesson.

title: Use compensation to add within 100.
objectives: Use compensation to add within 100.
i_can: I can use benchmark numbers to add.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to use benchmark numbers to add efficiently within 100.
key_questions: How do benchmark numbers help us add? How do models such as the number line and the arrow way help us use benchmark numbers to add?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students use compensation to find the solution to an addition problem in which one addend is close to a benchmark number. They use an open number line and the arrow way to show how to use benchmark numbers to add. Students reason about why compensation works and apply it to a measurement context.

title: Use compensation to add within 200.
objectives: Use compensation to add within 200.
i_can: I can use benchmark numbers to add numbers greater than 100.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to use benchmark numbers to add efficiently within 200. Orally justify why compensation is a helpful strategy.
key_questions: Why is compensation a useful strategy for addition?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students compare related expressions to advance their benchmark thinking to numbers beyond 100. They make connections between the open number line and the arrow way representations that show the use of benchmark numbers to add. The term compensation is introduced in this lesson.

title: Make a ten to add within 100.
objectives: Make a ten to add within 100.
i_can: I can make a ten to add.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to decompose an addend and use it to make a ten to add within 100.
key_questions: When is it helpful to make a ten to add?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students simplify addition problems by using the make a ten strategy and build capacity for mental addition. They recognize that the make a ten strategy is useful when one addend is close to a benchmark number.

title: Make a ten to add within 200.
objectives: Make a ten to add within 200.
i_can: I can make a ten to add numbers greater than 100.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to simplify addition problems within 200 when one addend is close to a ten. Analyze solution samples and identify the mistake to orally justify when making ten is a helpful strategy.
key_questions: When is making a ten a helpful addition strategy? How is making a ten a helpful strategy for some addition problems?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students make simpler addition problems by applying the make a ten strategy to adding within 200. They look carefully at problems before adding to develop the habit of determining when a strategy is useful.

title: Solve word problems by using estimation and simplifying strategies for addition.
objectives: Solve word problems by using estimation and simplifying strategies for addition.
i_can: I can estimate before I solve addition problems.
language_objectives: Listen to others’ reasoning about their choice of solution strategy to compare and contrast strategies. Orally justify the choice of a solution strategy.
key_questions: How do estimation strategies help us solve word problems? How do you decide which solution strategies to use?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.", "Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Estimate reasonable sums and differences when solving problems."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD1] Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown. [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod2.AD7] Estimate reasonable sums and differences when solving problems.
laag: Students apply previously learned strategies and the Read–Draw–Write process to solve put together and add to word problems. They make an estimate before solving and use their estimate to check the reasonableness of their answer. After solving each problem, students share their work by comparing and connecting solution strategies. This lesson introduces the academic verb defend.

title: Use concrete models to compose a ten.
objectives: Use concrete models to compose a ten.
i_can: I can compose a ten to add by using place value disks.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to compose a unit of ten.
key_questions: When do you compose a new unit of ten? How do place value models help us add?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod2.AD5] Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit.
laag: Students build on their understanding of making a unit of ten. They add one- and two-digit numbers by using place value disks and model the composition of a ten. The term compose is introduced in this lesson.

title: Use place value drawings to compose a ten and relate to written recordings.
objectives: Use place value drawings to compose a ten and relate to written recordings.
i_can: I can compose a ten to add by using a place value drawing.
language_objectives: Orally compare place value representations and explain how each representation shows when a ten can be composed.
key_questions: How do place value drawings help us add? How does a place value drawing relate to a written recording?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod2.AD5] Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit.
laag: Students represent and solve addition problems with place value disks before transitioning to pictorial place value drawings. Students relate place value drawings to other strategies and to written recordings.

title: Use concrete models to compose a hundred.
objectives: Use concrete models to compose a hundred.
i_can: I can compose a hundred to add by using place value disks.
language_objectives: Listen to, orally discuss, and confirm predictions about how to compose a unit of 1 hundred.
key_questions: When can we compose a new unit of a hundred? How does place value help us add?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod2.AD5] Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit.
laag: Students build on place value understanding to compose a unit of 1 hundred when they add. Students use place value disks to help compose a hundred to add two-digit numbers.

title: Use math drawings to compose a hundred and relate to written recordings.
objectives: Use math drawings to compose a hundred and relate to written recordings.
i_can: I can compose a hundred to add by using a place value drawing.
language_objectives: Orally determine a category in which three things belong, and justify why one does not fit by using place value language.
key_questions: How do place value drawings help us add? How does a place value drawing relate to a written recording?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod2.AD5] Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit.
laag: Students represent and solve addition problems with place value disks before transitioning to a pictorial place value drawing. They relate place value drawings to other strategies and to written recordings. The term sum is formalized in this lesson.

title: Use place value drawings to compose a ten and a hundred with two- and three-digit addends. Relate to written recordings.
objectives: Use place value drawings to compose a ten and a hundred with two- and three-digit addends. Relate to written recordings.
i_can: I can compose a ten and a hundred to add.
language_objectives: Through listening and speaking with a partner and as a class, explain how written recordings of addition are alike and different. Orally explain how to compose new units of ten and a hundred to find a sum.
key_questions: When do we compose a new unit? How do written recordings show place value understanding?
ad_texts: ["Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD3] Add within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod2.AD5] Rename 10 of a smaller unit as 1 of a larger unit.
laag: Students develop a conceptual understanding of addition as they make connections between place value drawings and written recordings. They compose a ten and a hundred and record by using expanded form. This lesson introduces totals below.

title: Estimate and represent to solve take from word problems.
objectives: Estimate and represent to solve take from word problems.
i_can: I can estimate to make sense of problems and help me solve them.
language_objectives: Read word problems involving subtraction, and write solution statements to put the answers in context. Through speaking and listening, compare and connect solution strategies and representations.
key_questions: How can representations of word problems help us estimate? What strategies can be used to help solve take from problems?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.", "Estimate reasonable sums and differences when solving problems."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD1] Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown. [2.Mod2.AD7] Estimate reasonable sums and differences when solving problems.
laag: Students solve a take from with change unknown problem by using self-selected strategies. They make an estimate before solving to make sense of the context and choose the correct operation. This lesson supports students as they make sense of change unknown and result unknown word problems with numbers that typically require renaming.

title: Use addition and subtraction strategies to find an unknown part.
objectives: Use addition and subtraction strategies to find an unknown part.
i_can: I can find an unknown part.
language_objectives: Orally analyze solution strategies that use benchmark numbers to add and subtract efficiently. Orally describe the relationship between addition and subtraction strategies to find an unknown part.
key_questions: How can we use addition to solve a take from problem? How do benchmark numbers help us to subtract?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
laag: Students represent and solve a take from with result unknown word problem. They use the part–total relationship to solve by using both addition and subtraction strategies. Students use benchmark numbers to efficiently add and subtract.

title: Use compensation to subtract within 100.
objectives: Use compensation to subtract within 100.
i_can: I can use benchmark numbers to subtract.
language_objectives: Orally explain how benchmark numbers and compensation make subtraction easier, and use a number line to support thinking.
key_questions: How does compensation make it easier to subtract? How does the number line help us use benchmark numbers to subtract?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
laag: Students reason about how compensation can be used to simplify subtraction problems. They use benchmark numbers and models, such as the open number line and the arrow way, to show why the strategy works.

title: Use compensation to subtract within 200.
objectives: Use compensation to subtract within 200.
i_can: I can use benchmark numbers to subtract from a number greater than 100.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to use compensation to subtract within 200 and use an open number line and the arrow way to explain why the strategy works. Read word problems involving subtraction and write a solution statement to put the answer in context.
key_questions: How does compensation make it easier to subtract? How does a number line help us use benchmark numbers to subtract?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
laag: Students reason about how compensation can be used to subtract with larger numbers. They use a number line and benchmark numbers to extend the strategy to numbers within 200. Students discuss similarities and differences between compensation as a strategy for addition and for subtraction.

title: Take from a ten to subtract within 200.
objectives: Take from a ten to subtract within 200.
i_can: I can take from a ten to subtract.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to decompose a total to make a simpler problem by subtracting from a ten, a benchmark number.
key_questions: Is it simpler to subtract from a benchmark number? Why? When does it make sense to decompose the total of a subtraction problem?
ad_texts: ["within 200", "Subtract by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction."]
ad_full: within 200 [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
laag: Students analyze the numbers in a subtraction problem and reason about how to decompose the total to simplify the problem. They use the take from a ten strategy by decomposing a total into a benchmark number and the remaining part.

title: Take from a hundred to subtract within 200.
objectives: Take from a hundred to subtract within 200.
i_can: I can take from a hundred to subtract.
language_objectives: Explain orally and record how to decompose a total to make a simpler problem by subtracting from a hundred, a benchmark number. Orally compare and contrast the take from a ten and take from a hundred strategies.
key_questions: How are the take from a ten and take from a hundred strategies related?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
laag: Students analyze the numbers and reason about how to decompose a total to simplify a subtraction problem. They use the take from a hundred strategy by decomposing a total into a hundred and the remaining part. Students reason about the relationship between take from a ten and take from a hundred.

title: Solve word problems with simplifying strategies for subtraction.
objectives: Solve word problems with simplifying strategies for subtraction.
i_can: I can estimate before I solve subtraction problems.
language_objectives: Read word problems involving subtraction, and write solution statements to put the answers in context. Orally justify the choice of strategy by using place value understanding. As a class, listen to then evaluate peers’ choice of subtraction strategies.
key_questions: How do simplifying strategies help us solve problems? How do you decide which strategies to use to solve?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.", "Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Estimate reasonable sums and differences when solving problems."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD1] Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown. [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod2.AD7] Estimate reasonable sums and differences when solving problems.
laag: Students share strategies to solve a subtraction problem in which the known part is close to a benchmark number. They apply strategies of their choice to solve a take from with result unknown word problem.

title: Reason about when to unbundle a ten to subtract.
objectives: Reason about when to unbundle a ten to subtract.
i_can: I can unbundle a ten to subtract.
language_objectives: Read word problems involving subtraction, and write solution statements to put the answers in context. Orally explain when to unbundle 1 ten and rename it as 10 ones.
key_questions: When do we need to unbundle a ten to subtract?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod2.AD6] Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit.
laag: Students use place value understanding to reason about when they need to unbundle a ten to subtract. They draw to represent subtraction problems and unbundle a ten to subtract.

title: Use concrete models to decompose a ten with two-digit totals.
objectives: Use concrete models to decompose a ten with two-digit totals.
i_can: I can rename a ten to subtract by using place value disks.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally retell a take from situation involving the need to decompose a ten. Orally explain how to rename 10 ones as 1 ten with place value disks. Orally compare modeling a problem with disks to using place value drawings.
key_questions: Does the total change when we exchange or rename units?
ad_texts: ["Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD6] Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit.
laag: Students use place value disks to model a subtraction problem. They determine when to rename a ten as smaller units to subtract. Students make connections between concrete models and place value drawings.

title: Use place value drawings to decompose a ten and relate them to written recordings.
objectives: Use place value drawings to decompose a ten and relate them to written recordings.
i_can: I can rename a ten to subtract by using a place value drawing.
language_objectives: In partners, orally describe how to rename a ten to subtract and how a place value drawing relates to a recording in unit form.
key_questions: How do place value drawings help us subtract? How does a place value drawing relate to a written recording?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod2.AD6] Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit.
laag: Students use a place value drawing to represent subtraction problems. They decompose a ten and rename it as 10 ones. Students relate a place value drawing to a written recording in which the total and known part are written in unit form.

title: Use concrete models and drawings to decompose a hundred.
objectives: Use concrete models and drawings to decompose a hundred.
i_can: I can rename a hundred to subtract by using place value disks.
language_objectives: Listen to and retell a subtraction situation and discuss how to exchange 1 hundred-dollar bill for 10 ten-dollar bills.
key_questions: How can we unbundle a hundred to help us subtract? How can unit form help us subtract like units?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod2.AD6] Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit.
laag: Students use place value disks to decompose a hundred and rename a three-digit total to subtract. Students learn that they can rename the total in tens and ones, write it in unit form, and subtract like units. Students make connections between concrete models and place value drawings.

title: Use place value drawings to decompose a hundred and relate them to written recordings.
objectives: Use place value drawings to decompose a hundred and relate them to written recordings.
i_can: I can rename a hundred to subtract by using a place value drawing.
language_objectives: Orally describe how place value drawings relate to unit form recordings. Read word problems involving subtraction, and write solution statements to put the answers in context.
key_questions: How do place value drawings help us to subtract? How does a place value drawing relate to a written recording?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod2.AD6] Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit.
laag: Students use place value drawings to represent subtraction problems. They decompose a hundred and rename it as 10 tens. Students relate place value drawings to written recordings.

title: Use place value drawings to subtract with two decompositions.
objectives: Use place value drawings to subtract with two decompositions.
i_can: I can rename numbers to subtract.
language_objectives: In small groups, orally describe different ways to rename a three-digit number. Orally describe how place value drawings relate to unit form recordings for subtraction problems.
key_questions: How do place value drawings help us subtract when there are not enough tens and ones? How does renaming help us subtract?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD4] Subtract within 200 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod2.AD6] Rename 1 of a larger unit as 10 of a smaller unit.
laag: Students subtract from three-digit totals with two decompositions by using both place value drawings and written recordings. They rename the totals in both standard and unit form to subtract when there are not enough ones and tens.

title: Solve add to and take from with start unknown word problems.
objectives: Solve add to and take from with start unknown word problems.
i_can: I can use part-total thinking to solve word problems.
language_objectives: Listen to, read, and retell a start unknown word problem and orally discuss how part–total thinking helps to solve the problem. Read start unknown word problems, and write solution statements to put the answers in context. Orally discuss how the relationship between addition and subtraction can be used to find the unknown.
key_questions: How can a tape diagram help make sense of a word problem? How can part–total thinking and the relationship between addition and subtraction help find the unknown?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown."]
ad_full: [2.Mod2.AD1] Represent and solve one-step addition and subtraction word problem types within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.
laag: Students use part–total thinking and the relationship between addition and subtraction to solve add to with start unknown and take from with start unknown word problems. They use tape diagrams to represent the word problems.

title: Solve two-step word problems within 100.
objectives: Solve two-step word problems within 100.
i_can: I can solve a word problem that has more than one step.
language_objectives: Read a two-step word problem, and write solution statements to put the answers in context. Orally discuss different equations that represent the different parts of the problem.
key_questions: How do we solve a word problem with more than one step? How does a tape diagram help us make sense of a word problem?
ad_texts: ["This lesson supports 2.OA.A.1 and introduces two-step word problems. Its content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module."]
ad_full: This lesson supports 2.OA.A.1 and introduces two-step word problems. Its content is intended to serve as a formative assessment and is therefore not included on summative assessments in this module.
laag: Students represent and solve two-step word problems. They reason about the problem to determine an efficient strategy to find the unknowns. They solve a two-step problem that requires interpreting a graph.

title: Determine the defining attributes of a polygon.
objectives: Determine the defining attributes of a polygon.
i_can: I can describe the attributes of shapes.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions involving the terms closed shape, attribute, side, and angle to create and draw polygons. Orally justify whether a shape is a polygon by using the terms closed shape, side, and angle.
key_questions: What is a polygon?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.
laag: Students create closed shapes and examine common attributes of the shapes to determine the defining attributes of polygons. This lesson formalizes side, attribute, polygon, and geometry and introduces the terms angle and vertex.

title: Use attributes to identify, build, and describe two-dimensional shapes.
objectives: Use attributes to identify, build, and describe two-dimensional shapes.
i_can: I can name polygons and describe their attributes.
language_objectives: Orally determine a category in which three shapes belong, and justify why one shape does not belong by using the terms side and angle. Orally classify polygons as triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons based on the number of sides and angles.
key_questions: How are polygons named?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.", "Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes. [2.Mod3.AD5] Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
laag: Students build, identify, and group polygons, such as triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons, based on their attributes. This lesson formalizes the terms quadrilateral and pentagon.

title: Identify, build, and describe right angles and parallel lines.
objectives: Identify, build, and describe right angles and parallel lines.
i_can: I can describe right angles and parallel lines.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to identify right angles and parallel lines in two-dimensional shapes by using the terms side, angle, vertical, horizontal, and parallel.
key_questions: What are parallel lines and right angles?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.", "Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes. [2.Mod3.AD5] Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
laag: Students identify right angles and parallel lines in two-dimensional shapes and around the classroom. They build right angles and parallel lines to uncover how these attributes compose shapes and determine whether all shapes have them. This lesson introduces the term right angle and formalizes horizontal and vertical.

title: Use attributes to identify, classify, and compose different quadrilaterals.
objectives: Use attributes to identify, classify, and compose different quadrilaterals.
i_can: I can describe and compare quadrilaterals.
language_objectives: Orally compare and classify shapes based on common attributes, and use attributes to identify different types of quadrilaterals. Listen to and build on the reasoning of others, and justify whether a given shape is a square, a rectangle, a quadrilateral, or a parallelogram.
key_questions: How are quadrilaterals the same or different? How are quadrilaterals classified?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.", "Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes. [2.Mod3.AD5] Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
laag: Students build a variety of quadrilaterals and make comparisons based on their attributes. They recognize that some quadrilaterals can be classified under multiple names. For example, a square is also a parallelogram and a rectangle. This lesson formalizes the term parallelogram.

title: Relate the square to the cube and use attributes to describe a cube.
objectives: Relate the square to the cube and use attributes to describe a cube.
i_can: I can describe the attributes of a cube.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions involving the terms face, cube, and edge to compose a cube and determine its attributes. Orally compare two- and three-dimensional shapes to identify similarities and differences.
key_questions: How is a cube similar to and different from a square? What are the attributes of a cube?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.", "Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes. [2.Mod3.AD5] Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
laag: In this lesson, students compose a cube by building a square first. They determine the attributes of a cube and note the differences between a two-dimensional shape and a three-dimensional shape. Students strengthen their knowledge of a cube’s attributes by drawing one. This lesson formalizes the terms two-dimensional shape, three- dimensional shape, face, cube, and edge.

title: Recognize that a whole polygon can be decomposed into smaller parts and the parts can be composed to make a whole.
objectives: Recognize that a whole polygon can be decomposed into smaller parts and the parts can be composed to make a whole.
i_can: I can decompose polygons.
language_objectives: Listen to and engage with the reasoning of others to describe how smaller polygons can compose a larger polygon and how a larger polygon can be decomposed into smaller polygons. With a partner and as a class, orally relate the decomposition of a polygon to the decomposition of a number.
key_questions: How are polygons composed or decomposed?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.", "Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes. [2.Mod3.AD5] Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
laag: Students search for polygons within a hexagon. They share their findings and relate the decomposition of a polygon to the decomposition of a number.

title: Combine shapes to create a composite shape and create a new shape from composite shapes.
objectives: Combine shapes to create a composite shape and create a new shape from composite shapes.
i_can: I can compose and decompose polygons.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions to decompose a tangram into smaller polygons and to create composite shapes by using the smaller polygons. Listen to and evaluate a statement and support agreement or disagreement with a model.
key_questions: How do composite shapes show a part–total relationship?
ad_texts: ["Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes.", "Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD4] Recognize and draw shapes based on defining attributes. [2.Mod3.AD5] Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
laag: Students use a tangram puzzle to decompose a square into many smaller polygons. They compose the tangram pieces to recreate the square. The class collectively combines all of their squares to create the largest composite shape possible.

title: Create composite shapes by using equal parts and name them as halves, thirds, and fourths.
objectives: Create composite shapes by using equal parts and name them as halves, thirds, and fourths.
i_can: I can compose and decompose polygons by using equal parts.
language_objectives: Listen to a scenario about decomposing a square into smaller shapes to evaluate the accuracy of two statements and orally defend reasoning. Listen to and follow directions involving the terms equal parts, units, halves, thirds, fourths, quarters, and whole to compose fractional units.
key_questions: What are halves, thirds, and fourths? How do the number of parts a whole is partitioned into relate to the size of the parts?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and the shares by using the words describe halves, thirds, fourths, etc."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD6] Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and the shares by using the words describe halves, thirds, fourths, etc.
laag: Students use manipulatives to show halves, thirds, and fourths. They compare the fractional units and determine the relationship between the number of parts that compose a whole and the size of the parts. This lesson introduces the term thirds.

title: Interpret equal shares in composite shapes as halves, thirds, and fourths.
objectives: Interpret equal shares in composite shapes as halves, thirds, and fourths.
i_can: I can find halves, thirds, or fourths in composed and decomposed polygons.
language_objectives: Listen to scenarios about equal shares to evaluate the accuracy of two statements and orally defend reasoning. Listen to and follow directions to cover halves, thirds, and fourths of a whole polygon. Orally explain how the part of the whole that is covered determines the fraction of the whole.
key_questions: How are halves, thirds, and fourths seen in shapes?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and the shares by using the words describe halves, thirds, fourths, etc."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD6] Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and the shares by using the words describe halves, thirds, fourths, etc.
laag: Students cover specified parts of a whole by using different combinations of pattern blocks. They recognize that the part of the whole that is covered determines what fraction of the whole is shown.

title: Partition circles and rectangles into equal parts and describe those parts as halves.
objectives: Partition circles and rectangles into equal parts and describe those parts as halves.
i_can: I can partition circles and rectangles into halves.
language_objectives: In partners, listen to, represent, and solve a problem. Orally describe the model and the solution. Listen to and follow directions to partition circles and rectangles into halves, and orally explain how some halves can have different shapes. Orally evaluate a statement about equal parts to determine whether it is always, sometimes, or never true.
key_questions: How do you know when a shape is partitioned into halves? Why can halves of the same whole look different?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, thirds, fourths, etc."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD6] Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, thirds, fourths, etc.
laag: Students partition a rectangle into halves in various ways and recognize that halves of identical wholes need not have the same shape. They apply this thinking to partition circles into halves and learn that, unlike a rectangle, a circle partitioned into halves creates halves that are always the same shape.

title: Partition circles and rectangles into equal parts, and describe those parts as halves, thirds, or fourths.
objectives: Partition circles and rectangles into equal parts, and describe those parts as halves, thirds, or fourths.
i_can: I can partition circles and rectangles into halves, thirds, or fourths.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions to partition shapes, and write to label them as 1 whole, 1 half, 1 third, and 1 fourth. With a partner and as a class, orally predict what happens when a whole is partitioned multiple times. Generalize that more equal parts mean smaller units.
key_questions: What relationships do you notice between halves, thirds, and fourths? How does the number of equal parts of a whole relate to the size of the equal parts?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, thirds, fourths, etc."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD6] Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, thirds, fourths, etc.
laag: Students partition same-size rectangles and circles into halves, thirds, and fourths. They notice that, when the number of parts increases, the size of the parts decreases.

title: Describe a whole by the number of equal parts in halves, thirds, and fourths.
objectives: Describe a whole by the number of equal parts in halves, thirds, and fourths.
i_can: I can tell how many equal parts of the same type make 1 whole.
language_objectives: Listen to a problem to identify an error in partitioning and orally explain how to correct the error. Orally describe a whole by the number of equal parts by using the terms halves, thirds, and fourths.
key_questions: Why does it take a different number of halves, thirds, and fourths to make 1 whole?
ad_texts: ["Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, thirds, fourths, etc."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD6] Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares and describe the shares by using the words halves, thirds, fourths, etc.
laag: Students compose a whole by combining the known part (e.g., 1 fourth) with the unknown part (e.g., 3 fourths). They describe the whole by the number of equal parts within a shape. This lesson formalizes the term fraction.

title: Recognize that equal parts of an identical rectangle can be different shapes.
objectives: Recognize that equal parts of an identical rectangle can be different shapes.
i_can: I can see that equal parts of the same whole can be different shapes.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions to partition shapes and arrange the pieces. Orally explain that equal parts of the same whole can be different shapes.
key_questions: Can equal parts from the same whole be different shapes? Why?
ad_texts: ["Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD7] Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.
laag: Students determine whether different shapes from identical wholes can be equal. They realize that two parts from the same-size whole can be different shapes and still be equal parts.

title: Distinguish between a.m. and p.m.
objectives: Distinguish between a.m. and p.m.
i_can: I can tell the difference between a.m. and p.m.
language_objectives: Read and write on a timeline to plot daily events to distinguish between a.m. and p.m. Sequence a set of daily events and orally justify the sequence by using a.m. and p.m.
key_questions: What is the difference between a.m. and p.m.?
big_idea: Represent Data Seeing Fractions in Shapes
ad_texts: ["Label a given daily event as taking place in the a.m. or p.m.", "Relate units of time."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD3] Label a given daily event as taking place in the a.m. or p.m. [2.Mod3.AD8] Relate units of time.
laag: Students compare a variety of clocks and notice that there are only 12 numbers on a clock, despite there being 24 hours in a day. This ignites a reason to study the repetitive cycle of hours and minutes and creates a need for a method to determine which part of the day a time references. Students distinguish the difference between a.m. and p.m. and use a timeline to plot daily events.

title: Recognize time as measurement units.
objectives: Recognize time as measurement units.
i_can: I can relate units of time to daily activities.
language_objectives: Orally explain how smaller units of time compose larger units of time by using the terms seconds, minutes, and hours and support thinking with examples. Orally determine a category in which three activities belong, and use units of time to justify why one activity does not fit.
key_questions: How do smaller units of time compose larger units of time?
ad_texts: ["Relate units of time."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD8] Relate units of time.
laag: Students participate in activities to experience the length of various units of time. They recognize that 60 seconds compose 1 minute and that 60 minutes compose 1 hour. Students select the appropriate unit of time to use when using benchmarks to estimate the duration of a given activity. They build upon previous experiences with length measurement to generalize that the smaller the unit, the more units it takes to measure.

title: Use a clock to tell time to the half hour or quarter hour.
objectives: Use a clock to tell time to the half hour or quarter hour.
i_can: I can show a fraction of an hour on a clock.
language_objectives: Write an explanation about a problem involving time and use a clock to justify the response. Read, ask questions about, and critique the responses of others. Listen in order to partition a clock into halves and fourths, and orally relate fractions to time by using the terms quarter past, half past, and quarter to.
key_questions: How do fractions relate to telling time?
big_idea: Represent Data Seeing Fractions in Shapes
ad_texts: ["Tell and write time to the nearest 5 minutes on analog and digital clocks."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD2] Tell and write time to the nearest 5 minutes on analog and digital clocks.
laag: Students fold a circle into halves and then into fourths to relate fractional units to benchmark times on the clock. They transform a circle into a clock by adding a minute hand and an hour hand. Students move the minute hand to show quarter past, half past, and quarter to. This lesson formalizes the terms quarter past and quarter to.

title: Relate the clock to a number line to count by fives.
objectives: Relate the clock to a number line to count by fives.
i_can: I can tell time by relating a clock to a number line.
language_objectives: Analyze the time shown on four different clocks. Listen to and build on the reasoning of others to justify which clock shows a given time. Orally describe the relationship between skip-counting by fives on a clock and skip-counting on a number line.
key_questions: How is a clock similar to a number line?
big_idea: Represent Data Seeing Fractions in Shapes
ad_texts: ["Skip-count by fives.", "Tell and write time to the nearest 5 minutes on analog and digital clocks."]
ad_full: [2.Mod3.AD1] Skip-count by fives. [2.Mod3.AD2] Tell and write time to the nearest 5 minutes on analog and digital clocks.
laag: Students develop an understanding of time as a continuous unit of measure. They unravel the yarn they used to create a class clock, and discover the analog clock is part of a number line shaped into a circle. Students determine the similarities and differences between a clock and a number line and count by fives to tell time. The academic verb create is introduced in this lesson.

title: Tell time to the nearest 5 minutes.
objectives: Tell time to the nearest 5 minutes.
i_can: I can tell time to the nearest five minutes.
language_objectives: Write an explanation about a problem involving telling time, and read, ask questions about, and critique the responses of others. Listen to the critiques of others to revise a written explanation.
key_questions: How does the movement of the hour hand relate to the movement of minute hand?
ad_texts: ["by fives.", "Skip-count", "Tell and write time to the nearest 5 minutes on analog and digital clocks."]
ad_full: by fives. [2.Mod3.AD1] Skip-count [2.Mod3.AD2] Tell and write time to the nearest 5 minutes on analog and digital clocks.
laag: Students read an analog clock to the nearest 5 minutes and write the time. They move the hands on an analog clock to show times and notice how the hour hand moves in relation to the minute hand.

title: Solve elapsed time problems.
objectives: Solve elapsed time problems.
i_can: I can find how much time goes by from the start of an activity to the end.
language_objectives: In small groups, listen to and engage with the reasoning of others to solve an elapsed time problem and orally explain thinking. In small groups, read elapsed time word problems. Through listening and speaking, describe the meanings of the problems and possible strategies for solving them. Write a solution statement to put each answer in context.
key_questions: What strategies can we use to help solve elapsed time word problems?
ad_texts: ["This lesson extends the grade 2 work with telling and writing time and supports the work in grade 3. This content is intended to serve as an extension and therefore is not included on summative assessments in grade 2."]
ad_full: This lesson extends the grade 2 work with telling and writing time and supports the work in grade 3. This content is intended to serve as an extension and therefore is not included on summative assessments in grade 2.
laag: Students use the Read–Draw–Write process to solve elapsed time word problems. They share recordings, such as the arrow way and the open number line, and strategies, such as skip-counting, counting on, counting back, and using benchmark numbers.

title: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
objectives: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
i_can: I can organize and count a collection using groups of ones, tens, or hundreds.
language_objectives: Orally describe strategies to accurately count a collection of objects, including grouping by tens and hundreds. Listen to others to compare and connect strategies. Write a reflection to explain which strategies worked well and why.
key_questions: How can we use place value units to help us count and organize? Why can we mentally add and subtract 10 or 100 from numbers?
ad_texts: ["Mentally add 10 or 100 to any number 100\u2013900.", "Mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number 100\u2013900."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD8] Mentally add 10 or 100 to any number 100–900. [2.Mod4.AD9] Mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number 100–900.
laag: This lesson is an opportunity for students to show growth in their application of place value concepts. They organize, count, and represent items in a counting collection. Collections are intentionally chosen to promote mentally adding and subtracting 10 and 100 from the totals. Students record their work, analyze the work of others, and discuss efficient strategies as a class. Due to the time needed to count collections, the Fluency component, the Problem Set, and the Exit Ticket are not included in this lesson. Use classroom observations and student recordings to analyze student thinking.

title: Mentally add and subtract multiples of 10 and 100 with unknowns in various positions.
objectives: Mentally add and subtract multiples of 10 and 100 with unknowns in various positions.
i_can: I can add and subtract tens or hundreds in my head.
language_objectives: Orally reason about part–total relationships to find the unknown in various positions. Listen to clues involving place value to find an unknown and make equal expressions.
key_questions: How can we add and subtract tens and hundreds mentally?
ad_texts: ["Mentally add 10 or 100 to any number 100\u2013900.", "Mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number 100\u2013900."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD8] Mentally add 10 or 100 to any number 100–900. [2.Mod4.AD9] Mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number 100–900.
laag: Students use their place value understanding and known facts to mentally subtract tens and hundreds. They apply their understanding of part–total relationships to find the unknown in an equation by adding or subtracting tens and hundreds.

title: Solve multi-step word problems and reason about equal expressions.
objectives: Solve multi-step word problems and reason about equal expressions.
i_can: I can write equations to solve word problems that have more than one step.
language_objectives: Read multi-step word problems. Through listening and speaking in groups, discuss problems’ meanings and describe possible strategies for solving them. Orally analyze equations and reason about equality.
key_questions: How do tape diagrams help me write equations to solve problems? What makes equations true?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve addition and subtraction word problems within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.", "Mentally add 10 or 100 to any number 100\u2013900.", "Mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number 100\u2013900."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD1] Represent and solve addition and subtraction word problems within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown. [2.Mod4.AD8] Mentally add 10 or 100 to any number 100–900. [2.Mod4.AD9] Mentally subtract 10 or 100 from any number 100–900.
laag: Students solve multi-step word problems by using mental math strategies to add and subtract multiples of tens and hundreds. They work in groups to solve a two-step problem, analyze equations, and reason about equality.

title: Represent and solve compare with bigger unknown word problems.
objectives: Represent and solve compare with bigger unknown word problems.
i_can: I can use tape diagrams to understand and help solve comparison word problems.
language_objectives: Read word problems involving the relationships between quantities in compare with bigger unknown problems. Orally describe problems’ meanings and possible strategies for solving them, and listen to others describe their strategies. Write a solution statement to put the answer to each compare with bigger unknown word problem into context.
key_questions: How does a tape diagram help us understand comparison word problems? How does understanding the part–total relationship help us understand how to solve compare problems?
ad_texts: ["Represent and solve addition and subtraction word problems within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.", "Add fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD1] Represent and solve addition and subtraction word problems within 100 by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown. [2.Mod4.AD4] Add fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
laag: Students use the Read–Draw–Write process and draw tape diagrams to reason about the relationships between quantities in compare with bigger unknown word problems. They then work independently to solve a comparison word problem.

title: Use the associative property to make a benchmark number to add within 1,000.
objectives: Use the associative property to make a benchmark number to add within 1,000.
i_can: I can make a benchmark number to help me add.
language_objectives: Listen to and build on others’ ideas to reason about and analyze strategies to add within 1,000. Orally evaluate when using benchmark numbers is an efficient strategy.
key_questions: How can knowing partners to ten help you simplify addition problems that are harder to add in your head? How is making a benchmark number a useful simplifying strategy for some addition problems?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Explain why addition strategies work by using place value or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD4] Add fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod4.AD6] Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod4.AD10] Explain why addition strategies work by using place value or properties of operations.
laag: Students use benchmark numbers to simplify addition problems. They make the next ten or the next hundred to build capacity for mental addition. Students study the digits in problems and evaluate when this strategy is useful.

title: Use compensation to add within 1,000.
objectives: Use compensation to add within 1,000.
i_can: I can use compensation to add.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to use benchmark numbers to add efficiently within 1,000. Orally justify why the compensation strategy works.
key_questions: How is compensation a useful strategy for addition? How do you decide when to use compensation?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.", "Explain why addition strategies work by using place value or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD4] Add fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod4.AD6] Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations. [2.Mod4.AD10] Explain why addition strategies work by using place value or properties of operations.
laag: Students advance their understanding of compensation to add numbers within 1,000. They model their thinking by using an open number line and the arrow way. Students reason about and explain why the compensation strategy works.

title: Use concrete models to add and relate them to written recordings.
objectives: Use concrete models to add and relate them to written recordings.
i_can: I can add by using place value disks and vertical form.
language_objectives: Orally compare and relate a place value disk model to the written vertical form of addition. Orally describe how to show a new unit of ten by using place value models and written recordings.
key_questions: How does my written recording relate to how I model addition? How can I show a new unit with models and written recordings?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 20.", "Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD2] Add fluently within 20. [2.Mod4.AD6] Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students use place value disks to represent addition problems with up to two compositions and relate the disks to vertical written recordings.

title: Use place value drawings to represent addition and relate them to written recordings, part 1.
objectives: Use place value drawings to represent addition and relate them to written recordings, part 1.
i_can: I can use place value drawings to model addition and record my work in vertical form.
language_objectives: Through listening and speaking with a partner and as a class, compare place value drawings to written recordings and describe how the recordings are alike and different.
key_questions: How does the place value drawing relate to vertical form? How can I show a new unit in my drawing and in vertical form?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 20.", "Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD2] Add fluently within 20. [2.Mod4.AD6] Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students use place value drawings to represent addition. They relate their drawings to a vertical recording called new groups below. Students then add and record their work by using both drawings and new groups below.

title: Use place value drawings to represent addition and relate them to written recordings, part 2.
objectives: Use place value drawings to represent addition and relate them to written recordings, part 2.
i_can: I can use place value drawings to model addition and record my work in vertical form.
language_objectives: Through discussion with a partner and as a class, orally analyze place value drawings and written recordings to identify errors. Justify claims by orally describing how to show new units on place value drawings and written recordings.
key_questions: How do you know when you can compose a new unit? How does using place value drawings and new groups below help us add?
ad_texts: ["Add fluently within 20.", "Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations."]
ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD2] Add fluently within 20. [2.Mod4.AD6] Add within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, or properties of operations.
laag: Students add within 1,000 by using place value drawings to support their understanding of the vertical recording, new groups below.

title: Choose and defend efficient solution strategies for addition.
objectives: Choose and defend efficient solution strategies for addition.
i_can: I can use an efficient strategy to add.
language_objectives: Orally evaluate a statement about the most efficient way to add to determine whether the statement is always, sometimes, or never true. Orally analyze addition problems to determine the most efficient solution strategy and defend the chosen strategy orally and in writing.
key_questions: How does place value understanding help you choose an efficient addition strategy? How does vertical form help you add like units efficiently?

laag: Students use place value understanding to determine efficient addition strategies. After working independently to solve the problems, students share their work and defend the efficiency of their methods.

title: Choose and defend efficient strategies to add up to four two-digit numbers.
objectives: Choose and defend efficient strategies to add up to four two-digit numbers.
i_can: I can use an efficient strategy to add four two-digit numbers.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe solution strategies to find the total and to compare and connect the strategies. Orally defend the efficiency of a chosen strategy.
key_questions: How do you choose an efficient strategy when you add up to four two-digit numbers? How does place value understanding help you add up to four two-digit numbers?

ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD2] Add fluently within 20. [2.Mod2.AD2] Add up to 4 two-digit numbers by using strategies based on place value or properties of operations. [2.Mod4.AD10] Explain why addition strategies work by using place value or properties of operations.
laag: Students apply their understanding of various addition strategies to add up to four two-digit numbers. After students solve independently, they compare and make connections among two or three strategies and defend the efficiency of their choices.

title: Take from a ten or a hundred to subtract.
objectives: Take from a ten or a hundred to subtract.
i_can: I can take from a ten or a hundred to subtract.
language_objectives: Through listening and speaking with a partner and as a class, analyze solution samples to describe similarities and differences. key_questions: When do I take from a ten or take from a hundred? Why can I use addition to check my subtraction strategy?

laag: Students use the familiar strategy of take from a ten or a hundred to subtract within 1,000. They reason about when to use this strategy and how to decompose efficiently. Students relate subtraction to addition by using an addition strategy to check their subtraction strategy.

objectives: Use compensation to subtract within 1,000.
i_can: I can use compensation to subtract from a number greater than 200.
language_objectives: Listen to, orally discuss, and confirm predictions about the next step in a solution process. Construct viable arguments to support reasoning, and critique the reasoning of others. Orally generalize about when compensation is a useful strategy.
key_questions: When is compensation a useful subtraction strategy? How does compensation help make it easier to subtract?

ad_full: [2.Mod4.AD5] Subtract fluently within 100 by using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod4.AD7] Subtract within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction. [2.Mod4.AD11] Explain why subtraction strategies work by using place value or properties of operations.
laag: Students reason about how compensation can be used to subtract numbers within 1,000. They use benchmark numbers and models, such as the open number line and the arrow way, to show why the strategy works.

title: Use compensation to keep a constant difference by adding the same amount to both numbers.
objectives: Use compensation to keep a constant difference by adding the same amount to both numbers.
i_can: I can use compensation to subtract.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to compensate by adding the same amount to both numbers in a subtraction problem and use a number line to support thinking.
key_questions: Why does this compensation strategy work? When is this compensation strategy useful?
ad_texts: ["Subtract within 1,000 by using concrete models or drawings, strategies based on place value, properties of operations, or the relationship between addition and subtraction.", "Explain why subtraction strategies work by using place value or properties of operations."]

key_questions: What are equal groups? How do repeated addition equations relate to equal groups?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array Number Strategies

ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD1] Represent and solve word problems involving equal groups by using manipulatives and drawings. laag: Students determine equal groups and articulate how they know groups are equal. They write repeated addition equations to represent the equal groups abstractly. Students identify the total, the number of equal groups, or the number in each group in scenarios with unknowns. This lesson formalizes the terms equal groups and repeated addition.

title: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
objectives: Organize, count, and represent a collection of objects.
i_can: I can organize and count a collection.
language_objectives: Orally describe strategies used to accurately count a collection of pre-grouped objects. Listen to others to compare and connect strategies and to analyze their efficiency. Write a reflection to explain which strategies for counting the collection worked well and why.
key_questions: How does the size of the group help us count? How can we use the unit 10 to help us count?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array
ad_texts: ["Represent equal groups of up to 5 groups of 5 objects by using manipulatives or drawings and apply an addition strategy (such as counting on, skip-counting, or doubles) to find the total number of objects."]
ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD4] Represent equal groups of up to 5 groups of 5 objects by using manipulatives or drawings and apply an addition strategy (such as counting on, skip-counting, or doubles) to find the total number of objects.
laag: This lesson provides an opportunity for students to apply their understanding of place value, equal groups, and repeated addition as they organize, count, and represent counting collections where the items have been pregrouped. They analyze the work of others and discuss how equal groups help them count and write equations. Due to the time needed to count collections, an Exit Ticket is not included in this lesson. Use classroom observations and student recordings to analyze student thinking.

title: Use math drawings to represent equal groups and relate them to repeated addition.
objectives: Use math drawings to represent equal groups and relate them to repeated addition.
i_can: I can use a math drawing to show equal groups and write a matching repeated addition equation.
language_objectives: Orally determine a category in which three pictures of equal groups belong and justify why one picture does not belong by using the phrase groups of. Orally reason about composing two smaller equal groups into one larger group to add more efficiently.
key_questions: How do repeated addition equations relate to equal groups? How can I use a repeated addition equation to make equal groups?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array

ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD4] Represent equal groups of up to 5 groups of 5 objects by using manipulatives or drawings and apply an addition strategy (such as counting on, skip-counting, or doubles) to find the total number of objects.
laag: Students use manipulatives and drawings to show equal groups and write repeated addition equations. They reason about using doubles to compose 2 equal groups and add more efficiently.

language_objectives: Through listening and speaking with a partner and as a class, compare representations of equal groups and describe how the models are alike and different. Orally analyze the accuracy of an equation to represent an equal groups situation, and explain how to correct the equation.

laag: Students represent and solve a word problem with equal groups. They compare solution strategies and make connections between representations. Students transition from drawing equal groups to drawing a tape diagram, and they write a related repeated addition equation.

title: Compose arrays with rows and columns and use a repeated count to find the total.
objectives: Compose arrays with rows and columns and use a repeated count to find the total.
i_can: I can use arrays to organize equal groups of objects to find the total.
language_objectives: Articulate how an array is useful for counting a set of objects efficiently by using the terms row, column, and array. Orally evaluate a statement about unequal groups to determine whether it is always, sometimes, or never true.
key_questions: How does an array help us count a set of objects? How does an array show equal groups?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array

laag: Students organize equal groups into rows and columns to compose an array. They determine that the total remains the same even when the array is reorganized. Students articulate why it is useful to organize objects into an array. This lesson formalizes the terms row, column, and array.

title: Decompose arrays into rows and columns and relate them to repeated addition.
objectives: Decompose arrays into rows and columns and relate them to repeated addition.
i_can: I can decompose arrays into rows and columns and relate the rows and columns to repeated addition.

key_questions: How are arrays and repeated addition equations related? How is decomposing arrays similar to decomposing numbers?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array

laag: Students represent a problem with square tiles organized into an array. They describe the array by using both rows and columns and write a related repeated addition equation. Students remove columns and rows of an array and talk about how doing that changes the total.

title: Distinguish between rows and columns and use math drawings to represent arrays.
objectives: Distinguish between rows and columns and use math drawings to represent arrays.

Listen to and engage with the reasoning of others to identify different representations of equal groups with the same total.

ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD3] Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. laag: Students describe the equal groups in an array as rows and columns. They determine that the total number of tiles in an array stays the same when they rotate or rearrange it. However, when they add or subtract a row or column, the total changes. Students identify an equal group as a unit.

title: Use square tiles to create arrays with gaps.
objectives: Use square tiles to create arrays with gaps.
i_can: I can create arrays with gaps and write repeated addition equations to represent the total.
language_objectives: Listen to and follow directions to compose arrays that match a context, and explain why some tiles are left over. With a partner, orally construct a context to match a given array. In small groups and as a class, orally justify how the context relates to the array.
key_questions: Why is the repeated addition equation the same for an array with gaps and an array without gaps? What is the effect of describing an array by rows or by columns?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array
ad_texts: ["Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4)", "Represent equal groups of up to 5 groups of 5 objects by using manipulatives or drawings and apply an addition strategy (such as counting on, skip-counting, or doubles) to find the total number of objects."]
ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD3] Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4) [2.Mod6.AD4] Represent equal groups of up to 5 groups of 5 objects by using manipulatives or drawings and apply an addition strategy (such as counting on, skip-counting, or doubles) to find the total number of objects.
laag: Students arrange equal groups of tiles into rows and columns and write repeated addition equations to match each array. They decompose the array into rows or columns with no gaps between the tiles and reason whether the gaps change the total number of tiles in the array. Students construct scenarios to match a given array.

title: Determine the attributes of a square array.
objectives: Determine the attributes of a square array.
i_can: I can describe the attributes of a square array.
language_objectives: Orally compare rectangular and square arrays and generalize that only one repeated addition equation can represent a square array by using the terms number of rows, number of columns, and equal. Explain in writing whether it is possible to make a square array for a given number.
key_questions: What are the attributes of a square array?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array
ad_texts: ["Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4)"]
ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD3] Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4)
laag: Students build a rectangular array, identify the number of groups and the number in each group, and then write a repeated addition equation to represent the array. They build square arrays and recognize that only one repeated addition equation can be used to represent the array because the number of groups and the number of objects in each group is equal.

title: Use math drawings to compose a rectangle.
objectives: Use math drawings to compose a rectangle.
i_can: I can draw arrays to help solve problems.
language_objectives: Orally determine a category in which three things belong and justify why one does not fit by reasoning about arrays. Orally reason about how to compose a larger rectangle by using smaller units. Orally discuss how to use arrays to represent and solve word problems.
key_questions: How is an array related to a repeated addition equation? How does a math drawing show composition?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array
ad_texts: ["Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4)"]
ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD3] Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4)
laag: Students use a square tile to draw rectangular and square arrays. They reason about how they can compose a larger rectangle by using smaller units.

title: Decompose an array to find the total efficiently.
objectives: Decompose an array to find the total efficiently.
i_can: I can decompose arrays to find the total.
language_objectives: Read and write the parts and the total of an array in unit form in a number bond, and orally determine that a decomposed array is equal to its total. Orally compare and discuss the efficiency of decomposing an array into equal groups rather than decomposing it into groups that are not equal.
key_questions: How does decomposing an array help us find the total?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Squares in an Array
ad_texts: ["Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4)", "Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares."]
ad_full: [2.Mod6.AD3] Write a repeated addition equation to represent an array, including writing an equation to express an even number as the sum of two equal addends. (2.OA.C.3, 2.OA.C.4) [2.Mod6.AD5] Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares.
laag: Students decompose arrays into parts to help them find the total. They compare the efficiency of decomposing an array into two equal parts versus two parts that are not equal.

title: Reason about how equal arrays can be composed differently.
objectives: Reason about how equal arrays can be composed differently.
i_can: I can compose and decompose arrays in different ways and see that the total stays the same.
language_objectives: With a partner and as a class, listen to and engage with the reasoning of others to discuss how arrays with the same total can be composed in different ways. Orally construct viable arguments to analyze and compare work with a partner, and critique the reasoning of others.
key_questions: How can arrays with the same total be composed in different ways?
big_idea: Skip Counting to 100 Seeing Fractions in Shapes Squares in an Array
