Through teacher-led instruction and peer discussion, students learn how to write ratios and how to use ratio language to describe the relationship between two quantities. This lesson introduces the term ratio.

title: Ratios and Tape Diagrams
objectives: Write multiple ratios to describe the same situation. Represent ratios with tape diagrams.

language_objectives: Orally describe and write ratios to represent situations. Orally and in writing, explain what ratios represent in context.
key_questions: How can multiple ratios describe one situation? What are the important characteristics of tape diagrams that represent ratios?
big_idea: Fraction Relationships Patterns Inside Numbers Generalizing with Multiple Representations Relationships Between Variables Model the World

language_objectives: Orally explain how to solve an inequality. Orally and in writing, explain restrictions to the solution set of an inequality based on context.
key_questions: How is solving inequalities similar to solving equations? How is solving inequalities different from solving equations? How can we determine whether the context creates a restriction on the solution set?
ad_texts: ["Write inequalities that represent real-world or mathematical situations.", "Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form or where and are specific rational numbers.", "Interpret solution sets of inequalities in the contexts of word problems."]
ad_full: [7.Mod3.AD6] Write inequalities that represent real-world or mathematical situations. [7.Mod3.AD9] Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form or where and are specific rational numbers. [7.Mod3.AD11] Interpret solution sets of inequalities in the contexts of word problems.
laag: In this lesson, students use various techniques to determine possible values for that result in a rectangle having a greater perimeter than a square. A class discussion leads students to write an inequality that helps them determine the solution set more efficiently. Students work in pairs to solve two-step inequalities and graph the solution set for each. In revisiting the perimeter problem, they learn that in context, restrictions on the variable are often necessary. Students work with their partner to write and solve the inequality that models a given context, graph the solution set, and state any restrictions that must be placed on the solution set due to the context.

title: Solving Problems Involving Inequalities
objectives: Write and solve inequalities comparing px + q and r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers, and graph the solution sets. Write and solve inequalities to represent context problems and identify restrictions to their solution sets.
i_can: I can solve inequalities, graph the solution set, and explain restrictions to the solution set.
language_objectives: As a class, orally describe and compare algebraic and arithmetic strategies to solve a real-world problem. Model a situation with an inequality, and in writing, explain restrictions to the solution set based on the context.
key_questions: What steps can we take to make the inequality simpler before using if–then moves? Why are there restrictions to solution sets of inequalities?
ad_texts: ["Write inequalities that represent real-world or mathematical situations.", "Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form or where and are specific rational numbers.", "Interpret solution sets of inequalities in the contexts of word problems."]
ad_full: [7.Mod3.AD6] Write inequalities that represent real-world or mathematical situations. [7.Mod3.AD9] Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form or where and are specific rational numbers. [7.Mod3.AD11] Interpret solution sets of inequalities in the contexts of word problems.
laag: This lesson begins with students watching a video depicting a context that can be modeled by an inequality. A class discussion highlights both an arithmetic and an algebraic approach to solving the problem, as well as different ways to write an inequality. In pairs, students draw cards to determine the order in which they complete a set of inequality problems. Some problems in the set require students to consider the contexts and describe restrictions to the solution sets.

title: Inequalities vs. Equations
objectives: Determine whether a situation should be modeled with an equation or with an inequality. Write a context that can be modeled by a given inequality.
i_can: I can determine whether to model a situation with an equation or an inequality and then write and solve it.
language_objectives: Orally explain why a situation should be modeled with an equation or with an inequality. Listen to and orally critique other explanations. Describe orally and in writing how to change a situation so it can be represented by an equation instead of an inequality or vice versa. Listen to and orally critique other suggestions.
key_questions: How can we change a situation so it can be represented with an inequality instead of an equation or represented with an equation instead of an inequality?
ad_texts: ["Write equations that represent real-world or mathematical situations.", "Write inequalities that represent real-world or mathematical situations.", "Interpret solution sets of inequalities in the contexts of word problems."]
ad_full: [7.Mod3.AD5] Write equations that represent real-world or mathematical situations. [7.Mod3.AD6] Write inequalities that represent real-world or mathematical situations. [7.Mod3.AD11] Interpret solution sets of inequalities in the contexts of word problems.
laag: In this lesson, students sort cards with contexts into two categories: model with an inequality and model with an equation. As a class, and then in groups of three, students describe how they would change each situation to fit into the other category. They work in groups to write contexts for given inequalities. Individually, students write a situation that a partner must model with an equation or inequality and then solve. Then they analyze their partner’s work.

title: Sketching, Drawing, and Constructing Geometric Figures
objectives: Construct geometric figures with given conditions. Construct geometric figures by using technology.
i_can: I can construct geometric figures with a given length or angle measure.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to use tools to draw and construct geometric figures.
key_questions: How can we construct a figure with a given length or angle measure?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.
laag: This lesson begins with students sketching a mandala and then geometric figures. In doing so, they realize the limitations of not using tools. Then they are provided with rulers, protractors, and notecards so they can accurately construct the same geometric figures. Students transition to constructing the geometric figures by using technology.

title: Constructing Parallelograms and Other Quadrilaterals
objectives: Construct parallelograms and other quadrilaterals, given conditions.
i_can: I can construct parallelograms and other quadrilaterals with given conditions.
language_objectives: With a partner, orally discuss and describe how to construct quadrilaterals with given conditions. Orally describe how to use patty paper to show that figures are identical.
key_questions: Which quadrilateral is the most challenging to construct? Why?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.
laag: This lesson begins with students examining a tessellation and trying to draw it. Students identify parallelograms in the tessellation, and they realize they need to know how to construct parallelograms before they can draw the tessellation. By using knowledge of how to construct geometric figures, students construct a parallelogram and then, more specifically, a rhombus. Students mark the figures to indicate parallel sides and side lengths with the same measure. By sorting cards that show different quadrilaterals, students review the characteristics of quadrilaterals. They then construct various quadrilaterals with given conditions.

title: Side Lengths of a Triangle
objectives: Determine whether a triangle with three given side lengths exists. Determine the relationship between the sum of two side lengths of a triangle and its third side length.
i_can: I can determine whether a triangle can be formed with three given side lengths.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, justify whether a triangle can be formed with three given side lengths.
key_questions: Can we make a triangle with any three side lengths? How are the three side lengths of a triangle related?
big_idea: 2D and 3D Connections Shapes in the World
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.", "Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. [7.Mod4.AD2] Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
laag: Students ponder whether a triangle can be formed with any three side lengths. Students investigate by trying to form triangles out of various lengths of uncooked spaghetti. They determine that a triangle cannot always be formed with three given side lengths. Looking to identify a relationship among the side lengths, students generate sample side lengths and predict whether a triangle can be formed with those lengths. Students test their predictions by using spaghetti. They determine that for three side lengths to form a triangle, the sum of any two side lengths must be greater than the third side length. Students use what they know about distances to justify their thinking, and they use this new learning to solve problems.

title: Angles of a Triangle
objectives: Determine whether a triangle can be formed with two given angle measures.
i_can: I can determine whether a triangle can be formed with given angle measures.
language_objectives: Write a conjecture about when a triangle can be formed with two given angle measures. Explain orally and in writing whether a triangle can be formed with two given angle measures.
key_questions: Can we form a triangle with two angles of any measure?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.", "Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. [7.Mod4.AD2] Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
laag: Students copy angles onto patty paper and try to form a triangle with three given angle measures. When they determine that a triangle cannot always be formed with three given angle measures, students embark on an exploration in which they try to form triangles by using two given angle measures and a line segment. Through this exploration, students form a conjecture about when a triangle can be formed with two given angle measures. After a discussion, they modify their conjecture to state that a triangle can be formed when two given angle measures sum to less than Students apply this discovery to determine whether a triangle can be formed with two given angle measures. In cases where a triangle can be formed, students construct the triangle, measure the third angle of the triangle, and compare their results.

title: Constructing Quadrilaterals and Triangles
objectives: Construct quadrilaterals given four side lengths and determine whether a unique quadrilateral is formed. Construct triangles given three side lengths and determine whether a unique triangle is formed.
i_can: I can determine when a unique quadrilateral or a unique triangle is formed.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, explain whether a quadrilateral constructed from four given side lengths is unique. Orally and in writing, explain whether a triangle constructed from three given side lengths is unique.
key_questions: How can we check to see whether we have identical figures? Given four side lengths, can we be sure that the quadrilateral we create with these side lengths is unique? Given three side lengths, can we be sure that the triangle we create with these side lengths is unique?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. (7.G.A.2) conditions that", "Recognize determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. (7.G.A.2) conditions that [7.Mod4.AD2] Recognize determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
laag: In this lesson, students construct quadrilaterals and triangles with given side lengths. After each construction, students compare their quadrilateral or triangle with those constructed by their classmates. When students construct equilateral quadrilaterals and equilateral triangles, they observe that the triangles appear to be identical, but the quadrilaterals do not. Through observation and discussion, students realize that they cannot construct a unique quadrilateral knowing only the four side lengths, but that they can construct a unique triangle knowing only the three side lengths. If time allows, students continue to construct triangles that meet specific conditions, including side lengths and angle measurements, and then make observations about the uniqueness of their constructions.

title: Unique Triangles
objectives: Determine that at least three conditions are needed to guarantee a unique triangle. Determine that three angle measures alone do not guarantee a unique triangle.
i_can: I can determine conditions needed to guarantee a unique triangle.
language_objectives: Orally describe the number of conditions and the types of conditions that guarantee a unique triangle. Determine whether a triangle is unique and explain the reasoning in writing.
key_questions: What number of conditions and what types of conditions guarantee a unique triangle?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. (7.G.A.2) conditions that", "Recognize determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. (7.G.A.2) conditions that [7.Mod4.AD2] Recognize determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
laag: This lesson begins with students determining whether triangles are identical by using patty paper to overlap them. Students then explore the minimum number of conditions needed to guarantee a unique triangle, and they realize they need more than one or two conditions. After creating triangles with the same three angle measures, students determine that three angle measures is not enough information to guarantee a unique triangle.

title: Two Angles and One Side
objectives: Determine whether two angle measures and an included side length guarantee a unique triangle. Determine whether two angle measures and a non-included side length guarantee a unique triangle.
i_can: I can determine sets of conditions needed to guarantee a unique triangle.
language_objectives: Orally describe the difference between an included side and a non-included side relative to two angles of a triangle. Orally and in writing, explain when two angles and one side length guarantee a unique triangle.
key_questions: Which sets of three conditions guarantee a unique triangle?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.", "Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. [7.Mod4.AD2] Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
laag: In this lesson, students continue to explore which sets of three conditions are needed to determine a unique triangle. Students examine whether a unique triangle can be formed given two angle measures and a side length. They test two cases: when the given measures relate to two angle measures and the included side length, and when the given measures relate to two angle measures and a non-included side length. Students use patty paper as a tool for exploring whether a triangle can be constructed under the given conditions. They also use it to compare triangles to find out whether they have constructed a unique one. Students determine that when two angle measures and an included side length are given, a unique triangle is formed, but when two angle measures and a non-included side are given, two triangles can be constructed.

title: Two Sides and One Angle
objectives: Determine whether two side lengths and an included angle measure guarantee a unique triangle. Determine whether two side lengths and a non-included angle measure guarantee a unique triangle.
i_can: I can determine whether a unique triangle can be constructed when given two side lengths and either an included angle or a non-included angle.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, explain when two side lengths and one angle measure guarantee a unique triangle.
key_questions: Given two side lengths and an included angle measure, is it guaranteed that a unique triangle is formed? Given two side lengths and a non-included angle measure, is it guaranteed that a unique triangle is formed?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.", "Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions. [7.Mod4.AD2] Recognize conditions that determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
laag: In this lesson, students construct triangles with two given side lengths and a given angle measure. Students explore two cases to examine whether two side lengths and one angle measure guarantee a unique triangle. When students construct a triangle with two given side lengths and the included angle measure, they determine that a unique triangle is guaranteed. When students construct a triangle with two given side lengths and a non-included angle measure, they determine that a unique triangle is not guaranteed. Students apply their new understanding by determining whether a unique triangle can be formed with given conditions.

title: Constructing a Circle
objectives: Define and construct circles given a radius or a diameter.
i_can: I can construct a circle given a radius or diameter.
language_objectives: Through speaking, listening, and writing with a partner, generate a definition of a circle. Orally describe measurements of a circle and characteristics of a semicircle, a quarter circle, and concentric circles.
key_questions: How can we accurately draw or construct a circle?
ad_texts: ["Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD1] Construct geometric shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles) with given conditions.
laag: The lesson begins with students revisiting triangles that can be created from only two given side lengths. With the aid of a digital interactive, they see what happens when one of the given sides of a constructed triangle is fixed and the other side is freely moved about their common vertex. They observe that a vertex of the triangle follows the path of a circle. Students sketch a circle and then watch two videos of people sketching circles to try to replicate those strategies. After being introduced to a compass, students construct circles, half-circles, quarter-circles, and concentric circles. This lesson introduces the terms radius and diameter and formalizes the term circle.

title: The Outside of a Circle
objectives: Describe the relationship between the circumference and diameter of any circle as a proportional relationship. Find the approximate circumference of a circle by using the value as the constant of proportionality. 3.1
i_can: I can describe the proportional relationship between circumference and diameter and use this relationship to find the approximate circumference of a circle.
language_objectives: Orally describe the relationship between the circumference and the diameter of a circle.
key_questions: How can we measure the distance around a circle? What is the relationship between the circumference and the diameter?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD4] Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle.
laag: The lesson begins with students trying to measure the distance around a circle with a ruler and then with a piece of string. The class discusses the differences in the measurements and the difficulties each method of measuring poses. In groups, students select circular- based items found in the classroom to measure. They use string to measure the diameter of the base and the distance around the base, and then they discuss the relationship between the measurements. Through an interactive, students examine the values of ratios and recognize that the distance around the circle and the diameter are in a proportional relationship. Students use an approximation for the constant of proportionality, to write an equation. They use this equation to find the approximate circumference of a circle given a radius or diameter and to find the approximate diameter given the circumference. This lesson introduces the term circumference.

title: The Inside of a Circle
objectives: Estimate the area of a circle.
i_can: I can estimate the area of a circle.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, explain how to estimate the area of a circle.
key_questions: How can we use what we know about finding the area of a polygon to estimate the area of a circle? Is the estimate for the area of a circle more accurate when the units are larger or smaller? Why?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD4] Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle.
laag: Students begin this lesson by examining different polygons with the same area. Then they estimate the areas of figures with curved sides by using the grid on the coordinate plane. Students extend this thinking to estimate the area of a circle. Students realize that a grid with smaller units enables a more accurate estimate of an area. Students find the area of the largest possible polygon that fits inside a circle. Then they find the area of the smallest possible polygon that goes beyond the boundary of the circle. Students reason that the area of the circle must be between the areas of these two polygons. They use the two areas to estimate the area of the circle.

title: Exploring the Area and Circumference of a Circle
objectives: Model and describe the relationship between the circumference and the area of a circle.
i_can: I can model and describe the relationship between the circumference and the area of a circle.
language_objectives: Orally describe the difference between finding the exact circumference of a circle and finding the approximate circumference of the circle. Orally describe the relationship between the circumference and the area of a circle.
key_questions: What is the relationship between the circumference and the area of a circle? What is the difference between finding the exact circumference of a circle and finding the approximate circumference of the circle?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle.", "Describe how the circumference and area of circles are related."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD4] Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle. [7.Mod4.AD5] Describe how the circumference and area of circles are related.
laag: Through a digital interactive, students realize that their constant of proportionality relating circumference and diameter is not exact. This drives the need for an exact constant, pi. After pi is introduced, students find the circumference of a circle. In pairs, students explore the area of a circle by cutting it into pieces and arranging the pieces into a rectangular shape. In a second interactive, students notice that as the circle is cut into more pieces, the rearrangement of the pieces appears more like a rectangle. They conjecture that the area can be determined by multiplying the length of the rectangular region by its width, and they calculate the area of a circle by using this approach. This lesson formalizes the term pi.

title: Finding Areas of Circular Regions
objectives: Solve problems by using the formula for the area of a circle. Model and describe the relationship between the areas of circles and the areas of semicircular and quarter-circular regions.
i_can: I can find the area and approximate area of semicircular and quarter-circular regions.
language_objectives: Develop a formula for the area of a circle and orally justify the process. Orally describe the relationship between the areas of circles and the areas of semicircular and quarter-circular regions.
key_questions: Is it possible to find the area of a circle without relating its area to a rectangular shape? How? How can we use what we know about the area of a circle to find the areas of semicircular and quarter-circular regions?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle.", "Describe how the circumference and area of circles are related."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD4] Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle. [7.Mod4.AD5] Describe how the circumference and area of circles are related.
laag: Students build on their understanding of how the circumference and the area of a circle are related to develop a formula for the area of a circle, By using this formula, students find the areas of circles, and they find the approximate areas by substituting a value for Students recall that quarter-circles are one-fourth of a circle and semicircles are half of a circle with the same radius. They use this understanding to find the areas of these figures by calculating the area of the circle and then multiplying by or .

title: Composite Figures with Circular Regions
objectives: Solve problems involving area and perimeter of composite figures.
i_can: I can solve problems involving the area and perimeter of composite figures.
language_objectives: Listen to and orally describe strategies to solve problems involving area and perimeter of composite figures.
key_questions: What makes a composite figure different from other figures for which we have found the perimeter and the area?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle.", "Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area of two-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, and polygons."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD4] Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle. [7.Mod4.AD6] Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area of two-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, and polygons.
laag: In this lesson, students analyze a complex geometric figure and discuss strategies to decompose it into familiar shapes. Then students work in groups to complete a sequence of perimeter and area problems based on composite figures. As they do, they use decomposition strategies to make simpler problems. Groups present their strategies and discuss solution pathways.

title: Watering a Lawn
objectives: Model a situation by using rectangular, circular, semicircular, and quarter-circular regions and calculate area to solve problems.
i_can: I can use what I know about area to model a situation.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to calculate the areas of rectangles, circles, semicircular regions, and quarter-circular regions by modeling a real-world situation.
key_questions: What factors are important when designing a plan to water an area? How can we use what we know about area to assess the efficiency of our models?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD4] Solve problems involving area and circumference of a circle.
laag: In this modeling lesson, students model the problem of designing an efficient plan to water a lawn. After watching videos of how different sprinklers move, students design a sprinkler system for a lawn. They assess the effectiveness of their design by using what they know about area. This lesson introduces the term design.

title: Solving Area Problems by Composition and Decomposition
objectives: Calculate the area of composite figures in real-world and mathematical problems by using composition and decomposition.
i_can: I can use composition to find the area of figures.
language_objectives: Orally compare composition and decomposition as strategies to calculate the areas of composite figures. Orally and in writing, explain how to use composition or decomposition to calculate the area of a composite figure.
key_questions: How can we use the information from a figure labeled with some measurements to find unknown lengths? When would we use decomposition to find area? When would we use composition to find area?
big_idea: Angle Relationships Shapes in the World
ad_texts: ["Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area of two-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, and polygons."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD6] Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area of two-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, and polygons.
laag: In this lesson, students apply what they know about familiar shapes to find the area of an irregular shape that resembles the front view of a bridge. They discover that composing a figure around it is helpful for finding its area. Students use decomposition and composition to find the areas of composite figures, and then they compare their strategies. While working with a stop sign, which is in the form of a regular shape, students determine they can decompose regular polygons into identical triangles to find their area.

title: Surface Area of Right Rectangular and Right Triangular Prisms
objectives: Calculate the surface area of right rectangular and right triangular prisms.
i_can: I can find the surface area of right rectangular prisms and right triangular prisms.
language_objectives: Write a description of a right prism. Orally describe strategies to calculate the surface areas of right rectangular prisms and right triangular prisms.
key_questions: How does a net of a geometric solid help us understand how to calculate the surface area of the solid? What strategies can we use to find the surface area of a right rectangular prism? What strategies can we use to find the surface area of a right triangular prism?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD7] Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.
laag: After watching a video of speed gift wrapping, students consider what the piece of wrapping paper would look like if it perfectly wrapped the outside of the box without overlap. Students use a two-dimensional net to represent the surface area of a three- dimensional solid. Then they decompose the net to help them find the surface area of the given prism. Students practice finding surface areas of right rectangular and right triangular prisms and look for efficient strategies for finding the surface area of prisms. Students build on their informal definition of right prism from previous grades and use that definition to learn how to name prisms based on their bases. This lesson formalizes the term lateral face.

title: Surface Area of Right Prisms
objectives: Calculate the surface area of right prisms by determining an efficient strategy for finding the sum of the areas of the lateral faces and bases.
i_can: I can find the surface area of right prisms by finding the sum of the areas of the lateral faces and bases.
language_objectives: Describe orally and in writing how to find the areas of the lateral faces of any right prism. Orally compare strategies to calculate the surface area of a right prism.
key_questions: What strategies can we use to find the area of the lateral faces of right prisms?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD7] Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.
laag: Students begin by finding the area of the lateral faces of a right nonregular hexagonal prism by calculating the area of each lateral face and adding them together, motivating the need for a more efficient strategy. Through class discussion, partner work, and an interactive, students realize they can find the area of the lateral faces by multiplying the height of the right prism by the perimeter of one of its bases. As a class, students compare these two strategies for finding the surface area of a right prism. In groups, students find the surface area of various right prisms.

title: Surface Area of Cylinders (Optional)
objectives: Calculate the surface area of right circular cylinders.
i_can: I can find the surface area of right circular cylinders.
language_objectives: Orally compare calculating the exact surface area with calculating the approximate surface area of a right circular cylinder. Through speaking, listening, and writing within groups, solve problems by calculating a right circular cylinder’s approximate surface area and lateral surface area.
key_questions: How is finding the surface area of a cylinder like finding the surface area of a prism? How is it different? How can we use nets to understand how to find the surface area of a cylinder?
ad_texts: ["Extension"]
ad_full: Extension
laag: Students contemplate how to calculate the surface area of a cylindrical object. With a partner, students form a net of a cylindrical object by wrapping it in paper with no overlaps. Students label the bases, height, and lateral surface on the paper before unwrapping it. The net reveals that a cylinder’s surface consists of two circular regions and a rectangular region. Students realize that the rectangular region represents the lateral surface, which has a width equal to the height of the cylinder and a length equal to the circumference of a base of the cylinder. Students use their understanding of a cylinder’s net to calculate its surface area. This lesson introduces the term lateral surface.

title: Surface Area of Right Pyramids
objectives: Calculate the surface area of right pyramids.
i_can: I can find the surface area of right pyramids.
language_objectives: Orally differentiate between the height and slant height of a right pyramid. Orally compare calculating the surface area of a pyramid with calculating the surface area of a right prism.
key_questions: How is finding the surface area of a pyramid different from finding the surface area of a prism? How does slant height differ from the height of a right pyramid?
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD7] Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.
laag: The lesson begins with students analyzing different geometric solids and deciding which one doesn’t belong. An interactive allows students to identify the key features of a pyramid that are used when sketching a net of the pyramid. By using the net, students find the surface area of the pyramid. Students analyze another pyramid and discuss which measurements are needed to find the surface area without creating a net. In groups, students calculate the surface area of various right pyramids. This lesson builds on students’ prior informal descriptions of pyramids to formally define them. This lesson also introduces the term slant height.

title: Surface Area of Other Solids
objectives: Calculate the surface area of solids composed of right prisms and right pyramids.
i_can: I can find the surface area of solids composed of right prisms and right pyramids.
language_objectives: Explain orally why the surface area of a composite solid is not the sum of the surface areas of the solids that compose it. Orally share strategies to calculate the surface areas of solids composed of right prisms and right pyramids.
key_questions: Is there more than one way to find the surface area of composite solids? Explain. When a solid is composed of cubes, can we find the surface area of the solid by finding the surface area of one cube and multiplying it by the number of cubes? Explain.
ad_texts: ["Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms."]
ad_full: [7.Mod4.AD7] Solve problems involving volume and surface area of three- dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.

They discuss the common error of forgetting to include the additional surface area created when a solid has a hole or cut out section.

Because the corresponding lengths in a scale drawing are in a proportional relationship, students can find an unknown side length of a cross section of a solid that is a scale drawing of the solid’s base.

By using familiar strategies for solving proportional relationship problems, students solve real-world problems for various pay structures. Students return to the original job offer problem and, as a class, make reasonable assumptions about unknown quantities in the situation. With a partner, students use these assumptions to determine which job offer results in the greatest expected earnings per week.

With a partner, they calculate fees and determine the rate as a percentage charged for a given fee. Students revisit the credit card situation and, given different purchase amounts, determine when the cash back amount is greater than the fees incurred.

Students lack the terminology to describe the translation precisely, which drives the need for a vector. After the class learns to precisely use a transparency for translations, students apply translations to the plane and find the images of points, segments, lines, and figures under the translation. Through observation and discussion, students articulate the properties of translations before participating in an Always Sometimes Never routine to formalize these observations. This lesson formally defines the terms vector and translation.

title: Reflections
objectives: Apply reflections to the plane. Identify the basic properties of reflections.
i_can: I can draw the image of a figure under a reflection across a given line.
language_objectives: Through listening to and speaking with a partner, identify the information needed to describe a reflection. Orally describe features and properties of reflections.
key_questions: Are reflections rigid motions? Why? What information do we need to apply reflections?
ad_texts: ["Verify experimentally the properties of translations, reflections, and rotations. (8.G.A.1, 8.G.A.1.a, 8.G.A.1.b, 8.G.A.1.c)"]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD1] Verify experimentally the properties of translations, reflections, and rotations. (8.G.A.1, 8.G.A.1.a, 8.G.A.1.b, 8.G.A.1.c)
laag: In this lesson, students classify cards with diagrams of translations and another rigid motion that is not a translation. Students recognize the other rigid motion as a reflection and describe the properties they notice. Students work in pairs to refine their precision of language by describing translations and reflections with sentence frames. Then students independently apply reflections by using a transparency. This lesson formally defines the term reflection.

title: Translations and Reflections on the Coordinate Plane
objectives: Apply translations and reflections on the coordinate plane. Use coordinates to describe the location of an image under a translation or a reflection.
i_can: I can use coordinates to describe the location of an image under a translation or a reflection.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe how to apply translations and reflections on the coordinate plane.
key_questions: How are translations and reflections on the coordinate plane the same as translations and reflections without the coordinate plane? How is the coordinate plane helpful for precisely describing a translation or reflection?
ad_texts: ["Use coordinates to describe the effect of translations, reflections, and rotations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD4] Use coordinates to describe the effect of translations, reflections, and rotations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students use their understanding of translations and reflections to explore both rigid motions on the coordinate plane. Students use a coordinate plane as a tool to describe a translation, similar to using a vector in the plane. Then they expand their study to include reflections by analyzing and precisely describing reflections across the - and -axes.

title: Rotations
objectives: Apply rotations to the plane. Identify the basic properties of rotations.
i_can: I can draw the image of a figure under a rotation around a given point.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe the features and properties of rotations.
key_questions: Are rotations rigid motions? Why? What information do we need to apply rotations?
ad_texts: ["Verify experimentally the properties of translations, reflections, and rotations. (8.G.A.1, 8.G.A.1.a, 8.G.A.1.b, 8.G.A.1.c)"]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD1] Verify experimentally the properties of translations, reflections, and rotations. (8.G.A.1, 8.G.A.1.a, 8.G.A.1.b, 8.G.A.1.c)
laag: In this lesson, students rely on previous work with circles to develop an intuitive understanding of rotation as a rigid motion. By trying to describe a rotation, students naturally develop the need for precise language about rotations. Students use transparencies to apply rotations and identify the basic properties of rotations. This lesson formally defines the term rotation.

title: Rotations on the Coordinate Plane
objectives: Apply rotations around the origin on the coordinate plane. Use coordinates to describe the location of an image under a rotation around the origin.
i_can: I can use coordinates to describe the location of an image under a rotation.
language_objectives: Orally describe the relationship between the coordinates of a point and the coordinates of its image under a rotation around the origin. In writing, summarize the cases in which a rotation maps a given line to a line parallel to it.
key_questions: How are rotations on the coordinate plane the same as rotations without the coordinate plane? How is the coordinate plane helpful for precisely describing a rotation?
ad_texts: ["Use coordinates to describe the effect of translations, reflections, and rotations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD4] Use coordinates to describe the effect of translations, reflections, and rotations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students build on their previous experience of rotations as a rigid motion to apply rotations of and around the origin on the coordinate plane. Students utilize the structure the coordinate plane provides to describe exact locations of a point and its image by using coordinates. They delve deeper into rotations of to identify patterns in the relationship between the coordinates of a point and the coordinates of its image. Students also engage in the Always Sometimes Never routine to explore whether a line maps onto a line parallel to it under a rotation of around the origin.

title: Working Backward
objectives: Precisely describe the rigid motion required to map an image back onto its original figure.
i_can: I can precisely describe how to map an image back onto its original figure.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe rigid motions that map images back onto their original figures.
key_questions: How can we describe a rigid motion that maps an image back onto its original figure? In what situations would we want to describe how to map an image back onto its original figure?
ad_texts: ["Verify experimentally the properties of translations, reflections, and rotations. (8.G.A.1, 8.G.A.1.a, 8.G.A.1.b, 8.G.A.1.c)", "Describe a sequence of translations, reflections, and rotations that exhibits the congruence between two given figures."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD1] Verify experimentally the properties of translations, reflections, and rotations. (8.G.A.1, 8.G.A.1.a, 8.G.A.1.b, 8.G.A.1.c) [8.Mod2.AD3] Describe a sequence of translations, reflections, and rotations that exhibits the congruence between two given figures.
laag: This lesson applies what students know about rigid motions and sets a foundation for understanding sequences of rigid motions. Through the Take a Stand routine, students are introduced to the concept of reversing a rigid motion that has been applied to a figure. Students compare the rigid motion that maps a figure to its image with the rigid motion that maps the image back onto its figure. By using observation and discussion, students conclude that each rigid motion can be undone. Then students draw a figure, apply a rigid motion, and use precise language to describe how to map the image back onto its original figure.

title: Sequencing the Rigid Motions
objectives: Describe a sequence of rigid motions that maps one figure onto another. Determine that the properties of individual rigid motions also apply for a sequence of rigid motions.
i_can: I can use a sequence of rigid motions to describe how to map another. one figure onto
language_objectives: Orally analyze how to determine a sequence of rigid motions that maps a figure onto its image.
key_questions: Do sequences of rigid motions have the same properties as individual rigid motions?

laag: In this lesson, students explore sequences of rigid motions by applying and describing rigid motions that map a figure onto its image. Students are first challenged to map one figure onto another with only one rigid motion, which motivates the need for sequences of rigid motions. After applying sequences of rigid motions and examining their properties, students determine a sequence of rigid motions that maps a given figure onto its image.

title: Ordering Sequences of Rigid Motions
objectives: Determine whether the order in which a sequence of rigid motions is applied matters.

language_objectives: Orally discuss whether the order in which a sequence of rigid motions is applied affects the location of the figure’s image.
key_questions: Does the order matter when applying a sequence of rigid motions? Why?

ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD2] Recognize that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rigid motions. [8.Mod2.AD4] Use coordinates to describe the effect of translations, reflections, and rotations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, student pairs work with different sequences of rigid motions to determine whether the order of a sequence affects the location of the image. In a gallery walk, students study the sequences of other pairs to find that the order matters in most of the sequences provided. Students then try to find sequences where the order does not matter. They conclude that the order matters when applying a sequence of rigid motions, except on rare occasions. Students learn the importance of applying a sequence in the given order to ensure that they find the correct location of the image of a figure.

title: Congruent Figures
objectives: Describe a sequence of rigid motions that maps one figure onto a congruent figure.
i_can: I can precisely describe a sequence of rigid motions that maps figure. one figure onto another
language_objectives: With a partner, write a sequence of rigid motions that maps a given figure onto a congruent figure. Listen to and orally analyze different sequences of rigid motions to determine whether they correctly map a given figure onto a congruent figure.
key_questions: What does it mean for two figures to be congruent? What is a strategy we can use for finding a sequence of rigid motions to map one figure onto a congruent figure?
ad_texts: ["Describe a sequence of translations, reflections, and rotations that exhibits the congruence between two given figures."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD3] Describe a sequence of translations, reflections, and rotations that exhibits the congruence between two given figures.
laag: In this lesson, students try to apply a sequence of rigid motions in which vectors, centers of rotation, and lines of reflection are not given. A discussion leads students to conclude that descriptions of sequences are clearest when figures share a point or segment. They immediately apply this knowledge to describe a sequence of rigid motions that maps a figure onto a congruent figure by first mapping a corresponding point or side. Students share these descriptions with a partner who asks clarifying questions to ensure that the descriptions are as replicable and precise as possible. This lesson formally defines the term congruent.

title: Showing Figures Are Congruent
objectives: Show figures are congruent by describing a sequence of rigid motions that maps one figure onto the other.
i_can: I can use rigid motions to show whether two figures are congruent.
language_objectives: Individually and with a partner, write, read, and orally critique arguments about the congruence of two figures.
key_questions: How do we show that two figures are congruent?
ad_texts: ["Recognize that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rigid motions."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD2] Recognize that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rigid motions.
laag: Students begin this lesson by analyzing an optical illusion and determining whether the figures in the illusion are congruent. They use rigid motions to show whether two given figures are congruent by using precise descriptions. Then students examine congruence in a historical context by analyzing patterns in traditional Navajo weavings. Students create their own pattern with sequences of rigid motions and precisely describe sequences of rigid motions within the pattern.

title: Lines Cut by a Transversal
objectives: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the angles created when pairs of lines are cut by a transversal.
i_can: I can describe the relationships between the angles that are formed when a line intersects two parallel lines.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe the angle relationships formed by a pair of lines cut by a transversal. Orally and in writing, explain why certain angle pairs formed by parallel lines cut by a transversal are congruent.
key_questions: When two lines are cut by a transversal, what angle relationships are formed? When two lines are cut by a transversal, how can we show that a pair of angles are congruent?

ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD2] Recognize that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rigid motions. [8.Mod2.AD6] Solve for unknown angle measures by using facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.
laag: Students begin this lesson by making predictions about angle congruence given a diagram of two nonparallel lines cut by a transversal and a diagram of two parallel lines cut by a transversal. By using a transparency, students recognize that there are more pairs of congruent angles when parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Then they begin to name the relationships between pairs of angles and show that pairs of angles are congruent by using sequences of rigid motions. Students continue naming angle relationships and identifying the rigid motions associated with those relationships as they find the unknown angle measures in a diagram. This lesson defines the terms transversal, corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, and alternate exterior angles.

title: Angle Sum of a Triangle
objectives: Use informal arguments to verify that the sum of the interior angle measures of a triangle is 180°.
i_can: I can explain why the sum of the interior angle measures of a triangle is always 180°.
language_objectives: Justify in writing that the sum of the interior angle measures of a triangle is

ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD5] Apply, establish, and explain facts about the angle sum and exterior angles of triangles.
laag: In this lesson, students analyze the sum of the measures of a triangle’s interior angles to verify that it is always . Students measure angles in triangles with different side lengths and look for any patterns in the sum of the angle measures. Exploring both a concrete model and an abstract model, students draw on their knowledge of angle relationships to verify that the sum of the interior angle measures of a triangle is °. Then they find the measure of an unknown interior angle of a triangle when given the other two interior angle measures. This lesson defines the terms interior angle of a polygon and same-side interior angles.

title: Showing Lines Are Parallel
objectives: Use informal arguments to conclude that lines cut by a transversal are parallel when angle pairs are congruent.
i_can: I can use pairs of angle measures to determine whether two lines cut by a transversal are parallel.
language_objectives: In groups and as a class, listen to and orally share reasoning to justify whether given lines are parallel.
key_questions: How can we use pairs of angle measures to show whether two lines cut by a transversal are parallel?
ad_texts: ["Solve for unknown angle measures by using facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD6] Solve for unknown angle measures by using facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.
laag: Student pairs analyze the truth of if–then statements as an introduction to analyzing the truth of the statement, If corresponding angles created by two lines cut by a transversal are congruent, then the two lines are parallel. Students then follow an informal argument that shows the truth of the statement. They extend this reasoning to other angle relationships and use a pair of angle measures to explain whether lines in a diagram are parallel. Pairs form groups of four and use the Five Framing Questions routine to analyze one another’s work and explanations.

title: Exterior Angles of Triangles
objectives: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the exterior angles of triangles. Determine the unknown measure of an interior or exterior angle of a triangle.
i_can: I can find the measures of interior or exterior angles of a triangle by using angle relationships.
language_objectives: Orally describe the relationship between an exterior angle of a triangle and the remote interior angles. With a partner, write equations to determine the unknown measure of an interior or exterior angle of a triangle.
key_questions: What do we mean when we refer to the interior and exterior angles of a triangle? What is the relationship between the measures of an exterior angle and the remote interior angles of a triangle?
ad_texts: ["Apply, establish, and explain facts about the angle sum and exterior angles of triangles.", "Solve for unknown angle measures by using facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal."]
ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD5] Apply, establish, and explain facts about the angle sum and exterior angles of triangles. [8.Mod2.AD6] Solve for unknown angle measures by using facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.
laag: Students use their intuitive understanding of the words interior and exterior to identify the exterior angle of a triangle in a diagram. Students apply prior knowledge about angle relationships to discover a new relationship; the measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the measures of the remote interior angles. Students work with a partner to write equations and solve for unknown angle measures in a sequence of problems that increase in complexity. They share and compare their strategies with the class to illustrate the many approaches that can be taken to solve a problem. This lesson formally defines the terms exterior angle of a triangle and remote interior angles of a triangle.

title: Find Unknown Angle Measures
objectives: Use facts about angle relationships to write and solve equations.
i_can: I can use angle relationships to write equations and solve them to find unknown values.
language_objectives: With a partner, discuss orally and record angle relationships used to find an unknown value in a diagram.
key_questions: How do we use angle relationships to write equations?

ad_full: [8.Mod2.AD5] Apply, establish, and explain facts about the angle sum and exterior angles of triangles. [8.Mod2.AD6] Solve for unknown angle measures by using facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.
laag: This student-centered lesson begins with student pairs finding the value of a variable by using what they know about angle relationships. The discussion that follows the opening problem serves two purposes. First, to emphasize that there is more than one acceptable solution pathway. Second, to highlight the differences between a numeric answer and an answer with units. Students then participate in an Angle Relationship Search activity. Throughout the activity, pairs must describe the angle relationships they intend to use, write a related equation, and solve the equation to find the value of the variable. Each answer leads pairs to their next problem. They repeat this process until they finish the activity, or time expires.

title: Proving the Pythagorean Theorem
objectives: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean theorem.

Students begin by completing a puzzle that is a visual representation of the Pythagorean theorem. Then they progress through another representation of a proof of the Pythagorean theorem. This lesson introduces the terms proof and prove.

title: Proving the Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem
objectives: Explain a proof of the converse of the Pythagorean theorem.
i_can: I can explain a proof of the converse of the Pythagorean theorem.
language_objectives: In writing, explain a proof of the converse of the Pythagorean theorem.

Then students apply that understanding to generate the converse of the Pythagorean theorem and to explore a proof of its converse. This lesson formally defines the term converse.

title: Using the Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse
objectives: Use the converse of the Pythagorean theorem to determine whether a triangle is a right triangle. Use the Pythagorean theorem to find unknown side lengths of right triangles.
i_can: I can use the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side length of a right triangle when given two side lengths.
language_objectives: Through listening to and speaking with a partner, identify combinations of side lengths that form right triangles. Orally explain whether a given statement about a right triangle is always, sometimes, or never true.
key_questions: When is it helpful to know and use the Pythagorean theorem?
ad_texts: ["Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse geometrically.", "Apply the Pythagorean theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions."]

laag: This lesson begins with students engaging in the Always Sometimes Never routine to spark thinking about possible side lengths in a right triangle. Throughout the lesson, students are prompted to revisit their choice of always, sometimes, or never based on new learning. They engage in a card sort activity that leads them to understand how to use the converse of the Pythagorean theorem to determine whether a triangle with the given side lengths is a right triangle. Before doing so, students must determine which of the given side lengths could represent the hypotenuse by comparing the side lengths. Then students find an unknown side length of a right triangle when given the other two side lengths.

title: Distance in the Coordinate Plane
objectives: Find the distance between two points in the coordinate plane by using the Pythagorean theorem.
i_can: I can use the Pythagorean theorem to find the distance between two points in the coordinate plane.
language_objectives: With a partner and as a class, discuss strategies for finding the lengths of segments in the coordinate plane. Orally compare finding the length of a segment in the coordinate plane to finding the distance between two points.
key_questions: How can we find the distance between two points in the coordinate plane?

Then students find lengths of segments and apply this new skill during a group activity to determine whether a triangle in the coordinate plane is a right triangle. Students transition from finding segment lengths to finding distances as they revisit a question about the set of points from the beginning of the lesson.

title: Exploring Dilations
objectives: Informally describe the effects of dilations. Classify a dilation as a transformation that is not a rigid motion.
i_can: I can determine whether a transformation is a rigid motion or is not a rigid motion.
language_objectives: Orally explain why a dilation is a transformation but not a rigid motion.
key_questions: How are rigid motions, dilations, and transformations related?

ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: This lesson begins with students visually comparing several examples of rigid motions to an example of a dilation. This drives the need to present the term transformation. A sorting activity underscores the relationship between rigid motions, dilations, and transformations. Through exploration, students build an intuitive understanding of how the center of dilation and the scale factor affect the resulting image. This lesson introduces the term dilation and formally defines the term transformation.

title: Enlargements
objectives: Apply a dilation with a whole-number scale factor greater than 1. Describe the effects of a dilation with a whole-number scale factor greater than 1.
i_can: I can draw the image of a point under a dilation with a scale factor that is a whole number and find an unknown distance.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe the relationship between the center of dilation, a point, and the point’s image under a dilation. Listen to the formal definition of dilation and compare it with informal definitions.

ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.

After learning to use a transparency to apply a dilation with a scale factor greater than students practice drawing images of points under a dilation. Students then analyze their work to refine their understanding of some of the features of dilations. This lesson builds on the previous exploration of dilations to formally define the term dilation.

title: Reductions and More Enlargements
objectives: Apply a dilation with a scale factor greater than 0. Describe the effects of a dilation with a scale factor greater than 0.
i_can: I can draw the image of a point under a dilation with a scale factor that is not a whole number and find an unknown distance.

They calculate distances and find the images of points under dilations with rational scale factors. Students conclude the lesson with an activity in which they match diagrams of dilations with scale factors.

laag: The goal of the activities in this lesson is to have students observe the properties of dilations. Students begin the lesson with an error analysis and conclude that a segment under a dilation, in which the center is not on the line that contains the segment, does not intersect with its image. Students build on this observation by using the parallel lines of a lined sheet of paper to notice that a segment and its image under a dilation are parallel. Students use different methods to measure the lengths of a segment and its image, and they find that the lengths are proportional by the scale factor of the dilation. By using what they know about the angles created by parallel lines cut by a transversal, students find that angles map to angles of the same measure under dilations.

title: Figures and Dilations
objectives: Draw images of figures under dilations with various scale factors.
i_can: I can draw the image of a figure under a dilation.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to draw images of polygons and other figures under dilations. Read a task involving a real-world application of dilations. With a partner, orally discuss a strategy to complete the task.
key_questions: How can we draw the image of a polygon under a dilation? How can we draw the image of a figure with curves under a dilation?
ad_texts: ["Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students use their knowledge of finding images of segments under dilations to find the images of polygons and curvilinear figures. They show that the segments in a polygon under a dilation, in which the center is not on the line that contains the segment, are parallel to the corresponding segments in the image. Furthermore, the lengths of the segments and their images are proportional. Students examine the dilation of a curvilinear figure and realize that finding the images of the endpoints is not enough to find the image of a curvilinear figure. Students then engage in a partner activity in which they apply dilations to enlarge and reduce a business logo to create a flyer and a business card.

title: The Shadowy Hand
objectives: Use a mathematical model to explain a real-world situation. Apply properties of dilations to make and test predictions.
i_can: I can use dilations to model real-world situations.
language_objectives: Through speaking and listening in groups, develop a solution strategy involving dilations for a real-world problem.
key_questions: How can we use dilations to model a real-world situation?
ad_texts: ["Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: This lesson is an open-ended modeling exploration. Students discuss the phenomenon of shadows. They question what makes shadows of the same object different sizes and find a mathematical model to represent this situation. Working in groups, students use the model to determine how far to place their hand from a light source so their hand’s shadow aligns to a fixed outline on the wall. Then they present their solution strategies to the class, compare results, and consider assumptions.

title: Dilations on a Grid
objectives: Apply dilations on a grid.
i_can: I can plot the image of a point under a dilation on a grid.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to use a grid to apply dilations.
key_questions: How can the properties of dilations help us plot the image of a point under a dilation on a grid?
ad_texts: ["Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students utilize the structure a grid provides to apply dilations. Students first rely on the grid as a measurement tool to determine distances between centers, points, and their images when they lie on rays that coincide with grid lines. Students then pair that understanding with the properties of dilations they discovered in the lined paper activity in lesson 4 to plot the image of a point along a ray that is neither vertical nor horizontal from the center of dilation. Students extend their skills by applying dilations involving single points on a grid to dilations involving polygons on a grid.

title: Dilations on the Coordinate Plane
objectives: Apply dilations centered at the origin on the coordinate plane. Determine the scale factor of a dilation centered at the origin.
i_can: I can graph the image of a figure under a dilation centered at the origin on the coordinate plane.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, summarize the relationship between the coordinates of a point under a dilation centered at the origin and the coordinates of the point’s image.
key_questions: What is the relationship between the coordinates of a point and the coordinates of its image under a dilation centered at the origin?
ad_texts: ["Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.", "Use coordinates to describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane. [8.Mod3.AD3] Use coordinates to describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students transition from using a grid as a tool to apply dilations to using the coordinate plane. Through a group activity, students look for patterns in the relationship between the coordinates of points and their images under dilations centered at the origin with various scale factors. Students then formalize this relationship as a rule by realizing that the coordinates of a point’s image can be found by multiplying the coordinates of the point by the scale factor. They apply this rule to graph the image of a figure on the coordinate plane and to determine the scale factor of a dilation given a figure and its image.

title: Describing Dilations
objectives: Precisely describe a dilation given a figure and its image.
i_can: I can locate the center of a dilation and determine the scale factor of the dilation.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to determine the center of dilation and the scale factor when given a figure and its image under a dilation.
key_questions: Can we locate the center of dilation? How? What information do we need to describe a dilation?
ad_texts: ["Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students study dilations to precisely describe them by using the center and scale factor. Students begin by examining a figure and several images of the figure. They recognize that points and their images are collinear with the center of dilation and use this fact to find the center of dilation. Students observe that the dilation that maps a figure to its image and the dilation that maps the image back onto its figure have the same center but reciprocal scale factors. With the skill of finding the scale factor of a dilation already established and the skill of finding the center of dilation just developed, students can precisely describe a dilation given a figure and its image.

title: Sequencing Transformations
objectives: Apply sequences of transformations. Recognize a sequence that involves a dilation and a translation as a single dilation.
i_can: I can graph the image of a figure under a sequence of transformations.
language_objectives: Read and apply sequences of transformations. As a class, orally describe how a single dilation with a different center can replace a sequence that involves a dilation and a translation.
key_questions: How can we apply more than one transformation?
ad_texts: ["Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD2] Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane.
laag: In this lesson, students build on their previous work with applying sequences of rigid motions by including dilations in the sequences they apply. Through a partner activity, students create and then apply sequences of transformations to draw images of figures, both on the plane and on the coordinate plane. Then they analyze a sequence involving a translation and a dilation. Students connect corresponding vertices of a figure and its image under the sequence to locate a new center for a dilation that maps the figure onto its image in a single step.

title: Similar Figures
objectives: Describe a sequence of rigid motions or dilations, or both, to show that two figures are similar. Identify properties of similar figures.

language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe a sequence of transformations that shows two figures are similar.
key_questions: What does it mean for two figures to be similar?

ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD4] Recognize that a two-dimensional figure is similar to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rigid motions or dilations, or both. [8.Mod3.AD5] Describe a sequence of rigid motions or dilations, or both, that exhibits the similarity between two given figures.
laag: Students engage in the Which One Doesn’t Belong? routine to begin forming an understanding of what it means for two figures to be similar. Building on their previous experience in applying sequences, students work with a partner to analyze pairs of similar figures, both on the plane and on the coordinate plane, to describe sequences that show the similarity between the figures. Students also compare corresponding lengths and angle measures in similar figures to identify the properties of similar figures. This lesson formally defines the term similar.

title: Exploring Angles in Similar Triangles
objectives: Recognize that triangles with two pairs of congruent angles are similar.

language_objectives: Orally explain why triangles with two pairs of congruent angles are similar.
key_questions: How can we determine if two triangles are similar without using transformations? What is the angle–angle criterion for similarity?

laag: This lesson begins with students determining which transformations they must use to map one triangle onto a similar triangle. Students then choose two angle measures for a pair of triangles and draw two unique triangles with those chosen angle measures. Students determine whether the triangles they drew are similar by describing a sequence of rigid motions or dilations, or both, that shows the triangles can be mapped onto one another. By studying a diagram where angles are congruent, but no measures are given, students observe that only two pairs of congruent angles are needed to show triangles are similar. Students practice determining whether two triangles are similar by using the angle measures in triangle diagrams. This lesson formally defines the angle–angle (AA) criterion for similarity.

title: Similar Triangles
objectives: Determine whether two triangles are similar by the angle–angle criterion.
i_can: I can determine whether two triangles are similar by the angle–angle criterion.
language_objectives: In writing, justify whether two triangles are similar by using angle measures and relationships.
key_questions: How can we use angle relationships to help us show that two triangles are similar?
