laag: Students begin the lesson within the context of a piece of art. Students’ previous work on the angle–angle criterion and its application to triangles is underscored by a comparison of triangles and quadrilaterals within the art. In the remainder of the lesson, students study increasingly complex diagrams in which they must decide whether the named triangles are similar. The problems require students to draw on their existing knowledge of angle relationships. Students take turns articulating their conclusions about angle relationships in response to a series of structured questions. They build on the angle relationships found by their classmates to determine whether a given pair of triangles in the diagram is similar.

title: Using Similar Figures to Find Unknown Side Lengths
objectives: Use properties of similar figures to find unknown side lengths.
i_can: I can find unknown side lengths of similar figures.
language_objectives: Orally explain how the relationship between similar figures can be used to find unknown side lengths.
key_questions: How can we use properties of similar figures to find an unknown side length of a figure?
ad_texts: ["Informally argue to establish facts about the angle\u2013angle criterion for similar triangles and apply the angle\u2013angle criterion for similarity."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD6] Informally argue to establish facts about the angle–angle criterion for similar triangles and apply the angle–angle criterion for similarity.
laag: Students begin this lesson by trying to find the height of a rectangle composed of similar right triangles when given the side lengths of one of the triangles. They then use the properties of similar figures to create an equation with corresponding side lengths from two similar figures. This equation, or proportion, is used to find an unknown side length. The work to find unknown side lengths continues as students discuss the proportionality of side lengths in figures that are not similar. Students conclude that using proportions to find unknown measures can be used only if the figures are similar.

title: Applications of Similar Figures
objectives: Use properties of similar figures to solve problems.
i_can: I can use similar triangles to solve real-world problems.
language_objectives: Summarize problem contexts involving similar triangles both orally and with diagrams.
key_questions: How is linear perspective related to dilations? How can we use similar triangles to solve real-world problems?
ad_texts: ["Informally argue to establish facts about the angle\u2013angle criterion for similar triangles and apply the angle\u2013angle criterion for similarity."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD6] Informally argue to establish facts about the angle–angle criterion for similar triangles and apply the angle–angle criterion for similarity.
laag: In this lesson, students are introduced to the concept of linear perspective. They observe how the idea of dilations gives linear perspective art the appearance of depth. Students work in pairs to solve three real-world problems presented in videos. After watching each video, students draw a diagram, which includes two triangles, and identify the unknown length in the diagram. Students then work to verify that the triangles used to represent the context are similar and solve the problem by using a proportion.

title: Similar Right Triangles
objectives: Apply dilations to create similar right triangles. Find unknown side lengths in similar right triangles.
i_can: I can find unknown side lengths in similar right triangles.
language_objectives: Orally describe how to use within-triangle ratios and between-triangle ratios to find unknown side lengths in similar right triangles. Through speaking and listening in groups, explain and analyze solution pathways for a problem involving similar right triangles.
key_questions: Given similar right triangles, how can we find an unknown side length?

[8.Mod3.AD7] Apply the Pythagorean theorem to determine unknown side lengths in similar right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.
laag: In this lesson, students apply dilations to create similar right triangles and discover that the values of the ratios of the height to the base for a right triangle and its images are equivalent. Students apply these within-triangle ratios to find an unknown side length given a pair of similar right triangles. Then they solve a problem that allows for various solution pathways, including using the Pythagorean theorem along with triangle ratios to find an unknown side length. Students engage in discourse within groups to analyze one another’s solution pathways for the problem.

title: Similar Triangles on a Line
objectives: Determine that right triangles with horizontal and vertical legs and with hypotenuses that lie on the same line are similar triangles.
i_can: I can find the height-to-base ratios of right triangles with horizontal and vertical legs and with hypotenuses that lie on the same line.
language_objectives: Justify orally that right triangles with horizontal and vertical legs and with hypotenuses that lie on the same line are similar triangles.
key_questions: Can we show that right triangles with horizontal and vertical legs are similar triangles? How?
ad_texts: ["Determine the values of the ratios of corresponding side lengths on similar right triangles that have horizontal and vertical legs and have hypotenuses that lie on the same line. (8.EE.B.6) coordinates", "Use to describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures in the plane."]
ad_full: [8.Mod3.AD1] Determine the values of the ratios of corresponding side lengths on similar right triangles that have horizontal and vertical legs and have hypotenuses that lie on the same line. laag: In this lesson, students are introduced to right triangles with horizontal and vertical legs and with hypotenuses that lie on the same line by first drawing an example of this type of triangle. They then compare their right triangle to those of their classmates and realize that the triangles are similar. They observe this similarity both in terms of sequences of rigid motions or dilations, or both, and by the angle–angle criterion. Students close the lesson by applying their knowledge of within-triangle and between-triangle ratios to solve for unknown lengths and to explain relationships between triangles.

title: Equations
objectives: Analyze an equation to make sense of how to solve it. Identify whether an equation is a linear equation.
i_can: I can solve linear equations and check my solutions.
language_objectives: Orally describe equations, listen to others’ descriptions, and read provided descriptions. Orally explain why some expressions are linear and others are not.
key_questions: How can we use our number sense to solve an equation? How do we know if an equation is a linear equation?
ad_texts: ["Solve linear equations with rational number coefficients."]
ad_full: [8.Mod4.AD11] Solve linear equations with rational number coefficients.
laag: Students begin this lesson by trying to find the solution to a challenging linear equation, which they revisit at the end of the lesson. As a class, they solve a simple linear equation by using their grade 7 skills and number sense. Then students work with a partner to match equations with the sentences that represent them and solve the equations by using a strategy of their choice. Students discuss their strategies with their partner, present differing strategies to the class, and then discuss their preferences. They determine which equations are linear by analyzing the expressions on both sides of the equal sign. This lesson formally defines linear expression and linear equation.

title: Solving Linear Equations
objectives: Identify the properties of equality. Solve multi-step linear equations in one variable with variables on both sides of the equations.
i_can: I can solve equations with a variable on both sides of the equation.
language_objectives: Orally discuss when and why the properties of equality are applied to solve equations.
key_questions: How do the properties of equality help us solve equations? How can we solve an equation that has a variable on both sides of the equation?

ad_full: and linear [8.Mod4.AD9] Write solve equations in one variable for real-world and mathematical problems. [8.Mod4.AD11] Solve linear equations with rational number coefficients.
laag: The lesson begins by presenting students with a linear equation that has a variable on both sides. Students cannot solve this equation with number sense, which leads to the need to apply the properties of equality. Through a card sort activity, students analyze true number sentences and classify them, first based on if–then moves and eventually based on the two properties of equality. They analyze one path for solving a given equation and identify the properties of equality applied in certain steps. Students work with a partner to solve linear equations with variables on both sides. Some equations require students to use the distributive property and combine like terms in the solution process.

laag: In this lesson, students continue to practice solving linear equations with variables on both sides, but the equations now include rational numbers. Students engage in the Five Framing Questions routine to analyze two different strategies used to solve an equation with rational numbers. One strategy uses rational coefficients to solve the equation. The other strategy involves rewriting the equation with integer coefficients. Students work with a partner to solve a variety of equations, culminating in applying their skills to solve a geometric problem.

title: Using Linear Equations to Solve Problems
objectives: Define variables and write equations that represent a given situation.

laag: This lesson begins with students by using guess and check, or another intuitive strategy, to solve a problem about consecutive integers. The class discusses how to define the variable and related expressions to represent a sequence of consecutive integers in a problem. The discussion develops into representing problems involving odd consecutive and even consecutive integers. Then students work individually to define variables and to write equations for problems with number relationships and geometric context. Through an activity, they discuss with various partners the variables and equations for these problems and then find solutions to the given problems.

laag: In this lesson, students participate in the Take a Stand routine to reactivate knowledge about the differences between the decimal forms of rational and irrational numbers. With a partner, students use the division algorithm to discover why the decimal forms of nonterminating rational numbers eventually repeat. Students learn how to use a linear equation and the properties of equality to write the fraction form of a decimal with one repeating digit. Then they write the fraction form of additional decimals with one repeating digit.

title: An Interesting Application of Linear Equations, Part 2
objectives: Use linear equations to write the fraction form of any repeating decimal.

language_objectives: With a partner, read and orally discuss a solution method for finding the fraction form of a decimal with digits that do not all repeat.

laag: In this lesson, students write the fraction form for repeating decimals with more than one repeating digit. They work with a partner to recognize that they need a whole number difference after applying the addition property of equality for the solution to the equation to be a fraction. Students then work individually on writing multi-digit repeating numbers as fractions by first determining which power of to multiply both sides of the equation by. Next, students study a strategy for finding the fraction form of a decimal with digits that do not all repeat. They analyze how the strategy is different from what they use when all of the digits repeat.

This activity establishes the foundation for identifying the numbers of solutions to a linear equation.

title: Writing Linear Equations

Given partial equations in various formats, students create equations with only one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solution by examining the linear terms and the constant terms on both sides of the equations. Students encounter problems that require taking algebraic steps, such as applying the distributive property, before the equation can be analyzed. The lesson concludes with a study of the distinction between no solution and a solution of

title: Using Linear Equations to Solve Real-World Problems
objectives: Solve real-world problems by using linear equations in one variable.

laag: Students begin the lesson by working with a partner to interpret an equation in context. Students recognize that how they define the variable, as a price or as a number of items, changes the meaning of the equation. Students analyze what the number of solutions to the equation means in the context of the situation as they summarize the solution in the last step of the routine. Students recognize that the solution to the equation does not always answer the question from the problem.

title: Planning a Trip
objectives: Solve a real-world problem by using linear equations in one variable.
i_can: I can write and solve equations in one variable to answer questions about a real-world situation.
language_objectives: Orally explain how to use linear equations to model and solve a real-world problem.
key_questions: How can we use equations to represent real-world situations?

Then they write and solve an equation to find the distance for which driving and flying take the same amount of time. key_questions: How can we use tape diagrams to help us solve systems of equations?
ad_texts: ["Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD2] Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.
laag: In this optional lesson, students begin by matching tape diagrams with the systems of linear equations they represent. They then work as a class to solve a system of equations by using a tape diagram before working with a partner to solve a system of equations by using a tape diagram. Students also work with their partner to analyze the work of a student who solved a system of equations in which neither variable term is isolated.

title: Rewriting Equations to Solve a System of Equations
objectives: Solve a system of linear equations by using the substitution method.
i_can: I can rewrite a system of equations before substituting solve. to
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe how and why one or both equations in a system of equations can be rewritten to create a new system with the same solution. As a class, orally describe and compare strategies for solving systems of equations.
key_questions: What do we look for when deciding how to rewrite an equation before substituting to solve?
ad_texts: ["Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.", "Determine the number of solutions to the system of two linear equations by inspection."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD2] Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically. [8.Mod5.AD4] Determine the number of solutions to the system of two linear equations by inspection.
laag: Students begin this lesson by analyzing the same system of equations written three different ways. They determine the number used to multiply both sides of an equation in the system and determine which rewritten system they prefer to solve. This analysis continues with a system that is rewritten in multiple ways using both multiplication and addition on both sides of the equation prior to substitution. Students then work with a partner to find solutions to systems of equations where rewriting at least one of the equations is necessary prior to substitution. They summarize how analyzing the equations within the system help identify the most efficient solution method.

title: Choosing a Solution Method
objectives: Analyze graphs and systems of equations to determine the number of solutions. Construct and critique arguments about the most efficient solution method.
i_can: I can use different methods to solve systems equations. of
language_objectives: With a partner, discuss which method to use to solve a given system of equations. Read solution paths for given systems of equations and provide written feedback. As a group, read and orally reflect on the feedback received.
key_questions: When given a system of equations, how do we determine which method to use to find the solution?
ad_texts: ["Verify that an ordered pair is a solution to a given system of two linear equations in two variables and explain what the solution means in terms of the system\u2019s graph.", "Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.", "Determine the number of solutions to the system of two linear equations by inspection."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD1] Verify that an ordered pair is a solution to a given system of two linear equations in two variables and explain what the solution means in terms of the system’s graph. laag: In this lesson, students analyze systems of equations in multiple forms to determine the best method to solve the system. Students recognize that the form of the equations within a system often indicates which method to use to efficiently solve the system. They are encouraged to consider inspection as a method to determine the number of solutions before attempting graphing or substitution methods. Then student pairs select and use different methods to solve a system assigned to them. They construct viable arguments to support their displayed solutions and critique the reasoning of others as they compare different methods during a gallery walk.

title: Writing and Solving Systems of Equations for Mathematical Problems
objectives: Write and solve systems of linear equations for mathematical problems.
i_can: I can write and solve systems of equations that represent problems. mathematical
language_objectives: Read a mathematical riddle and orally explain why modeling the situation with a system of equations is a more efficient way to find a solution than the guess-and- check strategy. Write a mathematical riddle that can be solved with a system of equations.
key_questions: What kinds of problems can we solve by using a system of equations?
ad_texts: ["Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.", "Solve mathematical and real-world problems leading to two linear equations in two variables."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD2] Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically. [8.Mod5.AD5] Solve mathematical and real-world problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
laag: This lesson begins with an opportunity for students to solve a mathematical riddle in any way they choose. Then they use the Read–Represent–Solve–Summarize routine to write a system of linear equations to represent the same riddle and solve the system. Students create a number riddle for a partner to represent as a system of equations and solve. They continue to work with a partner to represent and solve geometric problems related to measurements, such as determining angle measures and finding the side lengths and area of a rectangle.

title: Solving Historical Problems with Systems of Equations
objectives: Write and solve a system of linear equations given a historical situation.
i_can: I can write and solve systems of equations that represent problems. historical
language_objectives: Read and interpret historical problems to represent them with systems of equations.
key_questions: What kinds of problems can we solve with a system of equations?
ad_texts: ["Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.", "Solve mathematical and real-world problems leading to two linear equations in two variables."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD2] Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically. [8.Mod5.AD5] Solve mathematical and real-world problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
laag: In this lesson, students write and solve systems of equations to represent real-world situations based on problems from the text titled Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art. Students begin by observing and describing a single real-world constraint regarding the weights of different types of birds. After identifying a second constraint, students write and solve a system of equations. Students then move to a historical livestock trading context to write and solve more systems of equations.

title: Writing and Solving Systems of Equations for Real-World Problems
objectives: Write and solve a system of linear equations given a real-world situation.
i_can: I can write and solve systems of equations that represent problems. real-world
language_objectives: Read about real-world situations to represent them with systems of equations. Read and orally analyze sample work to identify an error. Explain the error orally and in writing.
key_questions: What kinds of problems can we solve by using a system of equations?
ad_texts: ["Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.", "Solve mathematical and real-world problems leading to two linear equations in two variables."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD2] Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically. [8.Mod5.AD5] Solve mathematical and real-world problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
laag: To begin the lesson, students analyze a word problem that leads to one equation in two variables. Students recognize that the equation has many solutions. They realize that at least two equations are needed to find one solution to a problem with two unknowns. For the remainder of the lesson, students work with a partner to write and solve real-world problems about an amusement park by representing each situation with a system of equations and finding the solution to the system.

title: Back to the Coordinate Plane
objectives: Write and solve systems of linear equations when given information about two lines to identify intersection points.
i_can: I can use information about lines to write and solve systems equations. of
language_objectives: In groups, orally discuss and summarize the relationship between the solution to a system of equations and the intersection point of the corresponding lines.
key_questions: What information do we need to write a system of equations to find the intersection point of two lines?
ad_texts: ["Verify that an ordered pair is a solution to a given system of two linear equations in two variables and explain what the solution means in terms of the system\u2019s graph.", "Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.", "Estimate solutions to systems of two linear equations in two variables by graphing the equations."]
ad_full: [8.Mod5.AD1] Verify that an ordered pair is a solution to a given system of two linear equations in two variables and explain what the solution means in terms of the system’s graph. [8.Mod5.AD2] Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically. [8.Mod5.AD3] Estimate solutions to systems of two linear equations in two variables by graphing the equations.
laag: In this lesson, students analyze given information about two lines to write and solve a system of linear equations by using substitution. The problems increase in difficulty by starting with one of the equations of the lines given and then progressing to problems where neither equation is given. Variation in the language in the lesson is intentional to emphasize the relationship between the intersection point of two lines, the ordered pair that represents the intersection point, and the solution to the system of linear equations.

title: Motion and Speed
objectives: Calculate the average speed of linear and nonlinear motion. Understand that a function is a special type of rule.
i_can: I can describe a function that relates distance and time and calculate average speeds over time intervals.
language_objectives: Listen to an informal definition of function. Orally determine whether a given context can be represented by a function.
key_questions: What does it mean for an object to move at constant speed? How can we use a function to make predictions?
big_idea: Data Explorations M ultiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD1] Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output.
laag: In this lesson, students use their understanding of speed and linear situations to make sense of average speed for linear and nonlinear motion situations. Students calculate average speeds over time intervals and see that nonlinear motion does not have constant speed. Students are introduced to functions as a rule in the context of distance and time related to linear and nonlinear motion. To make predictions, students observe patterns in tables that represent functions. They also explore how some values of time do not make sense for a given context. This lesson introduces the term average speed and informally introduces the term function.

title: Definition of a Function
objectives: Determine that a function is a rule that assigns to each input one and only one output. Identify functions that can be represented by an equation and those that cannot.
i_can: I can determine whether a relationship is a function and use a rule to find inputs and outputs.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, analyze tables and explain whether they represent functions. Orally explain why a given function can or cannot be represented by an equation.
key_questions: How can you determine whether the inputs and outputs in a table represent values of a function? Can every function be represented by an equation? Explain.
big_idea: Data Explorations M ultiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD1] Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output.
laag: This lesson opens with students comparing two tables of values in the familiar context of distance traveled over time. They recognize that the values in one table do not make sense in the context and do not represent a function. Students further explore a relationship that is a function by considering other possible input values that make sense in the context and writing an equation to describe the rule. Then they use that equation to determine output values not shown in the table. Students next encounter a function that cannot be represented by an equation. They conclude that some functions, but not all, can be represented by equations. This lesson formalizes the definition of function.

title: Linear Functions and Proportionality
objectives: Write equations that represent linear functions. Determine what inputs make sense in the context of a linear function.
i_can: I can write and use equations that represent linear functions and determine which inputs make sense in contexts.
language_objectives: Orally compare and contrast relationships represented by linear functions. Orally and in writing, determine which inputs make sense in the context of a given linear function and why.
key_questions: How do you determine the numbers that make sense as inputs in a given situation? How are linear functions and proportional relationships the same? How are they different?
big_idea: Data, Graphs, and Tables Data Explorations M ultiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Identify linear and nonlinear functions.", "Construct functions to model linear relationships by determining rate of change and initial value given a description or two values in a table or graph."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD3] Identify linear and nonlinear functions. [8.Mod6.AD4] Construct functions to model linear relationships by determining rate of change and initial value given a description or two values in a table or graph.
laag: This lesson begins with a video that introduces students to the context of paying an entrance fee at a state fair and then paying a fee for each ticket. Students write an equation for the relationship and learn that the relationship is a linear function because the equation is in the form In groups, students solve a context problem and then present it to the class. Through discussion, students compare the values that make sense for each context and discuss how proportional relationships and linear functions are related. This lesson defines the term linear function.

title: More Examples of Functions
objectives: Determine that not all functions have numerical inputs and outputs. Determine what inputs make sense for a variety of functions.
i_can: I can determine whether a relationship is a function that can be represented by an equation.
language_objectives: Through speaking and writing in groups, analyze and describe why a given relationship can be represented by a function, which inputs make sense for that function, and whether that function can be represented by an equation.
key_questions: What do all functions have in common? When can we represent a function with an equation? How can we determine what inputs make sense for a function?
big_idea: Data Explorations M ultiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD1] Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output.
laag: In this lesson, students work with a partner to sort relationships, described in words or represented in tables, into two categories and justify their choices. They realize that while all functions have each input paired with one and only one output, functions can be used to describe many different types of relationships. Using the Numbered Heads routine, students work in groups to determine that three different relationships represent functions. As they engage in the routine, they encounter relationships that have numerical and nonnumerical inputs and outputs, relationships that are linear functions and others that are nonlinear, and functions that can be represented with an equation and others that cannot. Students determine what inputs make sense for a wider variety of functions than they have been exposed to in previous lessons.

title: Graphs of Functions and Equations
objectives: Determine that if a function can be represented by an equation, then the graph of the function is the same as or some part of the graph of the equation. Determine whether a given graph represents a function.
i_can: I can write the equation for a function and use it to find input– output pairs and plot them as points in the coordinate plane.
language_objectives: In writing, compare graphs that represent equations to graphs that represent functions.
key_questions: How does the graph of a function relate to the graph of the equation that represents it? What characteristics must be satisfied for a graph to represent any function?
big_idea: Data Explorations M ultiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD1] Justify whether relationships are functions based on the understanding that functions are rules that assign each input to exactly one output.
laag: Students begin this lesson by using the Which One Doesn’t Belong? routine to analyze four graphs. By relating a table of values to one of the graphs, they recognize that if two or more points on a graph have the same the graph does not represent a function. Students then explore how the graph of an equation relates to the graphs of both linear and nonlinear functions. They determine that the graph of a function is the same as or some part of the graph of the equation representing the function. In pairs, students determine whether graphs represent functions or non-functions, by using what they have learned during the lesson. This lesson introduces the term graph of a function.

title: Linear Functions and Rate of Change
objectives: Calculate rates on a given interval to determine whether a function is a linear function. Determine the rate of change for a linear function and interpret the rate of change in context.
i_can: I can calculate rates of change on intervals to identify linear functions and interpret rates of change in context.
language_objectives: Orally explain the relationship between the rate of change of a linear function and the slope of the line that represents the function. In writing, justify whether given functions represented in different ways are linear functions and, if so, identify and interpret the rates of change in context.
key_questions: How can we determine whether a function is a linear function? In a linear function, how does the rate of change compare to the slope of the line that represents the function?

ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD3] Identify linear and nonlinear functions. [8.Mod6.AD5] Interpret rates of change and initial values of linear functions in terms of the situations that they model. (8.F.B.4, 8.SP.A.3)
laag: This lesson starts with an animation that shows how the batteries of two mobile phones lose their charges throughout the day. After analyzing tables, students determine that both situations represent functions. They recognize that when the rate is the same on any interval of time, the function is a linear function. With a partner, students analyze different representations of functions to determine whether the function is a linear function. They also describe what the rate of change means in context. Then students are challenged to create their own linear function and represent it in a table. Trading functions with a partner, students verify whether their partner has created a linear function. This lesson introduces the term rate of change.

title: Interpreting Rate of Change and Initial Value
objectives: Interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in context. Use rate of change to compare two linear functions.
i_can: I can use rate of change and initial value to compare and interpret linear functions in context.
language_objectives: Orally identify the rate of change and initial value for a given linear function and interpret these values in context. Read a description of a situation that can be represented with a linear function and mathematically interpret the situation’s parameters in writing.
key_questions: What does it mean for a linear function to be increasing? Decreasing? What strategies do we have to compare linear functions?
big_idea: Data, Graphs, and Tables Linear Equations Slopes and Intercepts Multiple Representations of Functions

(8.F.B.4, 8.SP.A.3)"]
ad_full: properties [8.Mod6.AD2] Compare of functions represented in different ways. [8.Mod6.AD4] Construct functions to model linear relationships by determining rate of change and initial value given a description or two values in a table or graph. [8.Mod6.AD5] Interpret rates of change and initial values of linear functions in terms of the situations that they model. (8.F.B.4, 8.SP.A.3)
laag: In this lesson, students are presented with two subscription plans and asked to consider which plan is better. After students recognize that both plans represent linear functions, they write an equation to represent each function. Students identify the rate of change and initial value and interpret the values in context. They are introduced to the ideas of increasing and decreasing linear functions and connect these new ideas to rate of change. Then they test input values to explore when one subscription plan is less expensive than the other. By using strategies such as substitution, graphing, and comparing tables of values, students determine when the subscription plans cost the same amount and then share their strategies with the class. In pairs, students examine two relationships presented as written descriptions and apply the new knowledge and skills they have acquired in the lesson. This lesson defines the terms initial value, increasing linear function, and decreasing linear function.

title: Comparing Functions
objectives: Compare two functions represented in different ways.
i_can: I can compare two functions represented in two different ways.
language_objectives: Through speaking and listening in groups, match one representation of a given function to other representations of the same function.
key_questions: Which representations of linear functions make it easiest to identify the rate of change and the initial value? Why? How can we find the rate of change and the initial value from different representations of functions?
big_idea: Data Explorations Multiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Compare properties of functions represented in different ways."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD2] Compare properties of functions represented in different ways.
laag: In this lesson, students are given a representation of a function and must find other students who have been given other representations of the same function. Through the activity, students are grouped according to which function they have. The groups then work on problems in which they compare two functions represented in different ways. By using the information provided, they answer questions about the context, sometimes representing the function in a new way to better understand the situation.

title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
objectives: Describe qualitative features of a function by analyzing a graph. Sketch the graph of a function given a description.
i_can: I can analyze graphs of linear and nonlinear functions and identify intervals where functions are increasing or decreasing.
language_objectives: Orally justify whether given functions are linear or nonlinear and whether they are increasing or decreasing.
key_questions: How do we determine where a function is increasing? How do we determine where a function is decreasing?
big_idea: Data, Graphs, and Tables Multiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Describe functions by analyzing their graphs.", "Sketch graphs of functions that exhibit qualitative features that have been described verbally."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD6] Describe functions by analyzing their graphs. [8.Mod6.AD7] Sketch graphs of functions that exhibit qualitative features that have been described verbally.
laag: In this lesson, students watch a video and then sketch a graph of the relationship between time and a rock climber’s height above the ground. Using the Take a Stand routine, students classify various functions represented by graphs or tables as linear and increasing, linear and decreasing, nonlinear and increasing, or nonlinear and decreasing. Through a digital animation, students explore the features of the graph of a function representing the time and height above the ground of a roller-coaster car.

title: Graphs of Nonlinear Functions
objectives: Sketch the graph of a function with certain qualitative features based on a description. Classify linear and nonlinear functions given a context, an equation, or a graph.
i_can: I can sketch graphs of functions and identify whether functions are linear or nonlinear.
language_objectives: With a partner, listen to a verbal description of the graph of a function and sketch the graph based on its description.
key_questions: What features of a graph help us classify it? How do we know whether a function is linear or nonlinear?
big_idea: Data, Graphs, and Tables Multiple Representations of Functions
ad_texts: ["Identify linear and nonlinear functions. (8.F.A.3) functions", "Describe by analyzing their graphs.", "Sketch graphs of functions that exhibit qualitative features that have been described verbally."]

laag: This lesson begins with students working in pairs to sketch graphs of linear and nonlinear functions without contexts. In each pair, one student is challenged to describe the qualitative features of a given graph in such a way that their partner can duplicate the graph without seeing it. Partners take turns describing and sketching the given graphs. Students then match each graph to a context that it may represent and interpret the qualitative features of the graph in context. They use their experience from this activity to sketch the graph of nonlinear functions given a written description of the context. Students conclude the lesson by analyzing a set of equations and corresponding graphs to determine whether the relationship is a function and describe some of its qualitative features.

title: Scatter Plots
objectives: Construct scatter plots and identify those that show an association between two variables. Describe the difference between an association and a cause and effect relationship for numerical variables.
i_can: I can construct scatter plots and recognize that an association between variables does not imply that changes in one variable cause changes in the other variable.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, interpret points on a scatter plot in context. Orally and in writing, informally describe patterns in a scatter plot that may suggest an association between the two variables.
key_questions: Why is a scatter plot useful when working with bivariate numerical data? What can an association tell us about two variables? What can it not tell us?
ad_texts: ["Interpret and describe patterns of association between two quantities shown in scatter plots."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD8] Interpret and describe patterns of association between two quantities shown in scatter plots.
laag: Students construct and interpret scatter plots of data for various T-shirt print shops. By examining a data set for two variables, students recognize a need for another way to organize the data. They then construct scatter plots and recognize the advantages of representing data in a scatter plot. After informally identifying patterns in scatter plots, students realize that these patterns do not imply cause and effect relationships. This lesson formalizes the terms observational unit, bivariate numerical data, scatter plot, and association.

title: Patterns in Scatter Plots
objectives: Identify and describe patterns of association between two variables represented in scatter plots. Identify and describe outliers and clusters in context.
i_can: I can identify patterns of association between variables in a scatter plot and describe clusters and outliers in context.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, describe the strength, direction, and shape of associations represented in scatter plots. In writing, interpret outliers or clusters in a scatter plot in context.
key_questions: In what ways can we describe data represented in a scatter plot?
ad_texts: ["Interpret and describe patterns of association between two quantities shown in scatter plots."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD8] Interpret and describe patterns of association between two quantities shown in scatter plots.
laag: In this lesson, students build upon their experiences from the previous lesson to describe patterns of association in scatter plots. Through the Which One Doesn’t Belong? routine, they compare and contrast scatter plots displaying different patterns of association. With further investigation, students analyze and describe associations as linear or nonlinear; positive or negative; and strong, moderate, or weak. They then explore graphs with outliers and clusters and describe these unusual features in context. This lesson introduces the terms contrast and outlier.

title: Informally Fitting a Line to Data
objectives: Informally fit a line to data displayed in a scatter plot. Make predictions based on the graph of a line fit to data.
i_can: I can draw a line that fits the data in a scatter plot and use the line to make predictions.
language_objectives: Orally and in writing, analyze lines fit to data in scatter plots and critique the strategies used to draw them.
key_questions: How is fitting a line to data with a linear association useful? What is an effective strategy for fitting a line to data in a scatter plot?
ad_texts: ["Informally fit lines that model linear relationships and assess the fit of the lines for two numerical variables displayed in scatter plots."]
ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD9] Informally fit lines that model linear relationships and assess the fit of the lines for two numerical variables displayed in scatter plots.
laag: Students consider how they might use a scatter plot to make predictions based on the pattern of association in the data. They recognize that a line can be useful for predicting values for future observations. Students then propose and examine various strategies for drawing a line that fits the data. They come to a consensus around an informal method that involves drawing the line as close as possible to each point. Students also recognize the effect that outliers can have on the line drawn to fit the data. This lesson formalizes the term outlier.

title: Determining an Equation of a Line Fit to Data
objectives: Determine an equation of a line informally fit to data displayed in a scatter plot and interpret the slope and y-intercept in context.

language_objectives: In writing, explain whether a line fit to data is a good predictor of the actual data values. Orally and in writing, determine the slope and of a line fit to data and interpret them in context.
key_questions: Given a context, how can we interpret the slope of a line fit to data in a scatter plot? What does a line fit to data that predicts the actual data values well look like?

ad_full: [8.Mod6.AD10] Solve problems by using the equations of linear models in the context of bivariate numerical data.
laag: Students examine a scatter plot with a linear pattern and predict by using a line fit to the data. The class discusses how determining specific values from the graph can involve some guesswork, especially when points are not at grid intersections. Students recognize they can apply methods from prior modules to write equations of the lines they fit to data. Then they write and use equations to calculate for given to make predictions. Students interpret the slope and the in context, and also interpret predictions they make for the dependent variable.

title: Linear Models
objectives: Use a linear function to model the association between two numerical variables. Informally assess the fit of a line to data in a scatter plot by judging the closeness of the data points to the line.
i_can: I can use a linear function to model the association between two variables, make predictions, and compare predictions to actual data points.
language_objectives: Through speaking, listening, and writing in groups, model the association between two numerical variables with a linear function. As a class, orally compare predictions about data made by different groups and discuss reasons why the predictions vary.
key_questions: How can we use linear functions to model associations between two numerical variables? How can we assess how well a line models an association in a data set?
big_idea: Interpret Scatter Plots Data, Graphs, and Tables Data Explorations Slopes and Intercepts

laag: In this lesson, students analyze a context where the association between two numerical variables can be modeled by a linear function. Students work in groups to model the association between the lengths and weights of three different types of fish. They create scatter plots, fit lines to the data, and write equations for the lines. Students use their equations to make predictions for the dependent variable given a value for the independent variable. They then informally assess the fit of their models by judging how close the data points are to the line. The lesson concludes with students analyzing and drawing conclusions from their models in context.

title: Using the Investigative Process
objectives: Use the investigative process to explore claims about proportional relationships in the human body.
i_can: I can make a plan, collect data, and analyze results to investigate claims about proportional relationships.
language_objectives: With a partner, write a proposal for a statistical investigation. As a class, orally identify difficulties encountered in the investigative process and discuss possible solutions to resolve them.

laag: In this two-day lesson, students engage in the modeling cycle to plan a three-dimensional scale model of the solar system. They begin by reasoning about whether a displayed picture of the solar system represents a scale model. They discuss the inherent challenges in representing the solar system with a model that accurately scales both the sizes of the sun and the planets and the distances between them. Students are presented with a task that requires them to propose a plan for a scale model of the solar system that fits on their school campus. As they formulate their plans, students consider appropriate units for quantities and determine the level of accuracy required in their calculations. They prepare a presentation of their plans. As groups share, students debrief the activity by using the Five Framing Questions routine and reflect on how they applied the steps of the modeling cycle.

laag: In this two-day lesson, students work in groups to design a fundraiser that satisfies a set of constraints. They find the maximum profit generated based on their choices. Groups engage in a gallery walk to review one another’s work. Then groups use peer feedback from the gallery walk to improve their models. They also read an excerpt and use a digital interactive to explore the concept of linear programming.

laag: In this lesson, students engage in the modeling cycle as they model a problem where they predict the number of doughnuts needed for an event intended to set a world record. Over two days, students work in collaborative groups to create and refine their models by developing working assumptions about the problem. Students may use drawings or small objects like pieces of cereal to test their theories on a small scale. They consider issues related to scaling up their models, including deciding which type of function is best and the cost of implementing their plans. They share their findings, analyze solutions, and use peer feedback to refine their models, if necessary, and reflect on alternate solution paths.
